1606.04474.tldr: Learned optimizers: a two-layer coordinatewise LSTM consumes each parameter's gradient history and emits its update, trained by backpropagating through the unrolled optimization of sampled functions. It beats tuned SGD, RMSprop, ADAM and NAG on quadratics, MNIST and CIFAR-10, and transfers to unseen architectures.
1606.04474.method: The update rule is itself a parameterized function: theta_{t+1} = theta_t + g_t with (g_t, h_{t+1}) = m(nabla_t, h_t, phi), so a two-layer LSTM (20 hidden units each layer) maps the optimizee gradient at one parameter into that parameter's update. The LSTMs are replicated coordinatewise with shared weights but separate hidden states, making the optimizer tiny, invariant to parameter ordering, and applicable to tens of thousands of optimizee parameters -- a learned RMSprop/ADAM. Training minimizes L(phi) = E_f[sum_t w_t f(theta_t)] over sampled functions, backpropagating through the unrolled trajectory (Fig. 2); gradients along the dashed edges, i.e. d(nabla_t)/d(phi), are dropped so no second derivatives of f are needed. Setting w_t = 1 at every step rather than only at T makes trajectory prefixes informative. Gradients are preprocessed as (log|nabla|/p, sgn nabla) with p = 10, outputs rescaled; the optimizer is trained with ADAM, a random-search learning rate, and early stopping.
results: Setup: optimizers are two-layer LSTMs with 20 hidden units per layer, each trained with ADAM (learning rate from random search) and early stopping to avoid overfitting the optimizer, then compared against SGD, RMSprop, ADAM and NAG with per-problem tuned learning rates. Initial optimizee parameters are IID Gaussian.

Quadratics: on 10-dimensional f(theta) = ||W theta - y||_2^2 with Gaussian W and y, each function is optimized for 100 steps and the optimizer is unrolled for 20 steps, with no preprocessing or postprocessing; the learned optimizer substantially outperforms the tuned baselines (Fig. 4, left).

MNIST: the base net is an MLP with one hidden layer of 20 sigmoid units, gradients estimated from minibatches of 128 examples, 100 steps, 20-step unroll, LSTM outputs rescaled by 0.1. NAG, ADAM and RMSprop perform roughly equivalently while the LSTM optimizer beats them by a significant margin, and it still beats them when allowed to run 200 steps despite being trained for 100 (Fig. 4, center and right).

Generalization: an optimizer trained on the 20-unit sigmoid MLP keeps beating the baselines when the optimizee becomes 40 hidden units or two hidden layers, but changing the activation to ReLU makes the learned optimizer no longer able to generalize (Fig. 5); sweeping optimizee depth and width (1/2/5/20/35/50 layers, 5/20/35/50 units, Fig. 6) shows the best transfer exactly where test problems resemble training problems.

CIFAR-10: on a model of three max-pooling convolutional layers plus a 32-unit fully-connected layer with ReLU and batch normalization, one coordinatewise LSTM per parameter type (fully-connected vs convolutional) learns much more quickly than the baselines, with significant boosts on CIFAR-5 and especially CIFAR-2; an LSTM-sub trained only on the held-out labels transfers to the remaining labels. Neural art: trained on one style and 1800 ImageNet content images at 64x64 with 128 steps and a 32-step unroll, the optimizer reaches tasks of 49,152 parameters from 12,288-parameter training tasks, changing style, resolution and content simultaneously.
advantages: Establishes the optimization procedure itself as a trainable object: end-to-end BPTT through the unrolled optimizee trajectory (with d(nabla_t)/d(phi) = 0 to avoid second derivatives) produces a learned rule that outperforms hand-designed competitors on four task families even though every baseline gets its learning rate tuned per problem. This is the founding demonstration that 'the improver can itself be improved'.

The coordinatewise decomposition is the enabling trick rather than a detail: one small LSTM with shared weights and per-parameter hidden states scales to tens of thousands of optimizee parameters, is invariant to parameter ordering, and is exactly a learned analogue of RMSprop/ADAM -- so the learned object stays comparable to the rules it replaces.

Transfer is measured, not asserted: 12,288 parameters to 49,152 parameters at once, new styles and content images, MNIST to 40 units and two layers, and CIFAR subsets including an optimizer trained only on held-out labels. The paper's No-Free-Lunch framing makes the specialization claim principled rather than an admission.

The learned updates are inspectable and land on recognizable optimization behavior: Appendix B traces single coordinates and finds the LSTM takes larger steps than SGD and ADAM and uses momentum with a shorter time scale than ADAM, with a step-like update-versus-gradient response that is sometimes inverted (bigger gradient, bigger update).
limitations: Generalization breaks when the dynamics shift, by the paper's own account: replacing sigmoid with ReLU activations makes the learning dynamics different enough that the learned optimizer can no longer generalize, and performance on a systematic depth/width sweep tracks how similar test problems are to the training distribution.

The architecture does not carry over unchanged: the coordinatewise LSTM was not sufficient for the convolutional model, which required splitting the optimizer into separate LSTMs for convolutional and fully-connected parameters, and the training objective had to be relaxed to w_t = 1 for all t because the true final-loss objective gives zero gradient on trajectory prefixes and makes BPTT inefficient.

Scale and horizons are small, and the optimizer itself overfits: training uses short unrolls (20 steps for quadratics and MNIST, 32 for neural art) requiring early stopping, and every experiment meta-trains on a narrow problem class (10-dimensional quadratics, one MLP, one CIFAR architecture, one style).

The more powerful variants are sketched rather than tested: global averaging cells and the NTM-BFGS / NTM-L-BFGS memory architectures (Appendix D) are argued to be able to simulate inverse-Hessian BFGS with one read head, three write heads and two GACs, but no experimental results are reported for them.
1606.04474.fits: Stage 1 (Foundations & Theory), in the Evolutionary & Open-Ended RSI section: the conceptual root of the whole list -- if the optimizer is learnable, the improver can be improved. Pairs with AutoML-Zero (2003.03384), which evolves update rules from scratch rather than learning them by gradient descent, and with GAC/NTM-style memory for its Newton-method ambitions.
1606.04474.reading: Section 2 for the objective and BPTT graph (Eq. 1-3, Fig. 2); Section 2.1 for the coordinatewise LSTM; Sections 3.1-3.3 for quadratic/MNIST/CIFAR transfer, 3.4 for neural art; Appendix A for gradient preprocessing, Appendix B for the learned updates.

2410.04444.tldr: An LLM agent that reads and rewrites its own Python source in runtime memory — monkey patching, not a fixed optimizer — lifting MGSM accuracy to 64.2% (Meta Agent Search 53.4%) and DROP F1 to 80.9 under GPT-3.5.
2410.04444.method: Gödel Agent is a single Python agent whose main function is recursive rather than a fixed loop, so its own code stays rewritable mid-run. Self-awareness comes from runtime memory inspection: it introspects the local and global variables holding its functions and classes. Self-modification comes from monkey patching — new code is written into runtime memory to add, replace or remove logic. Its action set is self_inspect, interact, self_update and continue_improve: an LLM decision function f0 emits an action sequence from the goal prompt g and environment feedback r=U(E,pi), the action function executes it, and continue_improve recurses one level deeper. Formally pi_t+1, I_t+1 = I_t(pi_t, I_t, r_t, g) — the optimizer updates itself, not just the policy, and the whole code base is rewritten after each execution. Auxiliary tools (think-before-acting, error handling, Python/Bash execution, LLM calls) only accelerate convergence.
results: Table 1, GPT-3.5 for all tests: Gödel-base beats Meta Agent Search on all four benchmarks — DROP F1 80.9±0.8 vs 79.4±0.8, MGSM 64.2±3.4 vs 53.4±3.5 (10.8 points, the paper's '11%'), MMLU 70.9±3.1 vs 69.6±3.2, GPQA 34.9±3.3 vs 34.6±3.2. Hand-designed baselines sit far below (CoT: 64.2/28.0/65.4/29.2).
Unconstrained Gödel-free scores 90.5 / 90.6 / 87.9 / 55.7 (DROP / MGSM / MMLU / GPQA), which the authors attribute to the agent spontaneously requesting help from GPT-4o.

Cost: one complete run — 30 recursive self-improvements across all four datasets — costs about $15 versus $300 for Meta Agent Search, because continuous self-optimization converges faster; the main cost driver is the agent's growing historical memory.

Game of 24 case study: after six failed optimization attempts the agent discards its LLM prompting strategy and rewrites itself to use a search algorithm, reaching 100% accuracy; adding code-assisted verification raises performance by over 10% and reattempting with additional data by more than 15%.

Robustness over 100 MGSM trials: 92% show temporary performance drops and 4% terminate unexpectedly (usually after it edits its own recursive-improvement module), but only 14% end worse than the initial policy. Ablating 'thinking' costs 13.4 points and error handling 14.8 (50.8 and 49.4 vs 64.2); code running (-7.1) and LLM calling (-3.8) matter little.
advantages: Removes the hand-designed meta-level that bounds ADAS / Meta Agent Search: because both the policy and the learning algorithm I are updated, the search space includes the optimizer itself, so the agent can replace its reasoning strategy outright — the Game of 24 switch from prompting to search is the concrete evidence.

One implementation transfers across reading comprehension, multilingual math, MMLU and GPQA with only a task-specific environment description and utility function, versus Meta Agent Search's per-task module design.

Cheap and empirically robust: roughly $15 per full evolution against $300 for Meta Agent Search, and in 86% of 100 trials it recovers from its own bad edits, often by reverting to a previously better algorithm.

Makes the Gödel machine measurable at LLM scale: an explicit recursion between policy and self-referential learning algorithm, a runnable Algorithm 1, and what the authors present as the first fully self-referential LLM agent framework, implemented with monkey patching.
limitations: No direct comparison with the most heavily engineered agent systems such as OpenDevin: the agent must construct all task code autonomously, and the authors say it is unrealistic to expect it to beat systems built over months or years — the experiments demonstrate feasibility of recursive self-improvement, not state of the art.

Gains are bounded by the base LLM: on Game of 24 no initial-policy variant let the agent outperform a hand-written Tree of Thought, and the authors doubt it can innovate beyond state-of-the-art algorithms until LLM capability improves.

Not goal-preserving by construction: self-modification caused 4% of trials to terminate irrecoverably by breaking the recursive-improvement module, and the unconstrained runs' large gains came partly from calling stronger models (GPT-4o), i.e. from leaving the intended setup.

The authors flag an unexplored ceiling — as the system grows more complex through self-optimization it may need exponentially more intelligence to understand itself, so a fully self-referential agent may lose that property as it evolves.
2410.04444.fits: Phase 1 (Foundations & Theory): the self-referential ideal the rest of the arc tests empirically. Pairs with Learning to Learn by GD-by-GD (the improver as a learnable object), STOP and ADAS (its fixed-meta-level foils), and above all DGM (stage 7), which keeps the edit-evaluate gate but adds a never-pruned archive.
2410.04444.reading: Section 3 for the formal recursion and Algorithm 1; Sections 4.1-4.2 for the monkey-patching, memory-inspection implementation and auxiliary tools; Section 5.3 with Table 1 for results; Sections 6.2-6.3 for robustness and Game of 24; Appendix D for the cost comparison.

2003.03384.tldr: Searches whole ML algorithms symbolically — Setup/Predict/Learn programs over 65 basic scalar/vector/matrix ops — and evolves two-layer nets trained by backprop, bilinear multiplicative interactions, unit-normalized gradients and accumulated-weight averaging that beat hand-designed baselines on CIFAR-10.
2003.03384.method: An algorithm is a three-function program — Setup, Predict, Learn — over a small zero-initialized virtual memory of scalar/vector/matrix addresses. Predict reads features (v0) and writes its prediction to s1 (sigmoid/softmax-normalized); Learn then sees the label (s0) and may update memory; validation runs Predict alone. The 65 ops are high-school math (add, dot, outer, sin, gauss, heaviside) — no derivatives, batches or convolutions — so any gradient used for training must be evolved. Search is regularized evolution: population P of initially empty programs; each cycle picks T=10 at random, copies the best, mutates it (insert/remove instruction, randomize a function, tweak an argument), evicts the oldest. Functional equivalence checking hashes 20 predictions to reuse cached scores (4x speedup); hurdles early-stop below the population's rolling 75th percentile (75% of compute saved); up to W=10,000 single-core workers migrate half their populations through a central server; half also search projected MNIST.
results: Best evolved algorithm on the original 3072-dim CIFAR-10 test set: 84.06 ± 0.10% vs logistic regression 77.65 ± 0.22% and a 2-layer fully connected net trained by gradient descent 82.22 ± 0.17%, all tuned with equal compute, 5 seeds.

Gains transfer to other binary classification datasets (evolved / linear / nonlinear): SVHN 88.12% vs 59.58% vs 85.14%; downsampled ImageNet 80.78% vs 76.44% vs 78.44%; Fashion MNIST 98.60% vs 97.90% vs 98.21%.

From empty programs it re-invents backprop: with one search task (D=1) evolution hard-codes the teacher net's weights into the forward pass; with D=100 it must find per-task weights and 'invents' gradient-descent code (Fig. 5: dot, ReLU, outer-product weight deltas, learning-rate scalar).

Motif ablations on the best algorithm (4 of 6 sections significant): removing weight accumulation costs −4.11, bilinear interactions −1.46, unit-normalized gradients −1.20, input-noise regularization −0.16.

Search-method ablation, 30 runs at 1k processes: best accuracy 0.703 ± 0.002 → 0.738 ± 0.008 and the fraction of runs beating a plain NN 0.00 → 0.53 after adding migration, FEC, 50% MNIST data and hurdles; the same ordering holds at 100 processes (0.700 → 0.714) and 10 processes (0.700 → 0.705).
advantages: Discovers complete algorithms symbolically rather than numerically — the output is readable code, not an opaque learned optimizer — and starts from empty component functions with no built-in assumption of a neural network, of layers, or even of gradients.

Shows evolution beats random search exactly where the space is sparse: ~5.6x on linear regression rising to 23,000x on affine-regression tasks as difficulty grows (Fig. 4) — the opposite of conventional AutoML spaces, where RS is competitive (linear regression has only 1 acceptable algorithm per 10^7; the paper estimates 1 in 10^12 in the freest space).

Task-conditioned adaptation emerges reproducibly from the same starting population: noisy ReLU / dropout-like regularization when data is scarce (8/30 experiments vs 0/30 control, p < 0.0005), iterated-arctan learning-rate decay that is nearly exponential when training is short (30/30 vs 3/30, p < 10^-14), and a learning rate derived from the transformed mean of the weight matrix for 10-class tasks (24/30 vs 0/30, p < 10^-11).
Engineered for scale and open-sourced: 2k–10k algorithms/second/CPU core, with baselines published at three compute scales so future search methods can be compared on the same space.
limitations: The space cannot express batch normalization or convolution: one example is processed at a time, with no loops or higher-order tensors, so a multi-layer network must be discovered layer-by-layer, and no derivative ops exist, so any gradient computation must be evolved.

Scale: the main experiment used W=10,000 CPU workers for 5 days (plus 100<W<1000 smaller runs); search happens on binary tasks projected to 8 ≤ F ≤ 256 dims, with the 3072-dim CIFAR-10 test set reserved for final evaluation only.
Only 13 of 20 search experiments produced candidates beating the hand-designed reference, and the headline win is ~1.8 accuracy points over a 2-layer MLP.

Hyperparameter coupling had to be fixed by hand — an expression such as s7 = v2·v2 can coincide with a good value on the search tasks but not generalize, requiring manual decoupling that the authors say 'could be automated by future work'.
2003.03384.fits: Stage 1 (Foundations & Theory). The minimal-human-bias limit of the pre-LLM AutoML line: pair with Learning to Learn by Gradient Descent by Gradient Descent (1606.04474) as the numeric counterpart, with AI-GAs (1905.10985) as Clune's pillar it instantiates, and with MAP-Elites / Quality-Diversity (1504.04909, frontiers-quality-diversity-2016) for the diversity machinery it lacks. Direct ancestor of AlphaEvolve and MLEvolve.
2003.03384.reading: §3.1–3.2 (search space; regularized-evolution upgrades FEC, hurdles, migration); §4.1 with Fig. 5 (backprop rediscovered); §4.2 with Fig. 6 and its callouts (the 84.06% algorithm); §4.3 (task-conditioned adaptations); Supplement S8 for motif ablation numbers.

2310.03714.tldr: DSPy replaces hand-written prompt strings with typed signatures, parameterized modules, and teleprompters that compile a pipeline against a metric, bootstrapping demonstrations so GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat self-improve GSM8K and HotPotQA programs without prompt engineering.
2310.03714.method: A program declares Signatures: typed input/output fields like "question -> answer", not prompt strings. Modules wrap a signature — Predict formats signature plus demonstrations into a prompt, calls the LM, parses output fields, and in compile mode records input/output traces. ChainOfThought merely prepends a rationale output field and delegates to Predict; ReAct, ProgramOfThought and MultiChainComparison are likewise built from Predict. Modules compose in a define-by-run forward() method (retrieve, then answer). A teleprompter compiles the program given a trainset plus metric in three stages: (1) candidate generation — recursively find unique Predict modules, simulate the program, and keep multi-stage traces whose final output passes the metric as demonstrations for each signature; (2) parameter optimization — select demonstration sets by random search or Optuna, or update LM weights via BootstrapFinetune; (3) higher-order optimization — ensemble the top bootstrapped programs by majority voting. What evolves is demonstrations and field instructions, not weights, unless finetuning.
results: GSM8K, GPT-3.5 dev/test: vanilla zero-shot 24.0 → bootstrap×2 64.7/61.7; CoT 50.0 → bootstrap 80.3/72.9 → +ensemble 88.3/81.6, matching the 8-shot fewshot+human-CoT baseline (78.6/72.4); reflection (5 sampled chains compared by MultiChainComparison) 83.0/76.0 and 86.7 dev ensembled. The paper's summary: composing modules instead of strings lifts LMs from 4-20% to 49-88% accuracy.

GSM8K, llama2-13b-chat dev/test: vanilla 7.0/9.4 → bootstrap×2 37.3/36.5; CoT 26.7 → bootstrap 43.3 (+ensemble 43.7 dev) vs 34.3 with human CoT demonstrations; reflection 36.7 → 44.3 bootstrap / 49.0 ensembled, 40.2/46.9 test.

HotPotQA answer EM, GPT-3.5 dev/test: CoT RAG fewshot 36.4 → bootstrap 42.3; multihop (two-hop query generation) 36.9 → 48.7 bootstrap (47.0 passage accuracy) → 54.7 ensemble dev, 31.2 → 39.6 → 45.6 test (ensemble scored on 50% of test due to cost). llama2-13b-chat multihop: 34.7 → 42.0 → 50.0 dev, 31.3 → 36.4 → 41.0 test.
HotPotQA ReAct dev EM: GPT-3.5 zero-shot 20.3, +human reasoning 33.0, bootstrap 31.0, bootstrap×2 39.0; llama2-13b-chat 20.0, 28.3, 24.7, 40.0 — bootstrap×2 beats the expert-written ReAct traces.

BootstrapFinetune distils a multihop program into T5-Large (770M): 39.3% answer EM and 46.0% passage accuracy on dev, from 200 labeled inputs plus 800 unlabeled questions and a teacher that is an ensemble of two llama2-13b-chat multihop programs.
advantages: Prompt strings stop being the interface: the same two-to-four-module programs and the same compilers run on GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat, and bootstrapped demonstrations match or beat expert-written ones (GSM8K CoT 80.3 vs 78.6 dev with human CoT; llama2-13b-chat CoT 43.3 vs 34.3).

Label-efficiency by construction: only final-output labels are assumed, while intermediate reasoning chains and retrieval contexts are bootstrapped, so a new pipeline is recompiled rather than re-annotated with step-specific data.

Compiling closes the LM gap — llama2-13b-chat multihop at 42.0 dev EM vs GPT-3.5 fewshot at 36.9 — and BootstrapFinetune pushes the pipeline into a 770M T5, which the paper argues means orders-of-magnitude cheaper inference than a proprietary LM.

One optimizer abstraction covers prompting and finetuning, and a teacher program can be composed in (an expensive large-LM ensemble supervises a cheap student), which is what makes the T5 result possible.
limitations: A well-defined automatic metric plus at least a few training inputs the LM can actually pass are prerequisites; bootstrapping works by rejection-sampling traces that satisfy the metric, so a program (or LM) that never passes yields no demonstrations.
The empirical evidence is two case studies, GSM8K and HotPotQA; the conclusion explicitly defers other tasks (information extraction, low-resource synthetic data generation) to future work.

Compiling is not free: minutes to tens of minutes and thousands of program runs (10-20 trials over 150-300 validation examples), and it was costly enough that the HotPotQA ensemble test number is marked as evaluated on 50% of the test set.

The optimizer scope in this version is narrow: "In this iteration of DSPy, we focus on demonstrations", Stage 3 control-flow optimization is only ensembling (dynamic test-time bootstrapping and backtracking are future work), and optional field data types are "not core to DSPy at the time of writing".
2310.03714.fits: Stage 2 (optimization-as-language): the substrate that turns prompt optimization into whole-pipeline compilation, and the direct ancestor of the harness-level optimizers in stages 4-6. Pairs with OPRO (2309.03409) and APE as the single-prompt optimizers it generalizes, and with Reflexion (2303.11366) for the feedback signal; its teleprompter/optimizer split recurs in later harness cards.
2310.03714.reading: Read §3 (signatures, modules, teleprompters) and §4 (the three compiler stages) first — that is the mechanism. Then §6 with Table 1 and §7 with Table 2 for the numbers, and Appendix E for BootstrapFewShot pseudocode.

2406.07496.tldr: Backprop for compound AI systems: every text variable — prompt, code, answer, SMILES, dose weight — is a parameter, and an LLM emits natural-language criticism at each edge that is chained backward and applied by a textual-gradient-descent step.
2406.07496.method: Wraps a compound system as a PyTorch-like computation graph v = f(predecessors), where variables are arbitrary text (system prompt, code snippet, an answer, a molecule SMILES, a radiotherapy importance-weight string) and functions are LLM calls, simulators, or numerical optimizers. The forward pass records each variable's predecessors; the objective may be nondifferentiable — unit-test results, an Autodock Vina docking score, or an LLM judge. The backward pass walks the graph in reverse topological order: for each edge an LLM gradient operator receives the successor's gradient plus the forward conversation and returns criticism of the predecessor (context concatenated with feedback), and feedback from all successors is aggregated, mirroring autograd through addition — which also yields minibatching via tg.sum. TextualGradientDescent.step then rewrites the variable from its accumulated criticism. The API mirrors PyTorch (tg.Variable, BlackboxLLM, TextLoss, loss.backward(), optimizer.step()), at most one gradient call per edge per iteration.
results: LeetCode Hard with gpt-4o, 5 seeds (Table 1): completion rate 0.26 zero-shot and 0.31 ± 0.012 for Reflexion run one-shot → 0.36 ± 0.018 for TextGrad, which used zero demonstrations.
Zero-shot question answering (Table 2): GPQA 51.0 CoT / 53.6 best reported → 55.0; MMLU-Machine Learning 85.7 → 88.4; MMLU-College Physics 91.2 → 95.1.

Prompt optimization for gpt-3.5-turbo with gpt-4o as the gradient engine (Table 3): Object Counting 77.8 CoT and 84.9 for DSPy BFSR with 8 demonstrations → 91.9 instruction-only; GSM8k 72.9 / 81.1 → 81.1; Word Sorting 76.7 / 79.8 → 79.8.

Molecules over all 58 DOCKSTRING targets: one PPARA run moves Vina -4.2 kcal/mol, QED 0.44 → -5.5 / 0.59 → -7.5 / 0.79 (Fig. 2a); across the 29 targets with approved drugs TextGrad matches clinical Vina and exceeds clinical QED, at median Tversky similarity 0.42 to the approved drug (range 0.14–0.90).

Prostate radiotherapy, 5 patients (Supp. Tables 1–2): PTV D95 hits the 70.20 Gy prescription (+0.00 ± 0.00 vs oncologist -0.10 ± 0.15) and mean dose is +0.51 ± 0.09 Gy over goal vs +1.97 ± 0.36 for the oncologist; rectum mean dose 23.88 → 17.18 Gy, bladder 22.39 → 20.92 Gy.
advantages: One fixed framework: the gradient operator and the TGD prompt are identical across all five domains — only the objective function and the graph change — so a new application costs a loss function plus a few lines of PyTorch-shaped code.

Extends the textual-gradient idea from prompt optimization to instance optimization, which the paper names as its advance over DSPy and ProTeGi: the artifact itself (code, answer, molecule, hyperparameters) is the parameter, optimized at test time without a training set.

Textual gradients are legible, so the edit carries its rationale: Fig. 1e's gradient finds the nums[i] == k edge case that breaks the first gpt-4o solution, and Fig. 3's gradients walk from 'increase the PTV weight' to 'slightly increase the bladder and rectum weights' as the tradeoff moves.

Complementary to program search rather than competing: it matches DSPy BFSR on GSM8k (81.1) and Word Sorting (79.8) with instruction-only prompts and no demonstrations, beats it by 7 points on Object Counting, and DSPy's demonstrations plus the TextGrad prompt reach 82.1 on GSM8k — while keeping test-time inference cheaper.
limitations: The authors' own §5 list: graph operations still do not cover tool use or retrieval-augmented components, and the molecule and radiotherapy results are in silico proof-of-concept — the ultimate test requires experimental and clinical assessment.

No convergence guarantee: variance reduction, adaptive gradients and LLM self-verification are named as future work, so nothing establishes that a textual-gradient step actually descends; gradients are unstructured text and can be noisy or uninformative.

Cost scales with the graph — up to one extra LLM call per edge per iteration plus the update call — and experiments are correspondingly small: 39 LeetCode problems, 12 prompt-optimization iterations at batch size 3, 10 molecule iterations per target.

Gradient quality rides on the critic model: prompt optimization uses gpt-4o to improve gpt-3.5-turbo, and the paper notes (citing prior work) that constraint-following reliability drops as natural-language constraints accumulate.
2406.07496.fits: Stage 2 (Optimization-as-Language) anchor: the general-purpose optimizer that later harness-search loops such as DGM, RRSI and Harness-Zero loosely analogize — they evolve whole scaffolds, TextGrad differentiates any text variable inside one. Pairs with DSPy as its sibling (program and demonstration search), OPRO and Promptbreeder as prompt-only ancestors, and Reflexion as the single-variable special case.
2406.07496.reading: Read §2 for the gradient operator, TGD.step and the general-case recursion (Eqs. 10–12); §3.1–3.3 for the code, QA and prompt numbers; §5 for the authors' own limitations. Skim §3.4–3.5 for molecules and radiotherapy.

2303.11366.tldr: Reflexion reinforces language agents through words, not gradients: after a failed trial the agent writes a first-person reflection on the error, appends it to an episodic memory buffer, and retries — reaching 91% pass@1 on HumanEval and +22 points on AlfWorld.
2303.11366.method: Training-free, inference-only loop over a frozen LLM, with no gradient update anywhere. Three roles: the Actor Ma (Chain-of-Thought or ReAct prompted) emits trajectory tau_t against the environment; the Evaluator Me scores it, rt = Me(tau_t), via exact-match grading (HotPotQA), a hand-written heuristic (AlfWorld: same action and same observation for more than 3 cycles, or more than 30 actions in one environment), self-written unit tests CoT-generated, AST-validated and sampled up to n = 6 (code), or an LLM judge (decision-making). The Self-Reflection model Msr consumes {tau_t, rt} and writes a first-person verbal summary sr_t of the mistake. Algorithm 1: sr_t is appended to long-term memory mem, the raw trajectory is short-term memory, and the Actor re-runs until Me passes or the trial cap hits. mem is a sliding window bounded at Omega = 1-3 entries (3 for AlfWorld and HotPotQA, 1 for code).
results: Table 1 pass@1, HumanEval Python 80.1 (GPT-4, previous SOTA) → 91.0 with Reflexion; also HumanEval Rust 60.0 → 68.0, MBPP Rust 70.9 → 75.4, Leetcode Hard Python 7.5 → 15.0 (40 hard Leetcode problems released after GPT-4's Oct 8 2022 pretraining cutoff, 19 languages). MBPP Python is the one regression: 80.1 → 77.1.

AlfWorld, 134 environments: ReAct + Reflexion solves 130/134 with the hallucination/inefficiency heuristic and keeps learning across 12 consecutive trials, while ReAct-only stops improving between trials 6 and 7 and settles at a 22% hallucination rate with no long-term recovery.

HotPotQA, 100 questions (Table 5): CoT (GT) + text-davinci-003 0.60 → 0.77, gpt-3.5-turbo 0.57 → 0.71, gpt-4 0.68 → 0.80; ReAct + text-davinci-003 0.30 → 0.55, gpt-3.5-turbo 0.26 → 0.38, gpt-4 0.39 → 0.51. CoT-only and ReAct-only baselines fail to solve any first-trial failure on retry at temperature 0.7. The intro's headline is a 20% HotPotQA gain; the largest table delta is +25 points.

Two ablations isolate the mechanism. On HotPotQA CoT (GT), self-reflection adds an 8% absolute boost over episodic memory alone (keeping only the most recent trajectory), so refinement-only loops are weaker than reflection-guided ones. On the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems (Table 3), Reflexion 0.68 vs 0.60 base, 0.60 for tests-without-reflection, and 0.52 for reflection-without-tests — removing test execution hurts more than removing the verbal reflection.

The MBPP Python failure is explained by test quality (Table 2): the false-positive rate of self-generated tests (tests pass, solution wrong) is 16.3% on MBPP Python versus 1.4% on HumanEval Python, where a flaky suite lets the agent submit early. Separately, starchat-beta gains nothing at all on HumanEval Python (0.26 → 0.26, average over 8 trials, Table 4).
advantages: Trains nothing and updates no weights: the 'policy' is literally {frozen LLM, memory buffer}, so it runs on closed models (GPT-4, text-davinci-003, gpt-3.5-turbo) and every improvement is stored as human-readable text, unlike policy- or value-based RL that needs fine-tuning and massive samples.

Feedback-agnostic by construction — the same loop consumes binary success, hand-written heuristics, exact-match grading, self-written unit tests, or an LLM evaluator, and the paper runs all of these across decision-making, reasoning and code. Feedback can be external or internally simulated.

Keeps code results pass@1-eligible: it gates on self-generated and AST-filtered tests rather than hidden ground-truth test cases (unlike AlphaCode, Self-Debugging and CodeRL), and is language-agnostic — Python and Rust via MultiPL-E — which is what makes 91.0 HumanEval and 15.0 Leetcode Hard legitimate single-sample numbers.

It separates reflection from mere retrying. The episodic-memory ablation (8% absolute) and the reflection-omission arm of Table 3 (0.60, no gain over baseline) both show that verbal error diagnosis is the causal ingredient, not extra attempts — blind trial-and-error debugging is ineffective on hard tasks.
limitations: Local minima, stated by the authors as the core risk and demonstrated on WebShop (Appendix B.1): ReAct + Reflexion over 100 environments was terminated after 4 trials having failed to significantly outperform ReAct, generating no useful self-reflections. Conclusion: it cannot solve tasks requiring a lot of diversity and exploration.

Memory is a fixed sliding window of 1-3 experiences with no retrieval structure — the paper explicitly defers vector-embedding or SQL memory to future work — so gains are bounded by the context window and vanish between sessions.

Self-evaluation is the load-bearing dependency and it fails silently: a flaky or wrong self-written test suite yields false positives (16.3% on MBPP Python) and premature submissions, and the authors prefer false negatives only because the agent may then repair its own test. Test-driven development also breaks for non-deterministic, impure, hardware-dependent or concurrent functions.

The ability to self-correct is emergent with model scale: starchat-beta showed zero improvement (0.26 → 0.26), and the authors state it is a quality of stronger, larger models. There is also no formal guarantee of success.
2303.11366.fits: The stage 3→4 hinge and the origin paper for verbal reinforcement plus episodic self-reflection memory. Pairs directly with Self-Refine (2303.17651) — same generate-critique-revise loop, but Reflexion crosses episodes with a persistent buffer — and with Self-Debugging (2304.05128) for the execution-gated code version. It is the ancestor of nearly every stage-4 memory agent (ExpeL, A-MEM, EvolveR).
2303.11366.reading: Read §3 (Actor/Evaluator/Self-Reflection, Algorithm 1, the Omega-bounded memory) and §4.1-4.3 (AlfWorld 130/134, Table 1 pass@1, Table 3 ablation), then §5 Limitations, Appendix B.1 (WebShop) and Appendix A (Tables 4-5) for where and why it breaks.

2305.16291.tldr: Voyager is a GPT-4 Minecraft agent that learns open-endedly with no gradients: an automatic curriculum proposes tasks, a library of self-verified executable code skills supplies reusable behavior, and environment feedback, execution errors and self-verification refine the code — 3.3× more items than baselines.
2305.16291.method: Three GPT-4 modules over a MineDojo + Mineflayer bot (§2). (1) Automatic curriculum: GPT-4 (temperature 0.1) gets the directive 'discover as many diverse things as possible', the agent state (inventory, equipment, biome, time, health/hunger, position, nearby blocks/entities), completed and failed task lists, and GPT-3.5 self-asked Q&A context, then emits the next task. (2) Skill library: each solved task is committed as a JavaScript program calling hand-written control primitives, keyed by the embedding of a GPT-3.5-written description; for a new task the plan plus environment feedback retrieve the top-5 skills into the code prompt. (3) Iterative prompting: execute the generated program, feed back bot.chat() progress messages and interpreter error traces, re-prompt GPT-4 to refine, and repeat; a separate GPT-4 self-verification agent returns success plus a critique. Success commits the skill and queries the curriculum again; four failed code rounds trigger a new task. No fine-tuning, no parameter access.
results: Exploration (Fig. 1): Voyager discovers 63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations, 3.3× more than ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT, which barely progress against the abstract goal.

Tech tree (Table 1, prompting iterations to unlock, 3 trials): Voyager 6±2 wooden, 11±2 stone, 21±7 iron (3/3 each) and, uniquely, diamond at 102 (1/3); AutoGPT 92±72 / 94±72 / 135±103 (3/3) but never diamond; Voyager without the skill library 7±2 / 9±4 / 29±11 but never diamond; ReAct and Reflexion never unlock even wooden (0/3). That is 15.3×, 8.5× and 6.4× faster than the best baseline at the three levels.
Map coverage (Fig. 7): Voyager travels 2.3× longer distances across diverse terrain, while baselines stay confined to local areas.

Zero-shot generalization (Table 2, fresh world, cleared inventory, 50-iteration cap): Voyager solves all four unseen tasks at 19±3 (Diamond Pickaxe), 18±7 (Golden Sword), 21±5 (Lava Bucket) and 18±2 (Compass) iterations, 3/3 each; no baseline solves any (0/3), and AutoGPT given Voyager's skill library reaches only 39 (1/3), 30 (1/3), 0/3 and 30 (2/3).

Ablations (Fig. 9): a random curriculum costs 93% of discovered items, deleting self-verification costs 73%, removing the skill library plateaus later stages, and swapping GPT-4 for GPT-3.5 in code generation yields 5.7× fewer unique items. Skill retrieval scores 80.2±3.0 top-1 and 96.5±0.3 top-5 accuracy over 309 samples (Table A.4).
advantages: Skills are executable, interpretable, compositional code, not text memories: each one is admitted only after environment execution and critic-confirmed success, is built on named control primitives, and composes into harder programs — the mechanism that lets later skills stand on earlier ones and keeps the agent off the plateau seen when the library is ablated.

The library transfers as an artifact: it works in a newly instantiated world and is plug-and-play for another agent, lifting AutoGPT from 0/3 on every unseen task to partial success on three of four — the paper's clearest evidence that the learned skills, not the prompting style, carry the capability.

Component attribution is measured rather than asserted: curriculum (−93%), self-verification (−73%), skill library and GPT-4-class code generation (5.7× items) are each individually ablated, isolating what actually drives open-ended progress.

Whole loop is gradient-free on a blackbox GPT-4: the model is queried through prompting only, needs no trajectory data, reward model or fine-tuning, and the results are robust across gpt-4-0314 and gpt-4-0613.
limitations: Cost and model lock-in: GPT-4 is 15× more expensive than GPT-3.5, yet the paper states the loop requires GPT-4's code-generation quality (GPT-3.5 loses 5.7× in unique items) and that open-source LLMs cannot substitute at the time of writing.

Failure modes persist despite the loop: the agent still gets stuck on some skills, self-verification misses cases (it does not read spider string as evidence of killing a spider), the curriculum hallucinates non-existent items such as 'copper sword' and 'copper chestplate', and generated code misuses invalid fuel (cobblestone) or calls absent API functions.

No perception: the GPT-4 API is text-only, so Voyager sees inventory/state text rather than pixels and acts through the high-level Mineflayer API — the paper explicitly declines comparison with pixel-and-low-level-control agents and leaves vision to future multimodal models.

The hardest demonstrations are human-scaffolded: building a Nether Portal or a house required a human as critic and as curriculum, and the domain is Minecraft only; transferring to physical robots would need added safety constraints.
2305.16291.fits: Stage 4's founding skill-library result and the ancestor of code-skill substrates (AgentFactory, DGM-lineage). Read next to Reflexion (2303.11366) — verbal reflections vs verified executable skills — and ExpeL/A-MEM for memory without environment-verified code. Pairs with the runnable Voyager repo card (stage 10) and MineDojo/Mineflayer as the substrate.
2305.16291.reading: §2.1–2.3 for the three modules (curriculum prompt, skill-library key/value + top-5 retrieval, the four-round iterative-prompting loop), §3.3 with Tables 1–2 for the numbers, §4 limits, B.4.4 for 96.5% retrieval accuracy.

2510.04618.tldr: Treats an LLM's entire context as an evolving playbook of ID'd, helpful/harmful-counted bullets, self-improved by a Generator/Reflector/Curator loop applying structured incremental delta updates with deterministic non-LLM merging — fixing the brevity bias and context collapse of monolithic prompt rewriting.
2510.04618.method: Context is a structured playbook of itemized bullets, each with metadata (unique ID, helpful/harmful counters) and content (a strategy, concept, or failure mode). Three same-model roles (DeepSeek-V3.1 non-thinking throughout, to isolate context effects) loop: the Generator solves a query while flagging which bullets helped or misled; the Reflector diagnoses the trace — up to 5 refinement rounds — extracting key insights and tagging each bullet helpful/harmful/neutral; the Curator emits compact JSON delta operations (ADD-only in the shipped prompts, IDs system-assigned) merged by deterministic non-LLM logic, so deltas batch in parallel. Grow-and-refine controls growth: counters update in place and semantic-embedding dedup prunes redundancy, either proactively after each delta or lazily when the context window is exceeded. Offline mode runs up to 5 epochs over training queries (system prompts); online mode updates after each test sample (agent memory).
results: AppWorld (DeepSeek-V3.1, ReAct base avg 42.4): offline ACE 59.4 (+17.0) with GT labels, 57.2 (+14.8) without; beats ICL by 12.3 and GEPA by 11.9 offline, and Dynamic Cheatsheet by 7.6 online (online ACE 59.5, +17.1) — the headline +10.6% agent average.

AppWorld leaderboard (09/2025): 59.4% avg matches top-ranked IBM CUGA (60.3%, GPT-4.1-powered) using smaller open-source DeepSeek-V3.1; online ACE surpasses CUGA by 8.4% TGC / 0.7% SGC on test-challenge.

Finance (FiNER+Formula, base 69.1 avg): offline ACE with GT 81.9 (+12.8), beating ICL/MIPROv2/GEPA by 10.9 avg; DDXPlus medical 75.2→90.2 (+15.0, vs GEPA's 76.4); BIRD-SQL 47.8→52.9 (+5.1) — the headline +8.6% domain average.

Cost: vs GEPA offline AppWorld −82.3% latency (53,898→9,517s), −75.1% rollouts (1,434→357); vs DC online FiNER −91.5% latency (65,104→5,503s), −83.6% token cost ($17.7→$2.9); 86.9% average latency reduction; 91.8% cache hit rate cuts billed input cost 82.6%.

Ablation: removing incremental delta updates drops test-normal TGC 76.2→67.3 and SGC 64.3→46.4 (−11.7%/−27.8% relative); gains hold across GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, and Llama-3.3-70B without algorithm changes.
advantages: First to name and quantify context collapse — a Dynamic Cheatsheet rewrite on AppWorld shrank 18,282 tokens to 122 in one step, accuracy 66.7→57.1, below the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline — and to fix it structurally via deterministic localized deltas rather than just scoring higher.

Self-supervised by construction: +14.8% on AppWorld offline with no GT labels, learning purely from execution feedback; the Reflector is separable and weak reflectors still gain (+5.9 with GPT-OSS-120B), with noise tolerated unless adversarial every single step.

The ADD-only, system-ID'd, helpful/harmful-counted bullet playbook merged by non-LLM code is directly portable discipline for any RSI harness with unboundedly growing notes — hyperparameters prove forgiving (dedup 50–90%, pruning trigger 10K–100K tokens, all stable).
Reframes long-context cost: richer playbooks don't scale billed cost linearly because KV/prompt caching amortizes reused context (91.8% of eval input tokens served from cache on GPT-5.1).
limitations: Feedback quality is load-bearing — the paper's own caveat: without GT labels or reliable execution signals, ACE degrades (FiNER online no-GT 67.3, −3.4) as spurious reflections pollute the playbook, and it drops below base under adversarial reflections every step (66.7 vs 70.7).

Relies on a reasonably strong Reflector: weak models show smaller gains (Llama-3.3-70B reflects noisily), and over-reflection hurts — 10 rounds degrade to 65.2 avg vs 67.6 at 5 ('overthinking' injects noisy updates).

Not for concise-context tasks: the paper concedes HotPotQA-style retrieval QA and fixed-strategy games like Game of 24 benefit more from terse instructions than comprehensive playbooks — detail-heavy domains are where it wins.
Context capacity is managed by dedup/pruning thresholds, not eliminated; leader-board comparison to IBM CUGA is explicitly a rough contextual reference, not a controlled baseline.
2510.04618.fits: Stage 4's context-as-evolving-artifact anchor: generalizes Dynamic Cheatsheet's test-time memory and GEPA's prompt evolution into structured playbook evolution with collapse resistance. The prompt-space complement to Voyager's code-skill library; its ADD-only delta discipline pairs with A-MEM's agentic memory organization.
2510.04618.reading: §2.2 for the collapse case study (Fig 2), §3.1–3.2 for delta updates and grow-and-refine, Tables 1–2, §4.6 + Appendix A.5 for the incremental-update ablation, Appendix C for ACE-vs-GEPA/DC mechanism contrasts.

2510.16079.tldr: EvolveR closes the experience loop inside RL training: the agent distills its own trajectories into guiding/cautionary principles kept in a scored, deduplicated, pruned base, retrieves them via a learned <search experience> action, and GRPO-trains on experience-conditioned rollouts — beating Search-R1 across seven QA benchmarks.
2510.16079.method: Three alternating phases (§3). (1) Offline self-distillation, policy frozen: the agent's own πθ reviews each trajectory under an expert persona and emits a principle — a natural-language description plus knowledge triples, typed 'guiding' (success) or 'cautionary' (failure). Same-problem candidates are pairwise-deduped by LLM votes; each survivor then passes a two-stage gate (BGE-M3 cosine retrieval + binary LLM equivalence check): add if max similarity < 0.85, else merge the source trajectory under the matched principle. Every principle carries a Laplace-smoothed trust score s(p)=(c_succ+1)/(c_use+2); scores below 0.3 are periodically pruned. (2) Online interaction: top-3 principles are retrieved on demand via a learned <search experience> action, alongside <search knowledge> document retrieval. (3) Policy evolution: GRPO (G=8 rollouts per prompt, 128 prompts/step) maximizes 1.0·exact-match + 0.1·format reward over experience-conditioned trajectories, after a ~700-sample GPT-4o cold-start SFT.
results: Seven QA benchmarks, EM: top average at both scales — 0.382 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 0.417 (7B) vs Search-R1 0.303 (base, 3B) / 0.385 (instruct, 7B); best in five of seven columns at 3B (NQ 0.434 vs 0.406, HotpotQA 0.373 vs 0.284, Bamboogle 0.328 vs 0.264), trailing Search-R1-base by 0.003 on TriviaQA (0.584 vs 0.587) and PopQA (0.434 vs 0.435).

Self- vs teacher-distillation reverses with scale (Table 2): GPT-4o-mini distillation wins at 0.5B (avg 0.220 vs 0.150) and 1.5B (0.290 vs 0.270), but self-distillation wins at 3B (0.382 vs 0.370) — the paper's 'cognitive alignment' claim.

Retrieval is load-bearing: the same trained weights denied the experience base at eval drop 0.382 → 0.340 (3B), 0.270 → 0.123 (1.5B), 0.150 → 0.078 (0.5B); swapping GRPO for SFT on the identical successful trajectories costs 0.382 → 0.357 (7% relative).

Quality control demonstrably works (manual audit of 100 principles): the high-score tier holds 82% ideal / 8% incorrect-misleading vs 26% / 24% in the low tier; the base grows to 49,934 principles with top-3 latency of 0.20 s and stable EM, peaking at 0.410 near 45k.

Scaling and learning dynamics: avg EM rises 0.150 (0.5B) → 0.270 (1.5B) → 0.382 (3B); principles distilled later score higher (interval-4 avg trust 0.500 vs 0.462 for interval 1), and pruning is threshold-robust (avg 0.265–0.276 for θprune ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9} on 1.5B).
advantages: Closes the loop inside RL rather than around a frozen model: distill every step (params frozen), retrieve during rollouts, GRPO over experience-conditioned trajectories — Reflexion/ExpeL/Memento never touch weights, Search-R1-style search RL has no experience channel. Component attribution: RL alone 0.325, retrieval without RL 0.357, full framework 0.382.

Memory with an audited trust ledger: the (c_succ+1)/(c_use+2) score decides survival (θprune = 0.3) and tracks human-judged quality (82% vs 26% ideal), robustly — performance moves only 0.265 → 0.276 across the whole θprune sweep.

Shows self-distillation can beat a stronger teacher at 3B: principles matched to the policy's own failure modes outperform GPT-4o-mini's, direct evidence against the external-scribing paradigm (ExpeL-style insights from a big model).
The experience base scales as an artifact: ~50k principles with 0.04–0.20 s top-3 retrieval (Milvus, BGE-M3) and no collapse under noise accumulation; full 3B lifecycle trains in ~39.4 h on 8×A100.
limitations: Scale-dependent distiller (paper's own finding): below 3B, self-distillation loses to GPT-4o-mini teacher distillation (0.5B avg 0.150 vs 0.220; 1.5B 0.270 vs 0.290); the conclusion concedes principle quality is 'inherently tied to the base model's capabilities'.

Capability is split between policy and base, not internalized: denying retrieval at eval costs 0.382 → 0.340 (3B) and 0.150 → 0.078 (0.5B), and the w/ exp-absorb attempt to learn from retrieved principle tokens degrades 0.382 → 0.371 (noisy top-k), left to future work.
Distillation failure mode is vagueness: low-score-tier principles are 50% vague and 24% incorrect/misleading (audit of just 100 samples) — scoring prunes but never eliminates bad advice.
Scope is QA-shaped: seven knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks with an exact-match headline; whether strategy principles transfer to non-QA agent domains is untested.
2510.16079.fits: Stage 4 (memory, reflection & skills): converts the Reflexion/ExpeL verbal-reflection loop into curated principles plus GRPO signal, closing experience → memory → weights end-to-end. Pairs with the EvolveR repo card (implementation detail), ACE (context-only evolution), A-MEM/MemoryBank (memory organization without RL), and Search-R1-lineage RL agents.
2510.16079.reading: §3.2 (distill/dedup/integrate, Eq. 1–2), §3.3 (reward + GRPO), §5.2–5.3 (Tables 2–7, the 100-principle audit), A.2.1/A.2.3 (SFT-vs-GRPO, learning dynamics), A.1 (hyperparameters).

2605.23904.tldr: SkillOpt treats a single 300-2,000-token skill document as the trainable state of a frozen agent: an optimizer model turns scored rollouts into bounded add/delete/replace edits, each accepted only on a strict held-out validation gain, best or tied-best on 52/52 cells.
2605.23904.method: SkillOpt freezes the target model, harness, and evaluator; only the skill text trains. Each step runs a rollout batch (B=40) from the train split; the optimizer model separates failures from successes, splits each into reflection minibatches (Bm=8, 16 parallel analysts), and returns structured JSON edits (append / insert_after / replace / delete). Failure patches merge, success patches merge, then a failure-prioritized final merge deduplicates and resolves conflicts; the pool is ranked and clipped to the edit budget Lt=4 (cosine decay, floor 2) - the textual learning rate. The candidate is scored on the selection split, accepted only on strict improvement (ties rejected), and the best accepted version exported as best_skill.md. A rejected-edit buffer conditions later reflection, and an epoch-boundary slow/meta update writes protected longitudinal guidance under the same gate. Default: four epochs; the optimizer-side meta skill is teacher-only.
results: GPT-5.5 direct chat, six benchmarks: average no-skill 58.8 -> 82.3 (+23.5), +5.4 clear of a per-cell oracle over human, one-shot LLM, Trace2Skill, TextGrad, GEPA and EvoSkill skills (76.9); SpreadsheetBench 41.8 -> 80.7, OfficeQA 33.1 -> 72.1, LiveMath 37.6 -> 66.9, ALFWorld 83.6 -> 95.5, SearchQA 77.7 -> 87.3, DocVQA 78.8 -> 91.2. Best-or-tied on 52 of 52 (model, benchmark, harness) cells.

Same interface under tool harnesses (GPT-5.5, five benchmarks): Codex average +24.8 over no skill and +14.0 over EvoSkill; Claude Code +19.1 over no skill, +3.2 over EvoSkill, whose own average is 57.8 -> 73.7; SpreadsheetBench under Claude Code 22.1 -> 80.4.

Not frontier-specific: per-model average gains are +12.7 (GPT-5.4), +15.4 (mini), +26.7 (nano), +16.6 (GPT-5.2), +19.2 (Qwen3.5-4B), +9.1 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), about +17.6 points per model; ALFWorld 34.3 -> 69.4 on GPT-5.4-nano and SpreadsheetBench 9.3 -> 23.9 (x2.6) on Qwen3.5-4B.

Ablations (GPT-5.5 student and teacher, SearchQA/Spreadsheet/LiveMath): removing the edit budget gives 84.6/75.7/57.3 vs 87.1/77.5/61.3 for the bounded default; dropping the rejected-edit buffer costs 1.6/4.6/2.4 points; removing both meta skill and slow update drops SpreadsheetBench 77.5 -> 55.0 (-22.5). Training evidence scales: 1 example -> 100% of the train partition lifts SpreadsheetBench 47.5 -> 78.0 and LiveMath 59.1 -> 70.5.

Transfer, and what it costs: a Codex-trained SpreadsheetBench skill reaches +59.7 on Claude Code (22.1 -> 81.8, above the in-domain 80.4) and the reverse adds +43.6 (27.5 -> 71.1); OlympiadBench -> Omni-MATH gains +3.7/+1.8/+1.3 across three scales. Deployed skills stay small (379-1,995 tokens, median ~920) and come from only 1-4 accepted edits (LiveMath's +29.3 and OfficeQA's +39.0 each from one); training costs 0.6M-46.4M tokens per test point.
advantages: The accept gate does visible work, and the edit economy proves it: the optimizer proposes many edits per epoch but only 1-4 survive into best_skill.md, because acceptance requires strictly beating the current selection score (ties rejected) - so the artifact cannot silently drift, and two of the largest single-benchmark gains come from exactly one gated edit.

Breadth of evidence unusual for a no-weight-update method: six benchmarks spanning extractive QA, spreadsheet codegen, document and multimodal QA, math and embodied interaction, seven target models from GPT-5.5 to Qwen3.5-4B, and three harnesses (direct chat, Codex, Claude Code) all consuming one best_skill.md, with the strongest per-cell competitor as the comparison point in every cell.

Optimizer strength is a free training-time lever: because the optimizer runs only offline, swapping in a frontier teacher costs nothing at deployment, and it measurably pays (GPT-5.4-nano SpreadsheetBench +19.0 vs +11.9, SearchQA +19.0 vs +14.1; GPT-5.4-mini +11.4 vs +7.1 and +4.3 vs +2.4). A target-matched optimizer still recovers 56-74% of that gain, so the loop itself, not distillation, carries most of the value.

The learned artifact is genuinely portable and auditable: cross-model, cross-harness (+59.7) and cross-benchmark transfers are all positive with no row below the target's no-skill baseline, every change is recoverable from edit_apply_report.json, the slow-update region is markup-fenced against step-level edits, and the meta skill never ships with the deployed skill.
limitations: The loop needs reliable automatic feedback: scored trajectories plus a held-out selection split mean it applies most directly where verifiers, exact-match metrics or executable checks exist; subjective or multi-dimensional domains may need stronger human or model-based evaluation (Appendix B).

Training is not free even though deployment is: rollouts plus optimizer calls cost 0.6M-46.4M training tokens per absolute test point (SearchQA 37.9M/pt, DocVQA 46.4M/pt), amortized only when the same skill is reused, and less attractive for one-off tasks.

It deliberately trains one portable skill rather than a library or model weights, which the authors concede may be insufficient for heterogeneous domains requiring many disjoint procedures - and it barely explores the self-distillation back into the target model.

Optimized skills encode heuristics from the training distribution, so held-out evaluation remains necessary before transfer; scope is also narrowed in places, with ALFWorld omitted from both harness rows because persistent embodied interaction is not representable in the standard Codex / Claude Code adapters.
2605.23904.fits: Stage 4's Harness & Scaffold Evolution group (ENRICHMENT row 30): the clearest 'skill document as trained parameter' discipline, and the strict held-out acceptance gate rsif borrows. Pairs with TextGrad and ACE on text-space optimization, SkillRise and MetaSkill-Evolve on evolving skills, MemoHarness and MemEvolve on the surrounding harness, and stage-5 ADAS/DGM for where the loop recurses.
2605.23904.reading: 3.2-3.6 for the loop (rollout batches, minibatch reflection, bounded updates, gate, slow/meta update); 4.2 with Tables 2-3 for the ablations; 4.3-4.4 with Tables 4-6 for transfer, edit economy and cost; Appendix B for limitations; C.2 for the verbatim optimizer prompts.

2408.08435.tldr: A meta agent (GPT-4o) programs new agents as complete `forward()` Python functions, scores each on a validation slice, and feeds the growing scored archive back into its own prompt — discovering designs that beat hand-designed baselines on DROP, MGSM, MMLU and GPQA.
2408.08435.method: The search space is Python, not prompts. The meta agent is handed a <100-line framework (`Info` namedtuple; `FM_Module` wrapping role/model/temperature and a `query()` that concatenates Info objects into a structured prompt) and must write one complete `def forward(self, taskInfo)` per candidate, which the harness executes. Loop (Algorithm 1): seed the archive with hand-designed baselines (COT, COT-SC, Self-Refine, LLM Debate, Quality-Diversity, Step-back, Role Assignment); the meta agent sees the full scored archive plus 'WRONG Implementation examples' and emits {thought, name, code}; two self-reflection rounds revise it for interestingness, implementation mistakes and improvement; it is evaluated on the domain validation split; runtime errors trigger up to five debug reflections; the agent and its metric are appended to the archive. Search runs independently per domain; one fixed meta agent (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) proposes while every candidate and baseline is scored by gpt-3.5-turbo-0125.
results: Table 1 (held-out test, 95% bootstrap CI): DROP F1 79.4 ± 0.8 vs best hand-designed 65.8 ± 0.9 (Role Assignment) and prompt-only OPRO 69.1 ± 0.9 — the paper's headline +13.6; MGSM accuracy 53.4 ± 3.5 vs 39.0 ± 3.4 (LLM Debate), +14.4; MMLU 69.6 ± 3.2 vs 65.9 ± 3.2 (COT-SC); GPQA 34.6 ± 3.2 vs 31.6 ± 3.2 (Self-Refine) — the gap shrinks where FM knowledge, not scaffolding, caps performance.

ARC (25 search iterations, 20-question validation / 60-question test, 5 evaluations each): top three discovered agents reach 13.7 / 13.3 / 12.7 % on GPT-3.5 vs best baseline 8.0 (LLM Debate); transferred unchanged to Claude-Sonnet they reach 38.7 / 39.7 / 48.3 % vs 31.7 baseline (Table 3).

Zero-shot transfer of the top-3 MGSM agents within math (Table 4): GSM8K 69.5 ± 3.2 vs best baseline 43.6 ± 3.4 (+25.9), GSM-Hard 31.2 ± 3.2 vs 18.0 ± 2.7 (+13.2), SVAMP 82.6 vs 78.5, ASDiv 91.8 vs 89.2. Beyond math (Table 5) DROP F1 70.4–71.9 vs 65.8 and MMLU 62.4–67.0 vs 65.9, but GPQA 28.6–29.9 stays under the 31.6 baseline — 'outperform or match', not a clean sweep.

Empty-initialization ablation (Table 6): with no seeded baselines Meta Agent Search still beats every hand-designed baseline in all four domains, and in math it beats its own seeded run (MGSM 67.5 ± 3.3 vs 53.4 ± 3.5), while seeding wins elsewhere (DROP 79.4 vs 73.9; MMLU 69.6 vs 68.5; GPQA 34.6 vs 32.7).
Cost (Appendix J): ~$500 per ARC search-and-evaluation run and ~$300 per reasoning-domain run, dominated by gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 evaluation calls rather than meta-agent proposals.
advantages: Whole-program search space: because the candidate is arbitrary Python, the loop learns prompts, workflows, ensembles, criticism and refinement together. The prompt-only baseline OPRO is beaten in all four domains (DROP 69.1 vs 79.4), which is the paper's direct evidence that code-space ADAS buys more than prompt optimization.

The stepping-stone story is documented, not asserted: on ARC a 'multiple COTs → refine → ensemble' pattern emerged at iteration 3 and was reused afterwards, and the best agent combined ideas first seen at iterations 5 (diverse feedback), 11 (trait-specific experts) and 12 (human-like critic) — LLM-mediated crossover over an archive rather than hill-climbing on one incumbent.

Generalization is measured three ways, not one: transfer to unseen math domains, to non-math domains, and across four FMs (GPT-3.5, Claude-Haiku, GPT-4, Claude-Sonnet), where the searched agents keep their lead at every model — evidence the discovered designs are not overfit to the searching model.

Extremely cheap substrate: <100 lines of framework, API-only, no GPUs, and the outputs are readable Python — the paper argues this makes the search space interpretable and auditable in a way graph/network search spaces are not.
limitations: One objective (performance) only: cost, latency and robustness are not optimized; multi-objective ADAS is left to future work, and the ~$300–500 per run is itself never treated as a search constraint.

By the authors' own account the evaluation function is the weak link — evaluating on a validation split and reading a scalar is 'both expensive and overlooks valuable information', discarding the run logs that carry failure modes, and it cannot handle subjectively judged tasks.

Scope is single-step QA plus ARC-style grid puzzles; multi-step interaction with real environments is untested, and the meta agent itself is fixed — the paper never improves the meta-agent's own prompt or search policy, listing self-referential 'Higher-order ADAS' explicitly as future work.
Where the FM lacks the knowledge, agent design cannot compensate: the GPQA/MMLU gains are small (34.6, 69.6) and the transferred math agents fall below the GPQA baseline (28.6–29.9 vs 31.6).
2408.08435.fits: Stage 5 (Harness-level RSI), the cleanest anchor of the Prompt & Program Optimization group: the evolving artifact is a whole agent program while the improver stays fixed. Successors (DGM, HyperAgents, AutoHarness, Continual Harness, MetaSkill-Evolve) extend the loop to the meta level or to online settings. Pairs with OPRO, Promptbreeder, STOP and DSPy as its prompt-only ancestors.
2408.08435.reading: §3 (the four-step loop), §4.1–4.3 with Tables 1–3 for the numbers, Appendix B (prompts, the two Reflexion rounds, the error-reflection prompt), H (pseudocode), I (empty-init ablation), J (cost); Appendix G for discovered agents' code.

2310.02304.tldr: GPT-4 is prompted with a seed improver's own source plus the meta-utility and returns a better improver; iterating I_t = I_{t-1}(meta-utility, I_{t-1}, LM) yields scaffolds that beat the seed on parity-with-noise and transfer to five unseen tasks.
2310.02304.method: Algorithm 1. The seed improver I0 (Fig. 2) is one prompt template carrying the solution string and the utility's source as a grey-box description string, run as batch_prompt with n = min(max_responses_per_call, budget) candidates at temperature 0.7, then extract_code and return the argmax under u. Meta-utility is u-hat(I) = mean over task set D of u(I(u,s,L)) (LPN: 10-bit parity with noise, 20 sampled instances, 5 copies of (u,s)). Crucially the self-improvement prompt holds only the template's placeholders, never the downstream task, so the LM cannot target it directly. Each round I_t <- I_{t-1}(u-hat, I_{t-1}, L) is a full improver run, costing O((budget_u + budget_L) * budget_u-hat). Selection is greedy: an improver is kept only if measured u-hat beats the incumbent, so nothing enforces monotonicity. The T=10 artifact (Fig. 5) is a top-3 population with epsilon-greedy temperature control and a no-improvement stop.
results: LPN with GPT-4: mean held-out meta-utility rises across 1-3 self-improvement rounds (Fig. 4, 5 runs, +/-1 standard error); the GPT-3.5 and Mixtral curves degrade over the same 4 rounds.
Baselines over 10 runs: chain-of-thought improver meta-utility 57.7% +/- 3.0% (49.6% +/- 3.5% counting errors) vs greedy iterative improver 64.2% +/- 0.9%.

Transfer of the T=4 LPN improver with no further optimization (Table 1, as u(s) -> u-hat(I0) -> u-hat(IT)): 3SAT 0% -> 21.2% -> 75.1%; Maxcut 0% -> 58.7% -> 74.2%; parity without noise 50.0% -> 59.3% -> 81.7%; String Grid Distance 43.9% -> 44.3% -> 56.7%; modified quadratic assignment 20.4% -> 20.6% -> 22.1%.

Smaller LMs: the seed improver scores higher with GPT-3.5 than GPT-4 (65% vs 61% meta-utility, attributed to GPT-4 proposing complex solutions that time out), yet only 12% of GPT-3.5 runs produced at least a 3% improvement; Mixtral mostly made harmless edits (prompt rewording, docs, caching).

Unsafe self-improvement, 10,000 sampled generations (Table 2): unsandboxing detected in 0.42% (0.31-0.57) of GPT-4 and 0.12% (0.07-0.21) of GPT-3.5 attempts; the warning variant raised the rate (0.46% / 0.17%) without significance. One LPN utility was reward-hacked into reporting >1000% accuracy by returning a differently-shaped prediction array.
advantages: First working demo that an LM can write code that improves the code calling it - the improver improves the improver - and the GPT-4 used was trained only to Sept. 2021, so the strategies appeared independently of the scaffolding literature that followed.

Real out-of-distribution transfer: an improver selected purely on LPN beats the seed on five qualitatively different tasks without any per-task tuning, including 0% -> 75.1% on 3SAT, even though the LM never sees the downstream task during self-improvement.

Names the recursive designs agent harnesses later adopted: GPT-4 proposed beam search, genetic/evolutionary search, function-level decomposition, simulated annealing, bandit/UCB selection, and temperature-as-exploration, with the generated code shipped in Appendix H and the repo.

Treats self-improvement safety empirically rather than rhetorically: a 10,000-sample measurement of sandbox circumvention, plus the observation that constraints written into the seed prompt get edited out as 'simplification' and one improver instantiated a new LM object with larger budgets.
limitations: Not full RSI, by the authors' own framing: the LM's weights and architecture are untouched, only the scaffold evolves, and improver quality is measured only indirectly through downstream task utility.
Improvement is not monotonic - a worse improver can be accepted, deterioration is possible, and with GPT-3.5/Mixtral the curve actually falls (Fig. 4).

Requires an efficiently evaluatable and describable utility; the meta-utility loop costs O((budget_u + budget_L) * budget_u-hat), far more than the improver it optimizes, and only a single improver is maintained per step (no population).

Dependent on a closed model (gpt-4-0314) that may be deprecated, and the authors doubt any open-source LM then available would work consistently; a fixed point of the recursion could equally be a minimizer, since nothing but the seed favors maximization.
2310.02304.fits: Stage 5's origin point. Unlike ADAS (search over agent programs) STOP searches the improver itself, and unlike the later DGM (self-modifying agent code under benchmark gates) it keeps a fixed LM and a hand-written utility. Pair it with RRSI for the recursive statement and DGM for where the loop went next.
2310.02304.reading: Read §3-4 for the problem statement and seed improver (Figs. 2-3, Algorithm 1), §5.1-5.2 with Table 1 for the numbers, and §6.2-6.3 with Table 2 for sandbox circumvention and reward hacking.

2605.09998.tldr: Harness engineering for embodied agents, previously human-in-the-loop (Gemini Plays Pokémon finished three RPGs), is automated: a Refiner rewrites the agent's prompt, sub-agents, skills and memory mid-episode with no resets, then an online DAgger+PRM loop updates the model's weights inside that same live-refining harness.
2605.09998.method: From a minimal interface (frame o_t, ASCII text map, eight buttons) the harness state is four editable stores: prompt p, sub-agents G, skills K, memory M. Inner loop: the agent model reads (s_t, H_t, tau_t) and emits an action. Outer loop: every F steps after a warm-up of W, the Refiner reads tau_{t-F:t}, names failure signatures — navigation loops, tool-call failures, stalled objectives — then runs four passes emitting Delta = (Delta_p, Delta_G, Delta_K, Delta_M) through the same meta-tool API (define_agent, run_code, process_memory): p is replaced, G/K/M get CRUD edits, and H_{t+1} = H_t + Delta enters context with no reset. At training scale each iteration runs pi_theta inside the live-refining harness for K=256 DAgger steps; a pairwise PRM scores transitions (progress 0.4, action 0.3, reasoning 0.2, format 0.1), a Gemini-3.1-pro teacher relabels low-reward windows, and soft SFT (LoRA r=256) produces theta_{k+1} from the carried-over emulator state.
results: On Emerald's 31-milestone set, Gemini 3 Pro with from-scratch Continual Harness reaches 100% of milestones at a $130 median, against the minimalist harness at 98% for $215 — a ~40% cost reduction with no completion loss; the two bootstrap variants reach 96–100% for $110–$140. On Red, bootstrap-updating is more efficient than from-scratch at every monitored milestone.

Gains scale with capability and invert below the floor: Flash bootstrap-updating reaches 80% of Emerald milestones at $42 vs Hmin's 77% at $30 (high variance across seeds), while Flash-Lite's Hmin gets 20% at $11 and every Continual Harness variant falls to 3–13% at comparable or higher cost.

Skills measurably self-improve toward an oracle: for the top-10% evolved navigation skills on a 24-hour Pro run, path-cost deficit against a Dijkstra oracle falls from a near-half-cost penalty to single digits, with the repair happening in the same episode as the failure. Hmin never invokes a navigation skill; every Continual Harness condition logs hundreds of invocations.

Co-learning drives sustained reset-free progress: five advancing Gemma-4 runs on Pokémon Red raise their milestone index across training iterations (net objective gains +2 to +5, judge-verified), from both the beginning of the game and mid-game checkpoints, against zero advance for the untrained baseline. Cross-family Qwen3.5 35B parses tool calls through the harness but cannot leave the starting area.

The human-in-the-loop predecessor is the existence proof: GPP is the first AI system to complete Pokémon Blue (May 2025), Yellow Legacy on hard mode (August 2025) and Crystal without a lost end-game battle (November 2025). On Crystal, Gemini 3 Pro matched Gemini 2.5 Pro's early milestones in roughly half the turns and ~60% fewer tokens, against 16,403 turns spent by 2.5 Pro before the Fog Badge.
advantages: Reset-free is a structural difference, not a convenience: failure signatures observed earlier stay available to every later refinement pass, so refinement quality compounds with episode length, and the loop can target failure modes that only appear deep in an episode (late-game battles, multi-step puzzles, dialogue chains) which reset-based prompt optimizers such as GEPA cannot reach by construction.

The evolved object is the entire harness state, not just the prompt — p, G, K and M are all rewritten by the same Refiner through the same meta-tool API the agent itself uses, with per-component mechanism attribution (Appendix C) instead of one aggregate ablation.

Skill quality is measured against an external oracle (BFS/Dijkstra path cost on navigation segments) rather than end-task efficiency, giving a task-independent mechanism-level read on self-improvement that most harness papers do not attempt.

It is the arm of the harness-school arc that closes the loop into weights: DAgger rollouts through the live-refining harness, pairwise PRM scoring, frontier-teacher relabeling and soft SFT produce model-harness co-learning, with capability-dependent evidence for whom it helps.
limitations: A hard capability floor: on Flash-Lite every Continual Harness variant reaches only 3–13% of Emerald milestones at comparable or higher cost than Hmin's 20% at $11, and Flash is high-variance. In the authors' own words the framework needs a model that will sufficiently utilize the harness components.
The residual gap to the hand-engineered expert harness concentrates in dialogue-heavy gym interiors and multi-turn battle strategy — components the loop does not yet synthesize reliably.

Co-learning couples a frontier teacher (Gemini-3.1-pro) to an open-source student; Gemma-4 up to 31B is not capable enough to serve both roles, the loop has no established convergence point, and no head-to-head comparison against reset-based batch accumulation was run.

Memory reuse is weak by the authors' own admission — most authored entries sit unused and the reference rate stays low in absolute terms. On Red the bootstrap-updating agent collapses its sub-agent budget to a handful of calls citing IDs absent from the bootstrap (inherited share 6.4% ± 5.7 vs 100.0% ± 0.0 frozen, Table 2), and the milestone staircase regresses below Hmin in lockstep; a reuse prior or sub-agent deletion policy is named as the fix.
2605.09998.fits: Stage 5 (Harness-level RSI): the capstone of the harness-school arc (ADAS → DGM → Hyperagents) and its reset-free, embodied anchor, with the DAgger+PRM arm pushing toward stage 6 co-evolution. Pairs with GEPA/TextGrad as the reset-based foils it generalizes, Meta-Harness and AutoHarness on what to evolve, and SIA's harness|weights split.
2605.09998.reading: §2–3 for the harness state and the two-loop architecture, §4.3–4.4 for the progression figure and the cost–completion Pareto plane, §4.6 plus Figure 8 for oracle-measured skill repair, Appendix C for per-component attribution, Appendix D for training hyperparameters.

2605.27276.tldr: A Feedback-Agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6) alternately rewrites a task agent's scaffold and RL-tunes its weights (LoRA on gpt-oss-120b), merging the harness-update and test-time-training silos into one loop that beats both single-lever variants on all three benchmarks.
2605.27276.method: Three LLM components: a Meta-Agent writes the initial scaffold A1 from the task spec and reference code; the task-specific agent (gpt-oss-120b) runs the benchmark in a sandbox (read-only data, private working dir); a Feedback-Agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6) reads the full trajectory — every prompt, response, tool call, and extracted answer per instance, not summary metrics — plus the scaffold and scores, then picks the next step: a harness update (A_{g+1} = F(A_g, τ_g, E_g, U); weights frozen) or a weight update (LoRA r=32, lr 4e-5 on gpt-oss-120b, H100s via Modal; scaffold frozen). It also selects the RL algorithm from a six-entry menu (PPO+GAE, GRPO, entropic advantage weighting, REINFORCE+KL, best-of-N behavioral cloning, DPO) from reward structure; in practice scaffold iteration runs first, switching to weights when harness progress stalls. Gate: a deterministic per-instance verifier scores every step.
results: LawBench 191-class Chinese charge classification (top-1 accuracy, 913-item held-out test): 13.5% initial → 50.0% harness-only — the scaffold converged on a TF-IDF + LinearSVC pipeline, abandoning the LLM path — → 70.1% after PPO+GAE weight updates; prior SOTA 45.0% (+25.1 points).

AlphaEvolve TriMul CUDA-kernel task (H100; score = 1500/runtime): harness-only stalled at 0.120 (12,483 µs, 1.14×); entropic advantage weighting drove runtime to 1,017 µs — 14.02× speedup, score 1.475 vs 1.292 prior SOTA (12.4% faster), a 91.9% runtime cut from the harness-only peak.

MAGIC scRNA-seq denoising on pancreas data (mse norm, higher = better): harness-only hyperparameter sweeps (k, diffusion steps, bandwidth) plateaued at 0.241; the first GRPO checkpoint added a np.clip + np.rint rounding step → 0.289 vs 0.240 prior SOTA (+20.4%).
Ablation (Table 3): SIA-W+H strictly beats SIA-H everywhere, but the dominant lever flips by domain — harness updates did most of the LawBench work, weights nearly all of TriMul's (0.120 → 1.475).
advantages: Table 1's only system that edits harness and weights inside one self-improving loop; the nearest neighbours each stop short — Hyperagents co-evolves agent and improver but freezes weights, EUREKA composes scaffold-side reward generation with RL training but one-directionally.

RL algorithm choice is part of what the Feedback-Agent searches: PPO+GAE when per-step rewards are dense, GRPO when rollouts are cheap and the verifier fires at episode end, entropic advantage weighting when the reward histogram is right-skewed, plus REINFORCE+KL, best-of-N behavioral cloning (cold start), and DPO — selected per trajectory, not a fixed schedule.

Conditions on full per-instance trajectories (every prompt, tool call, extracted answer) rather than aggregate scores, so edits diagnose specific failure modes instead of mutating toward summary statistics.

Isolates each lever's contribution empirically: weight updates are shown to deliver knowledge no scaffold generation reached (the np.clip+np.rint invariant, H100 tiling patterns), directly answering RQ2 rather than asserting synergy.
limitations: Coupled co-evolutionary Goodhart (§8, the paper's own analysis): both levers optimise the same fixed verifier, so the harness finds scaffolds the current policy can exploit while the weights train on data from a scaffold that will change — the joint fixed point is a Nash equilibrium of two mutually blind optimisers, fragile off-distribution.
Lever and algorithm selection is a frozen LLM prior, not learned (§9); the loop alternates in coarse discrete rounds — finer interleaving is left as future work.

Three single-task evaluations, one base model (gpt-oss-120b), no seeds or variance reported; and §7.3's algorithm-selection guidance is 'common patterns observed' across tasks not reported here, with a fuller treatment deferred to v2.
2605.27276.fits: Stage 5 harness-level RSI at its merge point with test-time training: the capstone of the harness-school arc (DGM → Hyperagents → Continual Harness) that adds SEAL/TTRL-style weight updates as a second lever. Read after Continual Harness; pair with the sia repo card, whose --focus harness|weights flags split the loop the paper auto-selects.
2605.27276.reading: §3.2–3.3 (Feedback-Agent inputs, trajectory), §5.1–5.3 (lever selection), Table 3 and §6.3 per-task numbers, §7.3 (the six-algorithm menu and when each fires), §8 (coupled Goodhart).

2505.15734.tldr: No-label self-evolution: run RCR-prompted multi-agent debate, keep the consensus answer plus a consolidated rationale, GRPO-train the single model on them, then swap the evolved policy back into the debate team and repeat. +8.92 pts average on GSM-Plus after one round.
2505.15734.method: Agents A={a1..aN} debate a query for up to T rounds under the RCR prompt, which enforces three phases per round: Reflect (self-critique of own rationale), Critique (exactly two peers), Refine (update the answer, and any changed answer must add a novel reasoning step absent from all prior traces). Debate stops on unanimous consensus, else majority vote. Traces are compressed into one consolidated rationale R by keeping steps that recur across agents or introduce novel symbolic manipulation, yielding (q, y*, R). Training is GRPO on that instance with reward r = 2.0·1[y=y*] + 0.5·f_format(y) + 0.5·exp(−|y|/120) — the correctness term is agreement with the debate consensus, not ground truth. G=8 samples/query, clip 0.2, KL β=0.02, LoRA r=128 on attention/MLP projections, AdamW lr 5e-6. After each round the evolved policy replaces its own predecessor in the debate pool.
