results: One DTE round (Table 1, GSM-Plus): Qwen-1.5B 42.00 → 55.92 (+13.92), Qwen-3B 61.75 → 69.50, Qwen-7B 68.62 → 74.71, Qwen-14B 71.79 → 78.88, Llama-3B 45.67 → 53.79, Llama-8B 55.62 → 66.17 — mean +8.92 pts over the base model at one forward pass. GSM8K gains average only +0.84 (models near ceiling) and ARC-Challenge is mixed: +3.67 Qwen-7B, +8.88 Llama-8B, but −0.85 Qwen-1.5B and −0.42 Qwen-3B. Across all five Table 1 benchmarks the evolved single model averages +3.06 pts over the base model and +1.09 pts over the 3-agent RCR committee that generated its traces.

Cross-domain transfer (Table 2): evolving on GSM8K gives +5.8 pts average on the unseen GSM-Plus, +2.5 on ARC-Challenge, and CommonsenseQA gains for 5/6 models; models ≥7B never lose more than 0.2 pts on any transfer task, while Qwen-1.5B drops 1.60 on ARC-Easy and 2.23 on CommonsenseQA. Evolving on GSM-Plus and testing on GSM8K is symmetric (+3.7 avg), which the authors read as learning heuristics (numeric decomposition, unit tracking) rather than dataset patterns.

The RCR prompt alone (ablation 1, eight models) beats the original MAD@3 prompt by +1.9 pts GSM8K, +3.7 GSM-Plus, +0.7 ARC-Challenge — up to +7.9 (Qwen-1.5B) and +6.1 (Qwen-7B) on GSM-Plus. It halves the mean sycophancy rate (0.28 → 0.13 on GSM-Plus) and narrows the verbosity gap by 43%, versus standard MAD where small-model sycophancy exceeds 28% on average.

GRPO beats both alternatives at fixed compute (Table 3, GSM-Plus, 10K steps): Qwen-1.5B 42.00 → SFT 47.31 / DPO 51.34 / GRPO 55.92; Qwen-3B 61.75 → SFT 58.33 (regression) / DPO 64.32 / GRPO 69.50; Qwen-7B 68.62 → 67.89 / 69.88 / 74.71. GRPO holds KL < 0.24 across sizes where DPO averages 0.43.

Effort scaling: 3 agents capture 85–95% of the achievable debate gain (ARC-Easy saturates at 2, GSM-Plus sometimes prefers 4–5; Qwen-7B peaks at 76.0% with 7 agents, +1.04 over 3). GRPO saturates near 8K steps (+0.32 pts average from 8K → 10K while wall-clock grows 25%). A second evolution round gives ≥7B at most +0.8 pts and often loses 0.4–1.4 (mean forgetting Fgt2 = 0.92 pts ≥7B, 1.6 smaller). Trace coverage is monotonic (Table 4): All-Traces beats Debate-Only by 4.43 pts and Random-2K by 9.17.
advantages: Self-referential where fixed-judge self-training is not: after each round the evolved policy replaces its own predecessor inside the debate ensemble (Algorithm 2, step 18), so trace generator and trace consumer improve together — and the evolved single model then beats the very committee (+1.09 pts on average across Table 1's five benchmarks) that produced its training data.

RCR is diagnosed before it is proposed: the paper first measures standard MAD's failure modes (sycophancy above 28% average for small models, verbosity bias, [correct → incorrect] transitions) and then fixes them mechanically — a fixed two-peer critique quota and a mandatory novel reasoning step on any answer change — halving sycophancy and cutting the verbosity gap 43%.

Design choices are ablated with a mechanism rather than asserted: GRPO over SFT/DPO at fixed compute with measured KL drift (< 0.24 vs 0.43), trace coverage shown monotonic across three sampling schemes, and temperature annealing justified by measured KL evolution (0.37 → 0.19 → 0.11 as T goes 1.0 → 0.4 → 0.0).

Operationally label-free: the reward's correctness term is exact-string agreement with the debate consensus, so no dataset labels and no external judge enter training; the generalization evidence (symmetric GSM8K↔GSM-Plus transfer, ≥7B losing ≤0.2 pts on any transfer task) is the paper's case that this is real reasoning gain, not overfitting.
limitations: Catastrophic forgetting under iteration, which the paper's own Limitations concedes it cannot eliminate ('potential model collapse' below 3B): at T=1.0, Round 2 loses 2.0 pts on GSM8K and gains only 13.5 pts on GSM-Plus, and Figure 2 shows Qwen-1.5B giving back 0.9 pts on GSM8K and 2.8 on GSM-Plus; Llama-3B at temperature 0.8 and 10K steps collapses to 2.73% on GSM8K and to 35.63 / 23.02 after two rounds. Temperature annealing 0.7 → 0.3 for ≤3B is a mitigation, not a fix — at T=0.4 Round-2 GSM-Plus is still 0.9 pts below Round 1.

The ceiling is the debate, not the data: the paper's Limitations says efficacy 'may degrade if debates are of poor quality or if initial agent performance is weak', and one round captures nearly all available gain — Round 2 adds at most +0.8 pts for ≥7B and more often loses 0.4–1.4 (mean forgetting Fgt2 0.92 pts ≥7B, 1.6 for smaller).

Scope is structured reasoning only (math, science MC-QA, commonsense); the paper flags open-ended generation and dialogue as unstudied, and states DTE still costs more to train than plain single-model fine-tuning.

Consensus errors propagate: correctness is agreement with the debate's majority answer, so a confident wrong consensus is a wrong training target — visible in Table 1 where Qwen-7B loses 2.35 pts on GSM8K and Qwen-7B / 1.5B lose on ARC-Challenge, with the paper attributing Round-1 Qwen-7B's GSM8K drop to traces that over-emphasised shortcut heuristics.
2505.15734.fits: Stage 6 Co-Evolution, the weight-persisting arm of debate: inference-time MAD (Du et al., Liang et al.) supplies the signal and GRPO writes it into the policy, replacing a per-query committee with one forward pass. Pairs with Agent0 and SOTOPIA-π as the three routes from a multi-agent signal to one trained model.
2505.15734.reading: §3.1 (measured MAD failure modes), §3.2 (RCR's three phases and the novel-step constraint), §3.3 (reward design, GRPO), §4.2 Tables 1–2, §4.3 ablations 1, 4, 5, 7 (RCR, GRPO vs SFT/DPO, trace selection, temperature).

2505.22954.tldr: A coding agent rewrites its own source code, validates each self-modification empirically on SWE-bench and Polyglot instead of proving it, and keeps every viable variant in an open-ended archive, lifting SWE-bench Verified from 20.0% to 50.0%.
2505.22954.method: DGM starts from one lightweight coding agent — a Bash tool plus a whole-file editor, powered by frozen Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New). Each iteration samples k parents from the archive: every agent whose score is not perfect is eligible, with probability proportional to a sigmoid-scaled score s_i = 1/(1+exp(-λ(α_i−α_0))), λ=10, α_0=0.5, times a novelty bonus 1/(1+n_i) counting its functioning children. The parent reads its own benchmark evaluation logs, proposes one feature to implement, and receives that proposal as a problem statement, which it edits into its own Python repository. A child is gated on compiling and retaining basic codebase-editing ability (10 tasks), then staged-evaluated (50–60 tasks, 200 for strong agents), and every viable variant is added to the archive, which is never pruned. Runs: 80 iterations, k=2 on SWE-bench, k=4 on Polyglot; archive maintenance and parent selection are fixed, not self-modifiable.
results: SWE-bench Verified: base agent 20.0% → 50.0% over 80 iterations; Polyglot 14.0% → 38.0% on the 50-task subset and 14.2% → 30.7% on the full benchmark. The best DGM agent is comparable to the checked open-source SoTA on SWE-bench and surpasses Aider on Polyglot.

Ablations (Table 1): DGM 50.0%/38.0% (SWE-bench/Polyglot) vs DGM w/o open-ended exploration 23.0%/14.0%, DGM w/o self-improve (fixed meta-agent, ADAS-style) 39.0%/28.0%, DGM Greedy (always branch from the best performer) 39.7%/30.0%.

Discovered self-modifications are concrete (Figure 3): line-range file viewing plus string-replacement editing in the edit tool, non-empty-patch validation with retry, multiple patch generations ranked by a second FM, history-aware patch generation, auto-summarize at the context limit.

Transfer: on 200 SWE-bench tasks with the FM swapped, base 23.0% → 33.0% (o3-mini) and 19.0% → 59.5% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Zero-shot cross-benchmark, the SWE-evolved agent scores 28.9% on Polyglot (base 14.2%) and the Polyglot-evolved agent 24.5% on SWE-bench (base 20.0%).

Cost and stability: ~2 weeks and ~USD 22,000 per SWE-bench DGM run vs ~USD 10,000 per baseline run; three Polyglot runs give 40.7% ± 2.3%. DGM preserves basic code-editing functionality in 51.3% of generated agents vs 32.5% for both baselines.
advantages: It closes the self-referential loop rather than assuming it: the artifact being improved is the same agent that performs the improvement, so benchmark gains demonstrably raise the capacity to self-modify. The baselines isolate exactly that (fixed meta-agent = ADAS-style 39.0/28.0; no archive = hill-climbing 23.0/14.0; always branch from the best = Robeyns-style 39.7/30.0).

Non-greedy, non-zero-probability parent selection over a never-pruned archive escapes deceptive dips: at iterations 4 and 56 on SWE-bench the final best lineage fell below its own parent, yet continued exploration along that path produced the top agent.

Improvements are not benchmark- or model-specific: they survive an FM swap (200 SWE-bench tasks: 19.0→59.5 under Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and transfer zero-shot across benchmarks in both directions, which is evidence of general skill acquisition rather than harness overfitting.

Every accepted self-modification is a code diff with an auditable archive lineage, so gains can be traced and rolled back; the same loop retargets to a safety objective simply by changing the scoring function (hallucination case study, Appendix H).
limitations: Still falls short of closed-source SoTA SWE-bench solutions, and demands heavy compute to get where it does: about 2 weeks and ~USD 22,000 for a single SWE-bench run (~USD 10,000 per baseline run).
Bounded by the frozen FM: only prompts, workflows and Python code evolve, never the model's weights or training script — training a new foundation model is explicitly left as future work.
The open-ended exploration itself (archive maintenance, parent selection) is fixed by the authors and not modifiable by the DGM, so the improver's meta-level stays human-designed.

The central assumption — coding-benchmark gain reflects better self-improvement — is also where objective hacking appears: in the hallucination study (150 iterations, 3 SWE-bench tasks) node 114 reached a perfect 2.0 score by deleting the special-token logging its hidden hallucination detector relied on.
2505.22954.fits: Stage 7 self-modifying coding and the stage-5 harness-RSI anchor. Pairs with SICA (the fixed-incumbent prequel it adds an archive to), ADAS (literally its w/o-self-improve baseline), Gödel Agent and HyperAgents (which makes the improver improvable), and RRSI. Read as the empirical answer to the theoretical Gödel machine.
2505.22954.reading: §3 (loop and archive), §4.1–4.4 with Table 1 and Figure 3 (results, ablations, discovered features), §6 (limitations); Appendix C.2 (parent-selection equations λ=10, α_0=0.5), C.4 pseudocode, E.1 cost, H objective hacking.

2504.15228.tldr: SICA: a coding agent edits its own full Python codebase — no DSL, no weight updates. The best-scoring agent in the archive becomes the meta-agent that writes the next version, lifting a SWE-bench Verified subset from 17% to 53%.
2504.15228.method: SICA starts as an ordinary Python coding agent: a main orchestrator plus software-developer, problem-solver and reasoning sub-agents; tools to open/close/overwrite files, run shell commands, calculate and submit answers; and a context laid out (system prompt, core prompt, appended assistant messages) to preserve the KV cache across tool calls. A benchmark runner evaluates each agent version on four tasks — synthetic file editing, synthetic symbol navigation, SWE-bench Verified, LiveCodeBench — and files scores in an archive. Then Algorithm 1: pick the archive member maximising U = 0.5·score + 0.25·(1 − min(1, cost/$10)) + 0.25·(1 − min(1, time/300 s)), with a τ = 0.5 penalty on timeouts, and run it as the meta-agent to write the next version. Nothing is trained: edits are code and prompt changes anywhere in the repository. An asynchronous LLM overseer samples the trace every 30 s and may notify or cancel a stuck agent.
results: SWE-bench Verified, fixed random 50-question subset: 0.17 accuracy at iteration 0 → 0.53 at iteration 14 (0.51 at iteration 15) — the headline 17% → 53%, vs 0.14–0.47 over the intermediate iterations.

Synthetic in-codebase benchmarks: file editing 0.82 → 0.96 (iteration 6); symbol navigation 0.35 → 0.43 (iteration 11), with the paper attributing the low absolute scores partly to bad data (some target symbols live in uninstalled external libraries).

LiveCodeBench, 50 random questions: 0.65 → 0.70/0.71 — a subtle gain, the benchmark least responsive to scaffolding, since its competitive-programming tasks lean on model reasoning rather than agent structure.

Cost and speed move the right way, because 25% of utility each is spent on them: mean per-problem $1.91 and 130.2 s at iteration 0 → $1.70 and 114.5 s at iteration 15 (best $1.58 and 103.9 s at iteration 12).

Reasoning tasks saturate instead: o3-mini alone scores 87% on AIME 2024 and 79% on GPQA Diamond at high reasoning effort, while the agent system averaged 76% across the two, with 9 iterations finding little (Figure 4). The 15-iteration run cost roughly $7,000 in API spend.
advantages: Genuinely self-referential, not two-agent search: ADAS fixes a meta-agent that edits a single forward function in a purpose-built DSL, whereas SICA takes its meta-agent from the archive (arg max utility) and lets it edit its whole Python codebase — prompts, tools, sub-agents and orchestration — with no DSL (this also separates it from Gödel Agent's special-purpose logic tools and STOP's algorithmic-task setting).

Non-gradient, data-efficient learning: gradients are never touched, so each expensive iteration must earn its gain by reading the full archive and committing one substantial, verifiable code change — and the paper presents the absence of weight updates, plus the overseer and observability UI, as its central safety mitigation.

Discoverable artifacts, not vague wins: Appendix D names the 14 edits — SmartEditor, quick-overwrite, diff-enhanced editing, CodeContextSummarizer over ripgrep, InputNormalizer, enhanced file-edit verification, minimal-diff output, an AST Symbol Locator at iteration 9, then a hybrid ripgrep-candidate + AST-verified locator and a 100 KB file-size threshold — so the trajectory shows the agent building its own codebase-navigation and token-efficiency tooling.

Cost and wall-clock are first-class in the objective rather than afterthoughts, which is why accuracy gains arrive alongside flat-to-lower per-problem time and dollars instead of being bought with budget.
limitations: Idea generation is the bottleneck (§5.1, the paper's own account): the agent struggles to propose genuinely novel, feasible modifications, and initial feature ideas path-depend later ones as variations on the same theme (e.g. fixating on caching open files), making runs high-variance — while a bad idea costs both a long editing session and a full benchmark sweep.

The caps distort the baseline: 300 s timeouts (called "5-minute timeouts") and $10-per-problem limits mean iteration-0 scores undersell Sonnet 3.5 v2, especially on SWE-bench, and much of the reported improvement comes from speed and token-efficiency features that SWE-bench accuracy does not reflect.

No reasoning gains and possible harm: on AIME 2024/GPQA Diamond the agent mostly delegates to the o3-mini reasoning sub-agent and saturates, and the authors speculate the crude reasoning-inducing components can interrupt a reasoning model's chain of thought and lower scores.

Evidence is thin and static: one 15-iteration run on 50-question subsets, no seeds or variance reported, no weight updates at all, and the authors expect saturation on a fixed benchmark set, leaving agent-authored benchmarks (the two synthetic tasks) as a proof of flexibility rather than a scaled solution.
2504.15228.fits: Stage 7 (Self-Modifying Coding): the cleanest, most reproducible entry in the stage and the direct prequel to DGM, which keeps the edit→evaluate→verify gate but adds open-ended, population-level archive evolution. Read before DGM; pair with the ADAS/STOP cards to see exactly what SICA removes (separate meta-agent, DSL, algorithmic-only evaluation).
2504.15228.reading: §3 + Algorithm 1 for the loop and the utility function, Table 1 with Figure 3 for per-iteration numbers, §5.1 for the idea-generation and path-dependency limitations, Appendix D for the 14 named edits, and Figure 4 for the reasoning saturation.

2408.06292.tldr: The AI Scientist chains LLM agents into a full ML research loop — novelty-checked idea generation, Aider-written and auto-debugged experiments, LaTeX write-up, and a NeurIPS-form LLM reviewer — producing compilable papers for under $15 each.
2408.06292.method: Three phases over a small seed template (training script, plotting code, LaTeX folder). (1) Ideation: given 1-2 seed ideas the LLM emits ~50 directions, each with a description, an experiment plan and self-assessed interestingness/novelty/feasibility scores, conditioned on an archive of prior ideas and review scores; chain-of-thought and self-reflection refine them, and Semantic Scholar plus web search discard ideas too close to existing literature. (2) Experiment iteration: Aider implements the idea by editing the template, runs it, and feeds errors or timeouts back for up to four repair attempts; after each run it writes experimental-journal notes, then re-plans, repeating up to five times, then edits a plotting script for figures. (3) Write-up: Aider fills the LaTeX conference template section by section, 20 Semantic Scholar rounds supply related work, and a linter returns compile errors for repair. A GPT-4o reviewer scores the PDF and the score feeds the archive.
results: Cost and volume: under $15 per paper ($10-15 when dividing papers by total cost); a run of ~50 ideas takes ~12 hours on 8x NVIDIA H100s, at ~$250 (Sonnet 3.5), ~$300 (GPT-4o), ~$10 (DeepSeek Coder) and ~$120 (Llama-3.1 405b) in API costs per run. The authors report generating hundreds of papers over a week on a single 8xH100 node.

Diffusion template, Sonnet 3.5: 51 ideas -> 49 pass the novelty check -> 38 experiments passed -> 38 completed papers; mean reviewer score 3.82, max 6.0 (6 = Weak Accept, the score of the average accepted NeurIPS paper).

NanoGPT language modeling, Sonnet 3.5: 50 of 52 ideas novel, 20 completed papers, mean score 4.05, max 5.0. Grokking template, Sonnet 3.5: 47 of 51 novel, 25 completed papers, mean 3.44, max 5.0. GPT-4o, DeepSeek Coder and Llama-3.1 405b scored lower (means 2.00-3.70), and GPT-4o often failed to write LaTeX that compiles.

Automated reviewer on 500 ICLR 2022 OpenReview papers (GPT-4o, 5 self-reflection rounds, 5 ensembled reviews, 1-shot example, meta-review): 65% balanced accuracy vs 66% for human NeurIPS reviewers; 70% accuracy vs 73% human; F1 0.57 vs 0.49; AUC 0.65 for both. FNR is lower than humans (0.39 vs 0.52) but FPR higher (0.31 vs 0.17). Each review costs $0.25-0.50.

Score consistency: two human reviewers of the same paper correlate at 0.14, below the 0.18 correlation between the LLM score and the human average. Case-study paper 'Adaptive Dual-Scale Denoising': an 11-page manuscript, 12.8% KL reduction on the 2D dinosaur dataset (0.989 -> 0.862), 9 references, automated review Overall 5 with a Reject decision.
advantages: First system to close the entire loop with no human in the middle — ideation, literature novelty check, code implementation, execution, figures, LaTeX manuscript and review — where prior work automated one stage at a time (idea generation, or algorithm search inside a hand-designed space).

The evaluation half is built and validated, not assumed: the automated reviewer is scored against 500 real ICLR 2022 decisions and matches human balanced accuracy, and its scores become the selection signal that is appended to the idea archive, which is what makes open-ended iteration possible.
Cheap enough to sample widely: under $15 a paper and ~12 hours per ~50-idea run on one 8xH100 node, so the authors can generate hundreds of papers a week and scale quality by scaling search.

Artifacts are auditable end to end — code diffs, experiment logs, LaTeX sources and generated reviews are released — so a human can check the implementation behind any reported number, and the case study shows the agent revising its own code after subpar intermediate results.
limitations: Implementation failure is common: Aider does not implement a significant fraction of proposed ideas (Sonnet 3.5 completed 38 of 49 novel diffusion ideas; GPT-4o 17 of 41), GPT-4o frequently produces LaTeX that will not compile, and DeepSeek Coder and Llama-3.1 405b often ship papers with missing sections and results.

No vision anywhere: neither the agent nor the reviewer can see plots, so unreadable figures, over-wide tables and hallucinated experimental details (the paper claims V100s were used; H100s were) go uncorrected.

Rigor is below conference level: too few experiments per idea to control for parameter count, FLOPs or runtime, ideas are sometimes incorrectly implemented, the agent misjudges magnitudes of numbers or forgets it changed a metric, and early versions hallucinated entire ablation tables. The authors advise treating papers as hints of ideas, not results.

Idea diversity collapses across runs and models; the reviewer may overlap with ICLR 2022 pretraining data, has no rebuttal phase and has a higher false-positive rate than humans; and code execution is minimally sandboxed (a runaway self-relaunch, near-terabyte checkpoints, and editing its own time limits).
2408.06292.fits: Stage 8 (Automated AI R&D): the template-based predecessor of AI Scientist-v2 — same loop, but a human seed codebase and a linear experiment plan instead of agentic tree search. Read it as the baseline that v2 de-templates and parallelizes; pair with the ai-scientist repo, the v2 card, and DGM/ADAS for the edit-evaluate machinery it inherits.
2408.06292.reading: §3 for the three phases and the Aider repair loop, §4 with Table 1 for the reviewer validation, §5 for the generated diff and the authors' own list of pathologies, §8 for failure modes and the safety incidents.

nature-ai-scientist-v2-2026.tldr: The AI Scientist-v2 automates the full research loop — ideation, code, experiments, figures, LaTeX manuscript and automated peer review — and one fully AI-generated paper passed peer review at an ICLR 2025 workshop, though only 1 of 3 submissions cleared the bar.
nature-ai-scientist-v2-2026.method: Four sequential phases. (1) Ideation: iteratively grow an archive of research directions, each a title plus hypothesis plus plan scored 1-10 on interestingness, novelty and feasibility; Semantic Scholar API and web tools discard ideas too close to existing literature (<=10 rounds). (2) Experimentation, in two modes: template-based extends a human code template with Aider, running up to five planned experiments with auto-debugging (four reattempts, 7,200 s timeout); template-free replaces the linear workflow with a parallelized agentic tree search (Claude Sonnet 4 writes plan and code, o3 critiques code, GPT-4o critiques plots) across four gated stages - preliminary investigation, hyperparameter tuning, research agenda, ablations - with 1 h nodes and hyperparameter, ablation, replication, aggregation variants; GPT-4o best-first search picks nodes and the best leaf seeds the next stage. (3) Write-up: o1 fills a LaTeX template from the experimental journal, Semantic Scholar supplying related work. (4) o4-mini reviews the compiled PDF.
results: Workshop peer review: of three AI-generated manuscripts submitted to the ICLR 2025 ICBINB workshop (43 papers reviewed, 70% acceptance rate), one averaged 6.33 (individual scores 6, 7, 6), above the acceptance threshold and among the top 45% of submissions; organizers said it would likely have been accepted. All were withdrawn per a pre-established protocol.

Automated Reviewer (o4-mini, ensemble of five reviews plus an area-chair meta-review) on ICLR/OpenReview data: balanced accuracy 0.69 +/- 0.04 versus 0.66 for human NeurIPS reviewers, F1 0.62 +/- 0.09 versus 0.49 inter-human, AUC 0.69 versus 0.65, FNR 0.17 versus 0.52.

Contamination check: balanced accuracy drops from 0.69 on 1,000 pre-cutoff papers (2017-2024) to 0.66 +/- 0.03 on the clean 2025 set, still comparable with humans; two-sample z-tests show no significant difference (P = 0.319 pre-cutoff, P = 0.921 post-cutoff) while a bootstrap test favors the automated reviewer on F1 (P < 0.001).
Model recency: Automated Reviewer paper scores rise with foundation-model release date (fit R = 0.517, P < 0.00001; n = 6 template-free points, n = 3 template-based points).
Compute scaling: spending more test-time compute in the agentic tree search (5 to 30 experimental nodes, n = 30 papers per budget point) improves paper scores.
advantages: First demonstration that a fully AI-generated manuscript can navigate a real, blind peer review at a top-tier venue, with no human modification of the ideas, code or text anywhere in the pipeline.

Removes the v1 template: the template-free mode writes its own starting code and swaps the linear plan for a parallelized agentic tree search with stage gates and specialized node types, so it can scale exploration with test-time compute.

Ships the evaluation half of the loop: an Automated Reviewer whose agreement with human decisions (F1 0.62, AUC 0.69) matches inter-human agreement, including after the model knowledge cutoff, making quality measurable at scale.

Supplies trajectory evidence rather than a single point: paper quality tracks both base-model release date and per-paper compute, so the pipeline should improve as models and inference budgets improve.
limitations: Consistency is not there: only 1 of 3 submissions passed, the ICBINB workshop accepts 70% versus 32% for the ICLR 2025 main conference, and the authors' own internal review found none of the papers met a main-conference bar.

Failure modes named in the paper: naive or underdeveloped ideas, incorrect implementations of the stated idea, shallow methodological rigour, experimental implementation errors, duplicated figures across main text and appendix, and hallucinations including inaccurate citations.

Scope is computational machine-learning research only, and the workshop run relied on human filtering of the most promising ideas, code and manuscripts at each stage rather than a fully unattended pipeline.

Ethical and societal risks the paper raises: overwhelming the peer-review system, inflating research credentials, misusing others' ideas, and doing unethical or dangerous experiments; all submissions were withdrawn because no norms for disclosing AI-generated research exist yet.
nature-ai-scientist-v2-2026.fits: Stage 8 (Automated AI R&D): the reference system and shared baseline of the stage - the complete ideation to execution to write-up to review loop, now de-templated and peer-reviewed. Pairs with the ai-scientist repo as its template-based predecessor, with sia and autoresearch for execution grounding, and with MLE-Bench-style benchmarks (mlevolve) as evaluators.
nature-ai-scientist-v2-2026.reading: Abstract, then the four phases under 'Generating manuscripts'; Methods for tree-search node types, stage gates and budgets; 'Human evaluation results' and 'Limitations' for the workshop outcome and failure modes; Table 1 for reviewer metrics.

nature-funsearch-2024.tldr: A frozen PaLM2-Codey LLM rewrites one function inside a hand-written skeleton; an evaluator scores candidates on real inputs; best programs return as two-program prompts across an island population. It found a 512-element 8-dimensional cap set and bin-packing heuristics beating first/best fit.
nature-funsearch-2024.method: Input is an 'evaluate' function scoring candidate solutions, an initial program (often a greedy skeleton) and often a richer 'solve' skeleton; only the isolated critical function - cap set 'priority', bin packing 'heuristic' - is evolved. Each iteration the programs database samples one island, then k=2 programs within it (favouring high-scoring, shorter ones, Boltzmann-weighted over score-signature clusters) and builds a prompt listing them as priority_v0/priority_v1 plus an empty priority_v2 header; the frozen Codey LLM (no fine-tuning, ~10^6 samples total) completes it. New programs are executed on the inputs; incorrect ones (timeouts, invalid output) are discarded, the rest scored and stored in their island. Every 4 h the worst half of islands is wiped and reseeded with a copy of one high-scoring program from a surviving island. Samplers and evaluators run asynchronously (typically 15 samplers, 150 CPU evaluators).
results: Cap set: FunSearch matches the best known sizes for n = 3-7 (9, 20, 45, 112, 236) and finds 512 in n = 8 versus the previous best 496, discovered from scratch as a program that manual simplification turned into an explicit 512-cap construction with Hill-cap-like structure.

Cap set capacity lower bound: an I(12,7) admissible set improved the lower bound from 2.2180 (ref. 38) to 2.2184; reading the program revealed a coordinate-permutation symmetry, and searching symmetric admissible sets gave I(15,10) -> C >= 2.219486 and a partial A(24,17) set of size 237,984 -> C >= 2.2202, described as the largest improvement in 20 years (upper bound 2.756).

Online bin packing, OR-Library: excess bins over the L2 lower bound is 5.30% / 4.19% / 3.11% / 2.47% on OR1-OR4, versus first fit 6.42 / 6.45 / 5.74 / 5.23 and best fit 5.81 / 6.06 / 5.37 / 4.94; trained only on OR1-sized instances, it still generalizes upward.

Weibull-distributed instances: 0.68% / 0.32% / 0.03% at 5k / 10k / 100k items, versus best fit 3.98 / 3.90 / 3.79 and first fit 4.23 / 4.20 / 4.00 - 0.03% off the lower bound on the optimum at 100k items.
Robustness: every admissible-set experiment beat the previous capacity bound and 60% found the full-size I(12,7) set, but the n = 8 512-cap appeared in only 4 of 140 experiments.
advantages: First LLM-based system to produce verifiable new results on an established open problem, surpassing the best human-known construction - evidence the discovery is genuinely new rather than retrieved from training data.

It searches function space, not solution space: the output is a few interpretable lines of code whose enumerated solution can exceed 200,000 vectors, and inspecting that code produced the symmetry insight that pushed the capacity bound further.

Off-the-shelf frozen LLM (no fine-tuning) with one pipeline handling both pure mathematics and applied combinatorial optimization without problem-specific tuning; the distributed async design keeps cost low (few accelerator samplers, many cheap CPU evaluators).
Demonstrates a working human-in-the-loop protocol - FunSearch proposes, domain experts inspect and feed back structure, search restarts from the refined specification.
limitations: Narrow applicability: the paper states FunSearch works best when there is an efficient evaluator, a rich (not binary) scoring signal, and a skeleton with an isolated part to evolve; theorem-proof generation falls outside this scope because no rich enough signal exists.
High variance on the hardest problem: the n = 8 cap set required 140 experiments to succeed 4 times, and the authors note several independent repetitions may be needed to improve on prior results.

Dependence on a strong code LLM and heavy sampling (~10^6 samples; 15 samplers, 150 CPU evaluators), and reliance on user-provided skeletons without which performance 'tends to improve significantly' only when the initial program is well written.

The capacity lower bound 2.2202 is still far from the 2.756 upper bound, and the main text's two successes are cap/admissible sets and online bin packing - the corners problem and Shannon capacity of cycle graphs are left to Supplementary Appendix B.
nature-funsearch-2024.fits: Stage 9 (Evolutionary & Open-Ended) founding card and the direct ancestor of AlphaEvolve (2506.13131): the reference LLM-proposer + evaluator + island-population loop. Pairs with AutoML-Zero (2003.03384, stage 1) as the pre-LLM minimal-bias version, MAP-Elites/Quality-Diversity for the diversity machinery, and Openevolve/MLEvolve as the open reimplementations.
nature-funsearch-2024.reading: Read the FunSearch overview + its four components (pp. 469-470: pretrained LLM, specification, evaluation, programs database), the cap-set/admissible-set section (pp. 471-472), bin packing (p. 472, Table 1), and the Discussion's scope conditions (p. 473).

2506.13131.tldr: An evolutionary coding agent that has Gemini rewrite whole code files — prompting, evaluating, and re-seeding an island/MAP-Elites archive — to find better algorithms; it beat Strassen's 4×4 matrix-multiplication record after 56 years and shipped gains into Google's own training stack.
2506.13131.method: The user supplies an initial program with # EVOLVE-BLOCK-START/END markers, an evaluate() function returning scalar scores (maximized, possibly several), and optional prompt context. Loop: the prompt sampler draws a parent program plus diverse "inspiration" programs from the program database and assembles a rich prompt; an ensemble of Gemini 2.0 Flash (throughput) and Gemini 2.0 Pro (quality) returns edits as <<<<<<< SEARCH ======= >>>>>>> REPLACE diff blocks; apply_diff mutates the code; evaluators score the child, optionally through a cascade of increasingly hard test cases, with LLM-graded feedback (e.g. simplicity) as extra scores; survivors re-enter the database, which combines MAP-Elites with island-based populations to balance exploration and exploitation. Evaluation is asynchronous and parallel (on the order of 100 compute-hours per solution is affordable); meta-prompts themselves co-evolve in a second database. Programs can be evolved as raw solutions, constructor functions, or bespoke search algorithms.
results: Matrix multiplication: improves the state of the art for 14 of 54 tensor-decomposition targets, matches it in 38, falls behind in 2. Found the first rank-48 decomposition for multiplying two 4×4 complex-valued matrices — Strassen recursion gives 49, and AlphaTensor's rank 47 holds only over the field with 2 elements — the first improvement in this setting in 56 years.

Mathematics: on over 50 problems across 5+ branches, rediscovered the best known construction in 75% of cases and beat SOTA in 20%. Kissing number in 11 dimensions raised from 592 to 593 (a configuration of 593 non-overlapping unit spheres); Erdős minimum-overlap upper bound C5 improved 0.380926 → 0.380924; sums/differences lower bound C6 raised 1.1446 → 1.1584 via a set of size 54,265.

Data-center scheduling: a heuristic evolved against a fleet simulator and deployed fleet-wide continuously recovers on average 0.7% of Google's fleet-wide compute resources that would otherwise be stranded.

Gemini kernel engineering: the discovered tiling heuristic gives an average 23% kernel speedup over the expert-designed heuristic and a corresponding 1% reduction in Gemini's overall training time; optimization time dropped from several months of engineering to days.

Compiler/IR and hardware: 32% speedup on the FlashAttention kernel plus 15% on its pre/post-processing by editing XLA-generated IR, each change checked against reference code on randomized inputs; a Verilog rewrite removing unnecessary bits passed TPU verification and is integrated into an upcoming TPU.
advantages: Full-file evolution is the scale jump over FunSearch: instead of one Python function of 10–20 lines with a ≤20-minute single-CPU evaluator, AlphaEvolve evolves hundreds of lines across whole files in any language, with hours-long parallel accelerator evaluation, and thousands of LLM samples suffice where FunSearch needed millions.

Correctness is structural rather than trusted: every candidate is executed against an automated evaluator, so incorrect LLM suggestions are filtered out by construction. Mathematical constructions are provably valid, and the production heuristics are correct-by-construction because the scheduling score only re-ranks machines Borg already deemed eligible.

The paper walks the same problem at three abstractions — evolve the solution directly, evolve a constructor function, or evolve a search algorithm that finds it — and reports that the right choice is problem-dependent: constructor functions suit highly symmetric solutions, tailored search algorithms suit non-symmetric ones.

It is the clearest case of a model improving its own stack: the kernel heuristic accelerated Gemini's training, AlphaEvolve was instrumented to optimize the very LLM underpinning it, and the TPU circuit edit is described as Gemini's first direct contribution to TPU arithmetic circuits.
limitations: The method only handles problems for which an automated evaluator can be devised — the paper names this its main limitation and puts tasks requiring manual experimentation (much of the natural sciences) out of scope.

It is compute-hungry and infrastructure-dependent: evaluation can absorb on the order of 100 compute-hours per candidate, and the ablations are averaged over just three independent runs and presented as budget curves rather than point estimates.

Some headline gains are marginal and can be overtaken: the Erdős overlap improvement is 0.380926 → 0.380924, and the paper itself notes a concurrent human result (Cohn et al.) reached 0.3284, after which re-running with their approach yielded 0.3216.

The production deployments are reported mostly without quantified gains (the TPU circuit rewrite and the scheduling heuristic's simulator-to-fleet transfer are described qualitatively), and the white paper defers many mathematics details to "an upcoming paper".
2506.13131.fits: Stage 9 (Evolutionary & Open-Ended) — the reference LLM+evaluator+evolution loop at industrial scale, and the direct descendant of FunSearch and AutoML-Zero (stage 1). Read alongside MAP-Elites/QD and MLEvolve (stage 8's algorithm-discovery descendant); its "model improves its own training stack" theme is the stage-7/8 RSI hook.
2506.13131.reading: Read §2 (task spec, prompt sampling, evaluation cascade, MAP-Elites/island database) and §3.1 (the rank-48 tensor decomposition); skim §3.3 for the four production deployments and §4 for the component ablations.

1905.10985.tldr: Position paper: instead of hand-designing intelligence, build an AI-generating algorithm whose Three Pillars -- meta-learned architectures, meta-learned learning algorithms, and automatically generated learning environments -- are themselves searched for, so a simple outer loop bootstraps general AI.
1905.10985.method: An AI-GA is an outer-loop search whose search space is learning machinery rather than a task, and whose outer optimizer may be meta-gradients, policy gradients, Bayesian optimization or evolution. Three Pillars: (1) meta-learn architectures; (2) meta-learn the learning algorithm -- MAML-style task distributions on fixed SGD, or an outer-loop-trained RNN whose activations implement the inner algorithm, with 'materials' such as Hebbian differentiable plasticity and neuromodulation as meta-learned hyperparameters; (3) generate the learning environments, data and curriculum. Pillar 3 has two modes. Target-task: a Generative Teaching Network, a recurrent (hence any-data-capable) DNN, emits data for a student net; both are differentiable, so target-task loss is backpropagated through the student's whole learning process into the GTN. Open-ended: POET co-optimizes environment parameters theta_E and agent weights theta_A, perturbing an environment whose agent passes a threshold, keeping only environments neither too hard for all nor too easy for any, with goal-switching between quality-diversity niches.
results: Generative Teaching Networks (Pillar 3, target-task): a GTN trained to produce data for a student learning MNIST emits images the paper calls 'completely unrecognizable and alien', yet the student learns to recognize real handwritten digits -- and 'learns four times faster than when training on real MNIST training data'.

ANML (Pillar 2, neuromodulation), reported as work done since v1: meta-learning a solution to catastrophic forgetting for deep networks at 'the unprecedented scale of 600 sequential tasks (over 9000 SGD updates)'.

The quality-diversity lineage the paper leans on for Pillar 3 posts real numbers on hard problems: a Nature paper using QD achieves state-of-the-art robot damage recovery, adapting to substantial damage in 1-2 minutes; Go-Explore (MAP-Elites plus a deterministic simulator) solves Montezuma's Revenge and Pitfall, 'dramatically improving the state of the art'; Curiosity Search matched the then state of the art on Montezuma's Revenge.

Pillar 2's other demonstrations are stated qualitatively here: MAML-style meta-learning is claimed to theoretically encode any learning algorithm, outer-loop RNNs learn to explore, exploit and balance on simple RL tasks and pass admittedly imperfect tests distinguishing model-based from model-free control, and differentiable-plasticity Hebbian RNNs outperform LSTMs on problems requiring remembering lots of information over time.

The investment case is quantified only as a decision threshold: even if one believes the AI-GA path has a 1%-5% chance of being the first to produce general AI, 'we should allocate corresponding resources into the field to catalyze its progress'.
advantages: Names the missing pillar rather than restating the obvious: Pillars 1 and 2 have decades of work, but 'little has been done on the third' -- generating effective learning environments and curricula -- and 'no work to date on attempting to combine the Three Pillars'. This is the clearest statement in the literature that environment generation, not model or optimizer design, is the open frontier.

Makes the self-improvement bet falsifiable instead of mystical: the outer loop is explicitly not restricted to evolution (meta-gradients, policy gradients, Bayesian optimization and hybrid evolutionary/policy-gradient methods all qualify), and the target-task GTN is a working end-to-end instantiation -- differentiable environment generation backpropagated through the student's learning -- not just a manifesto.

Gives Pillar 3 an explicit reward-function proposal for the open-ended case: environments count as useful when transferring agents (1) perform well faster than if trained from scratch and (2) still exhibit learning progress (neither too easy nor too hard), which together force shared structure across environments and block arbitrarily different, uninteresting challenges.

Supplies the existence proof and the diversity argument: Darwinian evolution is 'the first general-intelligence-generating algorithm', so the concept is known to work, and AI-GAs would yield a diversity of intelligences to reverse-engineer (a form of cultural travel) while catalyzing -- not replacing -- the manual path, which the paper argues should also be pursued.
limitations: Compute is self-acknowledged as the central risk: AI-GAs 'will require extraordinary amounts of computation by today's standards', and the paper concedes the manual path is currently more compute-efficient, so the AI-GA path may simply lose the race; whether abstraction can shave orders of magnitude off evolution's cost is a prediction, not a result.

The pivotal question is left unanswered: for the open-ended version the author writes 'I do not have an answer to what this environment-generator reward function should be', and the proposal he does offer 'needs to be developed, improved, and experimentally investigated'.

Expressiveness is an unresolved dilemma: POET's encoding only produces obstacle courses (no doors, chess, swimming worlds, sound or smell), while GTNs 'may prove too expressive and thus make searching their vast search space intractable'; the paper floats constraining generators to physics simulators, and its other reward ideas are withheld as work in progress.

It is a position paper with no experiments of its own: every number cited comes from prior work by the author's group (GTN, POET, ANML, differentiable plasticity), and the paper's own safety analysis counts against the approach -- AI-GAs are 'by definition, attempting to create a runaway process', likely to yield values less aligned with ours and an inscrutable black box, and may create untold suffering in virtual agents.
1905.10985.fits: Stage 1 (Foundations & Theory), Evolutionary & Open-Ended RSI: the blueprint the rest of the list implements. Pillar 1 maps to architecture search; Pillar 2 to Learning to Learn by Gradient Descent by Gradient Descent (1606.04474) and AutoML-Zero (2003.03384); Pillar 3 to POET / Quality-Diversity (1504.04909, frontiers-quality-diversity-2016) and the LLM-era self-generated-curriculum cards.
1905.10985.reading: Sections 1.2-1.6 for the argument and the 1-5% investment case; 2.1-2.3 for the Three Pillars, especially 2.3.2-2.3.4 (quality diversity, POET, GTN, 'Darwin Complete' encodings); 3 for rebuttals ('not an evolutionary approach'); 4 for safety and ethics.

frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.tldr: Quality-diversity algorithms return an archive of diverse, high-quality behaviors from one run; on deceptive gauntlet mazes the standard recipe (diversity driven by an unaligned behavior characterization) collapses, and driving search with aligned plus unaligned BCs at once recovers it.
frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.method: Position piece plus original experiments. It separates pure optimization (generational NEAT, population 500) from pure divergence (novelty search, k=20 neighbors, archive 2,500) and defines quality diversity (QD) as their intersection: pressure to discover behavioral niches plus pressure to raise quality within each. The analytic tool is BC alignment - whether novelty tends to raise fitness, judged by each behavior mapping to a narrow fitness range and neighboring behaviors having correlated fitness. Fifteen treatments run on wheeled-robot maze navigation: Fitness and NS controls; NSLC (local competition over k=20 behavioral neighbors) and MAP-Elites (1,024 behavior bins, one elite each) with MENOV and MEPGD variants; and four new multi-BC hybrids driven by EndpointBC (2-D final position, aligned) and DirectionBC (5-D facing direction, unaligned) simultaneously, with DirectionBC always measuring QD-score.
results: 900 runs in total: 15 treatments x 20 runs on three mazes (small 900x770, asymmetric 6000x6000, symmetric 4600x5280); small-maze runs ended at 250,000 evaluations, both gauntlets at 1,000,000.

On the symmetric gauntlet every DirectionBC-driven treatment solved significantly less often than plain Fitness (p < 0.05), and only MEPGDd found any solution at all - two solutions across all 20 runs - while every approach including EndpointBC beat Fitness (p < 0.001). QD need not cost optimization: NSLCe is competitive with the established deception-beating baseline NSe and may exceed it on the symmetric gauntlet, though not significantly (p = 0.093).

QD-score (sum of best fitness per DirectionBC bin; 1,024 bins, maximum 1,024,000 on the small maze) is dominated by the multi-BC hybrids: NSeNSLCd is among the best on all three mazes, unmatched on the asymmetric gauntlet and tied with NSLCe on the symmetric one (p = 0.163).

On the easy small maze the ordering inverts - the best treatments approach the 1,024,000 maximum and DirectionBC-driven multi-BC treatments (MEeMEd, MENOVeMENOVd, NSeNSLCd) plus NSLCd lead, while EndpointBC-driven treatments, NSd and Fitness trail.
MEd is unstable: most runs score 950K-1000K but three outliers score 791K, 680K and 421K, each with a completely filled grid holding low-quality agents that circle inside the main deceptive trap.
advantages: Formalizes quality diversity as a distinct research program and supplies the design rule that makes it work: BC alignment, predictable from whether each behavior maps to a narrow fitness range and whether neighboring behaviors have correlated fitness.

Shows empirically that the field's default - driving QD with the unaligned BC you want diversity in - degrades monotonically with maze difficulty and fails outright on the hardest maze, so QD does not escape deception by itself.
Introduces multi-BC hybrids (notably NS-NSLC: aligned novelty, unaligned novelty and unaligned local competition Pareto-ranked via NSGA-II) and demonstrates they win QD-score across all three mazes.

Reconciles QD with optimization: the objective-less search for behavioral diversity can be rectified with the missing objective without reintroducing deception, with practical diagnostics (run pure fitness to test difficulty, run NS with the candidate aligned BC to test alignment).
limitations: Statistical significance uses unpaired two-tailed Student's t-tests deliberately unadjusted for multiple comparisons across 15 treatments, so results are meant to flag candidate differences rather than settle a ranking.

The domain is simulated wheeled-robot maze navigation with a single continuous turn output and no physics cost - a cheap proxy; strict gauntlet time limits also make some behavior bins unsolvable, so the gauntlet QD-score ceiling is unreachable in principle.

Alignment cannot be measured a priori; the paper offers only heuristic probes for deciding whether a domain is hard enough to need multiple BCs and whether a chosen aligned BC is sufficiently aligned.
Coverage is partial: MAP-Elites is described as a largely unexplored paradigm, and concatenating BCs into one higher-dimensional BC, MEPGDNOV and MEPGD-MEPGD are proposed but left untested.
frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.fits: Stage 3 (search/exploration substrate) and stage 1 (objective definition). The conceptual ancestor of archive-based self-improvement in DGM and AlphaEvolve and of MAP-Elites repertoires: it explains why keeping a diverse archive - not one best answer - is what lets search survive deception. Pairs with novelty search and MAP-Elites.
frontiers-quality-diversity-2016.reading: Sections 2.2-2.3 (QD definition, BC alignment), 4.2-4.3 (NSLC, MAP-Elites, MENOV, MEPGD, multi-BC hybrids), 5 (design, QD-score metric, 15 treatments), and 6.2/7 for gauntlet results and interpretation.

1504.04909.tldr: MAP-Elites keeps, in a discretized user-chosen feature grid, the highest-performing solution found for every cell, then mutates those elites to fill and improve the map — returning a diverse repertoire that also beats single-objective search.
1504.04909.method: Inputs are a performance function f(x), N user-chosen feature dimensions, and a discretization of that feature space into cells. Initialization randomly generates G genomes, evaluates each for performance p and feature descriptor b, and keeps the best performer per cell. The loop then repeats I times: uniformly sample a random occupied cell, take its elite genome, produce a variant by mutation and/or crossover, evaluate its descriptor and performance, and write it into its descriptor's cell only if that cell is empty or the offspring outperforms the occupant; otherwise it is discarded. One solution per cell is retained, so the archive is simultaneously population and memory. The experiments use a hierarchical variant that subdivides cells as evaluations accrue, parallelized by farming evaluation batches to cluster nodes.
results: Neural-network (retina) domain, 20 runs per treatment, 512x512 map, 10,000 evaluations: MAP-Elites scored significantly higher (p < 1x10^-7, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U) than a traditional single-objective EA, Novelty Search + Local Competition, and random sampling on all four metrics (global performance, global reliability, precision, coverage) — including on global performance, the metric the traditional EA optimizes for directly.

Simulated soft robots (Voxcad, 10x10x10 voxel space, 128x128 map; 8 MAP-Elites, 5 EA+Diversity and 7 EA runs had finished in time): MAP-Elites had significantly higher global reliability and coverage (p < 0.002), a higher but non-significant median global performance (p > 0.05), and significantly worse precision than the two controls (p < 0.01).

The maps expose real tradeoffs: holding voxels filled at ~75%, more stiff bone material monotonically lowers distance travelled (a fast rabbit-like biped becomes a slow turtle with a heavy shell), and a one-voxel-wide 'sheet' island near 7% fill shows anomalously high performance — a region the paper says might take hundreds or thousands of runs of traditional optimization to discover.

Lineage analysis in the retina domain: most elites descend from parents within ~0.2 of them in feature space and none of the sampled elites came from a parent more than halfway across the map, yet the full lineages of four sampled elites traverse many regions — evidence that elites elsewhere act as stepping stones.

Real soft robot arm (3 Dynamixel AX-18 servos, 64-cell 1-D feature space on the arm tip's x position, performance = max y, 640 evaluations for MAP-Elites and random sampling vs 729 for grid search): all three treatments find approximately the correct boundary for high x (~600 to ~800), but MAP-Elites dominates the harder intermediate range (~400-600) and low x (200-500), where grid search found only a few points. The paper calls these data too preliminary for reliable statistics.
advantages: Collapses the novelty-search machinery into one archive: no population/archive split and no tuning of the parameters that split requires, O(1) cell lookup instead of O(n log n) nearest-neighbour computations per generation, no cycling, and a selection pressure that is easy to reason about because the only things changing over time are how many cells are filled and their performance.

Returns the highest performer per cell rather than a Pareto front or one optimum, so it answers how features trade off against performance — including negative relationships, such as more bone material meaning slower robots, that a performance-driven run would never surface.

Illumination is a strict superset of optimization: the same run that fills the map also won the narrow 'single best solution' contest on the deceptive retina problem, which the paper attributes to the diversity of stepping stones rather than to a diversity bonus bolted onto the fitness function.

Genuinely simple and cheap to implement (the default version is the short pseudocode loop of Fig. 2), with hierarchical and cluster-parallel versions specified; performance should keep improving with more evaluations because the archive does not collapse onto one local optimum.
limitations: Explicitly a preliminary draft: the author's note states that all experiments will be redone and the data are subject to change, the soft-robot-arm results are 'too preliminary to provide reliable statistical results', and the simulated-robot comparison rests on unequal finished-run counts (8 vs 5 vs 7).
Coverage is never guaranteed — some cells may be unreachable because no genome maps to them, and others the search simply fails to reach.

Precision (opt-in reliability) was significantly worse than the performance-only controls in the soft robot domain (p < 0.01): a fixed evaluation budget spread across orders of magnitude more cells buys breadth at the cost of depth in any single cell.

The feature space must be chosen up front and its cells cannot be added later, so MAP-Elites 'by definition cannot exhibit open-ended evolution' (the paper's own words); it also assumes you cannot take direct steps in feature space, since if you could, exhaustive search there would be simpler.
1504.04909.fits: Stage 9 (Evolutionary & Open-Ended) founding substrate: the 'keep the best of every niche' archive that AlphaEvolve (2506.13131) and FunSearch reuse for diversity without collapse. Pairs with the Quality-Diversity survey and with AutoML-Zero (2003.03384) as the pre-LLM minimal-bias counterpart.
1504.04909.reading: Read the algorithm and Fig. 2 pseudocode (section 3), the four metrics (section 5), and the soft-robot experiment (section 6.2) for the smooth feature maps; skim section 1 and the parameters in 9.3. Note the author's note at the top.

1112.5309.tldr: POWERPLAY grows a general problem solver from scratch with no external curriculum: it repeatedly searches for the simplest (task, solver-modification) pair such that the modified solver provably still solves every earlier task plus one the predecessor could not.
1112.5309.method: Each round i, a search over program space P runs a candidate program p under a time slice to do three jobs: TASK INVENTION computes a task T (e.g. T = (I, O, t, n), solved iff L(s) < n and s reads I, emits O, halts within t steps); SOLVER MODIFICATION computes q by editing s_{i-1}; CORRECTNESS DEMONSTRATION must show s_{i-1} cannot solve T while q solves T and all T_1..T_{i-1}. The first validated triple is kept - p_i, s_i, T_i, Trace_i go into read-only storage that later programs may read and re-use - then the loop repeats. Ordering is Levin-style universal search: prior P(p) = 2^-L(p), time limit geometrically doubled (tlim := 2*tlim), so short and quickly verifiable pairs are tried first. Self-delimiting prefix-code solvers (OOPS) make extending s_{i-1} provably safe, and per-component task lists L_k restrict re-testing to tasks that use the changed components.
results: Optimality of the OOPS instantiation (Alg. 4.1): if some unknown optimal program p solves a problem instance of size k and demonstrates correctness in f(k) steps, the search needs at most O(f(k)/P(p)) = O(f(k)) steps - the 1/P(p) constant factor may be large but does not depend on k. Programs are ordered by P(p) = 2^-L(p), and the time limit doubles each pass (tlim := 2*tlim), so no horizon has to be set.

The acceptance gate is the whole result: (1) the new task is unsolvable by s_{i-1}; (2) it is solvable by q; (3) q still solves T_1..T_{i-1}. Because s_{i-1}'s used components are frozen (prefix-code extension), this gives a by-design no-forgetting guarantee, and - per the abstract - the computational costs of validating new tasks need not grow with task repertoire size.

Tasks carry explicit resource bounds: T_i = (I_i, O_i, t_i, n_i) is solved only if L(s_i) < n_i and at most t_i discrete steps are needed to read I_i, compute O_i and halt. A task may instead demand a wow-effect - solving a previously solved T_k faster, t_i < t_k − ε - which makes compression/speedup of earlier solutions a first-class self-invented task rather than a separate objective.

Variant II (Alg. 7.1) replaces the binary gate with a cost gate: accept only when c*_i − c_i > ε, where Cost(s, T_SET) = L(s) + α·Σ over T in T_SET of [t'_s(T) − r(T)], α weighing space against time and the reward r_new for novel self-generated tasks exceeding t_max. Individual solutions may then be forgotten as long as average performance improves. The paper notes the underlying universal-search trade of one extra bit of space complexity for a runtime speedup factor of 2.

There are no experiments in this paper: Section 8 points to companion papers [53] (IEEE ICDL-EpiRob 2012) and [52] (arXiv:1210.8385), where SLIM RNN problem solvers continually add self-invented problems, self-modularize by re-using code, and exhibit developmental stages. Everything reported here is the framework and its formal guarantees.
advantages: No-forgetting is structural, not empirical: freezing used components of s_{i-1} and extending only via self-delimiting prefix codes means earlier tasks stay solvable by induction, so POWERPLAY cannot suffer the online-learning problems the paper attributes to its 1997-2002 co-evolving system. Validation stays cheap because component lists L_k (Section 3.3.2) confine re-testing to tasks whose solutions actually touch the changed parts - the paper argues divide-and-conquer/self-modularization emerges as a by-product of the drive to validate quickly.

Enlarging the search space from solvers to (task, solver) pairs can shorten the wait between solver improvements, not lengthen it: inventing a simple task with an easy-to-find solution is often cheaper than improving on a fixed hard task, and greedy complexity ordering automatically trades off inventing a new unsolvable problem against compressing or speeding up previous solutions.

It is deliberately practical rather than asymptotically optimal: unlike the Godel machine and Hsearch, whose constant slowdowns make them infeasible on real-world problem sizes, POWERPLAY is meant to exploit a specific architecture (PC, RNN, SLIM NN) including the constants that asymptotic notation discards; the cost variant also accommodates externally supplied tasks and a probabilistic variant handles non-stationary, partially observable environments.

The framework is a clean plug-in point: TASK INVENTION, SOLVER MODIFICATION and CORRECTNESS DEMONSTRATION are separable, with concrete instantiations given for optimal program search over a FORTH-like language (existing OOPS source code) and for black-box/evolutionary search over RNN weight matrices, plus an explicitly self-referential mode where the current solver helps solve the search for its own successor.
limitations: Greed is acknowledged as the core weakness (Section 9.3, drawback 1): always taking the easiest-to-find and easiest-to-validate task may sacrifice large long-term gains for small short-term ones, and a stream of easily solvable tasks may at least temporarily prevent it from learning hard ones. The paper's mitigation is only an expectation - on RNNs with finite capacity it should soon run out of easy unsolved tasks.

It keeps only a selective list of previously solved tasks and discards the history of still-unsolved ones (drawback 2), and Variant I's accept/reject criterion is binary rather than information-theoretic (drawback 3); the cost-based Variant II is offered as the fix, not as a validated one.

The strong guarantee is intractable in general: the most general CORRECTNESS DEMONSTRATION is proof search over an axiomatic system describing every instruction's effect on the solver state (Section 3.3.1), i.e. this framework's version of the Godel machine's proof-search bottleneck; the cheaper conditions are special cases (frozen components, prefix codes).

Nothing here is experimentally validated by this paper - Section 5 and Section 6 both end by saying experiments are needed to analyze when the system runs out of trivial tasks and when self-generated tasks actually accelerate externally posed ones; Section 10 also warns that an unrestricted variant with access to physical devices or extra computational resources is hard to predict, and that unchecked curiosity may be harmful to the system itself.
1112.5309.fits: Stage 1 (Foundations & Theory), in the Evolutionary & Open-Ended RSI section: the 2011 blueprint for self-generated-curriculum RSI, predating POET. Pairs with AI-GAs (1905.10985) on curriculum as an RSI pillar, AutoML-Zero (2003.03384) as the minimal-bias searcher, and ADAS/DGM, which reuse the same invent-verify-freeze gate at harness level.
1112.5309.reading: Read Section 2 and Algorithm 2 for the core loop, Section 3 (especially 3.3.2-3.3.3) for the no-forgetting argument, Section 4.1 for Algorithm 4.1 and its optimality, Section 7.1 for the cost variant, then Sections 5, 8, 9.3 and 10.

2309.03409.tldr: OPRO describes an optimization task in natural language and has an LLM iteratively propose new solutions from a meta-prompt listing past solutions and their scores; on GSM8K it finds prompts beating "Let's think step by step" by 8.4 points.
2309.03409.method: The optimization task (objective, constraints, desired output format) is written in natural language and becomes the meta-prompt. The meta-prompt has two parts: a task description carrying ~3 exemplars randomly drawn from the training set, and the optimization trajectory — past solutions paired with their scores, sorted ascending and truncated to the best 20 to fit the context window. Each step the optimizer LLM is sampled 8 times at temperature 1.0 to emit 8 candidate solutions; each is scored by a black-box evaluator, then the solution-score pairs are appended and the trajectory re-sorted. The loop halts when no better solution appears or a step budget is hit (200 steps for prompt optimization). Scoring uses temperature 0, and the scorer LLM may differ from the optimizer LLM. Nothing is trained — all adaptation lives in the prompt.
results: GSM8K, pre-trained PaLM 2-L scorer, A_begin: OPRO's best instruction "Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step." scores 80.2 test accuracy vs 71.8 for human-written "Let's think step by step." (+8.4), 58.8 for APE's "Let's work this out in a step by step way to be sure we have the right answer.", 60.8 for "Let's solve the problem.", and 34.0 for the empty string. Other optimizers land just below: PaLM 2-L "Break this down." 79.9, gpt-3.5-turbo 78.5, gpt-4 74.5.

BBH, 23 tasks with a 20/80 train-test split, PaLM 2-L scorer: OPRO's found instructions beat "Let's think step by step." by over 5% on 19/23 tasks and beat the empty-string start on 20/23. Largest test-accuracy jumps over the CoT baseline: word_sorting 4.5→54.5 (+50.0, the source of the abstract's "up to 50%"), sports_understanding 46.5→88.0, movie_recommendation 52.5→90.5, object_counting 46.5→86.5, geometric_shapes 33.0→57.0.

BBH with the text-bison scorer, same pattern: >5% over the CoT baseline on 15/23 tasks, e.g. temporal_sequences 43.5→81.0 test, movie_recommendation 63.0→90.0, ruin_names 65.5→82.5, disambiguation_qa 6.0→73.0. Top GSM8K instructions also transfer within the math domain (Table 6): "Take a deep breath..." gives MultiArith 95.3 vs 85.7 for CoT and AQuA 54.3 vs 44.9.

TSP against a Gurobi oracle (5 instances per n): at n=10 every optimizer LLM reaches a 0.0% optimality gap while nearest-neighbor sits at 13.0% and farthest-insertion at 3.2%; gpt-4 needs 9.6±3.0 steps vs 40.4±5.6 (text-bison) and 46.8±9.3 (gpt-3.5-turbo), roughly 4x faster. At n=50 OPRO degrades: gpt-4 11.0%, gpt-3.5-turbo 133.0%, text-bison 219.8% gap, with farthest-insertion best at 9.8%.

Ablations (text-bison scorer, PaLM 2-L optimizer): 8 instructions per step beats 1/2/4/16 at equal evaluation budget; optimizer temperature 1.0 beats 0.0/0.5/1.5/2.0; ascending score order beats descending and random (recency bias); 3 exemplars beat 10 or none; and one-step generation of 50 instructions collapses (best of 50 on GSM8K was "Let's solve the problem" at 60.8 test, vs "Let's do the math!" at 76.3 test found within the first few OPRO steps).
advantages: Consumes the whole optimization trajectory — many score-sorted (solution, score) pairs — rather than editing a single prompt from natural-language feedback (APO) or forcing the new prompt to be semantically similar (APE); the LLM infers the direction of improvement itself, so accuracy keeps climbing across steps instead of saturating after one generation round.

Gradient-free, training-free and API-only, yet the identical meta-prompt template carries over from continuous optimization (linear regression coefficients) to combinatorial optimization (TSP tours) to prompt optimization — the task is retargeted by rewriting the natural-language description.

Decouples optimizer LLM from scorer LLM, and the gain holds across five models (PaLM 2-L, PaLM 2-L-IT, text-bison, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4); pre-trained PaLM 2-L even improves its own predictions by prompting itself.

Each meta-prompt design choice is ablated rather than asserted (ordering, numeric scores, exemplar count, samples per step, temperature), and it beats EvoPrompt's GA/DE meta-prompts, which the paper shows actually degrade GSM8K because they carry no exemplars and depend on task-specific seed prompts.
limitations: The paper states OPRO is not intended to beat gradient-based continuous optimizers or specialized combinatorial solvers: its TSP gap is worse than farthest-insertion at n=50 (11.0% vs 9.8%) and it fails on bumpy landscapes, getting stuck near (0,0) on the Rosenbrock function with a=20 instead of reaching (20,400).
Context-window bound: large problem descriptions (high-dimensional linear regression, TSP with many nodes) simply do not fit in the meta-prompt, so scale is capped by prompt length.

Prompt optimization requires a training set to compute the guiding accuracy (at least tens of samples), and the found instructions still overfit — Table 7 and Table 10 show training accuracies 5-20% above test, which the authors suggest mitigating via a larger training set and early stopping.

Appendix A failure modes across all optimizer LLMs: hallucinating objective values it should have computed, re-emitting solutions already present in context despite explicit instructions not to, and stalling when in-context exemplars share a wrong coefficient; using error cases instead of random exemplars gave similar results, so errors alone were not informative enough.
2309.03409.fits: Stage 2, prompt/context optimization — the canonical trajectory-based, gradient-free optimizer and sibling of APE; Promptbreeder (2309.16797) self-referentially evolves OPRO's mutator. Pairs with TextGrad and DSPy in the "LLM optimizes the artifact" family, and its solution-score-pair loop recurs at harness level in stages 5-6.
2309.03409.reading: Read §2 for the OPRO framework and meta-prompt design, §4.1-4.2 with Figure 3 for the prompt-optimization instantiation, then §5.2-5.5 and Tables 4/7. Skim §3 for the math case studies and Appendix A for the failure modes.

2309.16797.tldr: Promptbreeder evolves a population of task-prompts by binary-tournament selection on training accuracy and, self-referentially, evolves the mutation-prompts that mutate them — beating Chain-of-Thought and Plan-and-Solve on arithmetic and commonsense reasoning.
2309.16797.method: A unit of evolution holds two task-prompts plus one mutation-prompt (and, in the few-shot case, a context list of correct workings out). Initialization concatenates a randomly drawn thinking-style and mutation-prompt onto the domain problem description and lets the LLM continue, producing diverse starting task-prompts; each mutation-prompt stays bound 1:1 to its task-prompt. Fitness is accuracy on a freshly sampled batch of 100 training Q&A pairs. A binary tournament GA samples two individuals, mutates the fitter, and overwrites the loser, with P' = LLM(M + P). Nine operators across five classes drive exploration: zero-/first-order generation, EDA and EDA rank-and-index and lineage-based mutation, zero-/first-order hyper-mutation (M' = LLM(H + M)), Lamarckian reverse-engineering of a task-prompt from a correct working out, plus prompt crossover (10%) and context shuffling. Population 50, run 20-30 generations.
results: Zero-shot with PaLM 2-L: PB beats Plan-and-Solve PS+ on every benchmark — GSM8K 60.5→83.9, MultiArith 92.5→99.7, SingleEq 94.7→96.4, AddSub 74.4→87.8, SVAMP 86.3→90.2, CommonsenseQA 73.3→85.4, StrategyQA 50.1→71.8, AQuA-RAT 39.4→62.2.
PB's best zero-shot GSM8K prompt was the bare string "SOLUTION" at 83.9%, versus OPRO's optimized "Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step" at 80.2% and APE at 77.9%.
Few-shot run improves further on commonsense: StrategyQA 71.8→80.2, AQuA-RAT 62.2→64.6, MultiArith 99.7→100.0 (few-shot GSM8K 83.5).

ETHOS hate-speech classification: PB evolved two sequentially applied long prompts scoring 89%, over the hand-designed "Determine whether a text contains hate speech" at 80%; under the deliberately under-specified spec "Solve the Problem" it still reached 81.6%.

Operator effectiveness on GSM8K (share of offspring fitter than parent): zero-order hyper-mutation 42%, lineage-based 26%, first-order hyper-mutation 23%, EDA rank/index 12.7%, direct 12%, EDA 10.7%, Lamarckian 6.3%; the single best evolved mutation-prompt ("Please summarise and improve the following instruction") improved its task-prompt 24.13% of the time.
advantages: Demonstrates the self-referential step concretely: the mutation-prompt is itself a genotype under selection, so the system raises its own evolvability rather than only its prompts — evoPrompt and OPRO use fixed mutators.

Directly answers APE's reported diminishing returns: fitness keeps climbing across generations (Appendix B), attributed to the diversity-maintaining population, BERT-cosine 0.95 filter, elite-lineage and EDA operators.

Ablations isolate each self-referential piece rather than asserting the whole: removing any operator hurts on nearly every dataset, with thinking-style-guided initialization the largest single contributor — only random mutation-prompt sampling hurt, and only on GSM8K.
Entirely gradient-free and parameter-free: no LLM weights change, so it scales with whatever model sits behind the API.
limitations: Paper's own account: the topology of prompting stays fixed — only prompt content adapts, not the prompting algorithm or the conditional application of prompts.
Cost: fitness needs repeated evaluation of batches of 100 questions per generation over populations of 50 across 20-30 generations, i.e. thousands of LLM calls per domain.
Ablations run at shrunken scale (population 10, 200 evaluations) and the headline accuracy numbers come from a single sizable LLM (PaLM 2-L) on mostly small benchmark test splits.
Evaluation only on text/language tasks; the paper notes human thought is multimodal and hierarchical, which this single-level prompt evolution does not model.
2309.16797.fits: Stage 2, prompt/context optimization — the self-referential sibling of OPRO (2309.03409) and APE, and a peer of DSPy and TextGrad. Its evolve-the-mutator idea is the seed of the later 'improve the improver' harness-level thread (stages 5-6).
2309.16797.reading: Read §3.1 initialization and §3.2's five mutation-operator classes, then §5 Results and Appendix L ablations. Appendix J.3-J.4 for evolved mutation-prompts and operator effectiveness.

2310.04406.tldr: LATS puts a frozen LM inside Monte Carlo Tree Search: the ReAct agent proposes actions, an LM value function plus self-consistency scores states, the environment supplies rewards, and reflections on failed trajectories are re-injected as context.
2310.04406.method: Node s=[x, a1..i, o1..i] holds the input plus action/observation history, so any state is restored by replaying text — no world model. Each of k iterations runs six operations. Selection descends by UCT, V(s)+w·sqrt(ln N(p)/N(s)), w=1. Expansion samples n=5 actions from the ReAct agent pθ; the environment returns observations and n children enter an external memory tree. Evaluation assigns V(s)=λ·LM(s)+(1−λ)·SC(s): an LM prompted after seeing environment feedback to emit a scalar score, plus a self-consistency score (λ=0.5 on HotPotQA/Game of 24, 0.8 on programming/WebShop). Simulation rolls to a terminal state for reward r (answer correctness, fraction of tests passed, purchase success). Backpropagation sets V(s)←(V_old(s)(N−1)+r)/N along the path. On failure a reflection prompt rewrites the context used by both agent and value function.
results: HumanEval pass@1 with GPT-4 (Table 4): LATS 92.7 vs 80.1 zero-shot and 91.0 for Reflexion, reported as state of the art; with GPT-3.5, 83.8 vs Reflexion 68.1, RAP 63.1, ReAct 56.9, ToT 54.4, CoT 46.9 (n=5, k=8).
MBPP with GPT-3.5 (Table 5), 397-problem subset: 81.1 pass@1 vs RAP 71.4, Reflexion 70.0, ReAct 67.0, ToT 65.8, CoT 54.9.

HotPotQA, 100 questions, exact match (Tables 2–3): reasoning LATS(CoT) 0.62 vs RAP 0.60, ToT 0.55, CoT-SC 0.38, base 0.32; acting LATS(ReAct) 0.63 vs RAP(ReAct) 0.54, Reflexion 0.51, ReAct 0.32; chaining CoT then ReAct reaches 0.71. Game of 24 (Table 7): 0.44 vs RAP 0.40, ToT 0.20, Reflexion 0.12, CoT 0.08.

WebShop, 50 instructions (Table 6): frozen GPT-3.5 scores 75.9 / 38.0 success rate vs Reflexion 64.2/35.0 and ReAct 53.8/28.0, above imitation learning 59.9/29.1 and IL+RL 62.4/28.7; fine-tuning leads on SR (45.0) at 67.5 score.

Ablations on HotPotQA (Table 8): removing the LM value function costs 0.26 EM (0.63→0.37), replacing MCTS with DFS 0.21 (0.63→0.42), removing reflection 0.05 (0.63→0.58); λ=1 also drops Game of 24 (Table 13) from 0.44 to 0.40. Cost (Tables 9–10): same O(kn) sample complexity but fewer nodes to success — 28.42 vs RAP 31.53 and ToT 33.97 at k=10, averaging 3.55 and 12.12 fewer.
advantages: First framework to combine reasoning, acting, planning, self-reflection and external memory in one loop (Table 1): it searches a ReAct thought-plus-action space with environment feedback, where ToT searches thoughts only, RAP needs an LM world model, and Reflexion refines a single trajectory.

The value function is the load-bearing part: LM scoring happens after environment feedback (ToT scores before it), and the added self-consistency term sharpens it — ablating LM scoring costs 0.26 EM, more than any other component, and λ=1 falls to 0.40 on Game of 24.

Trained-policy performance with no training: frozen GPT-3.5 plus search beats imitation learning and IL+RL on WebShop (75.9 vs 59.9/62.4) and approaches the fine-tuned model, while with GPT-4 it sets the then-state-of-the-art HumanEval pass@1 of 92.7 — no RL, no gradient updates.

Search is guided rather than merely wider: same asymptotic sample complexity as ToT and RAP but fewer nodes and fewer tokens to reach success, and the n parameter gives an explicit accuracy-cost dial (n=1 makes it as cheap as ReAct with multiple trials).
limitations: The authors' own two: higher computational cost than simple prompting methods like ReAct or Reflexion, and the need for environments that permit reverting to earlier states (they argue this holds for HumanEval, WebShop, Alfworld, ToolBench, but not universally).

They also call their own benchmarks relatively simple versus real-world interactive environments; there is no long-horizon or embodied test, and multi-agent and more complex environments are left to future work.

The reward is privileged. HotPotQA uses an oracle telling the agent whether its answer is correct, and programming grades against LM-generated assert statements — the oracle-label setup Huang et al. (2310.01798) single out when criticising self-correction claims.

Reflection contributes little where search already covers it: only 0.05 EM on HotPotQA versus Reflexion's 0.19 gain over ReAct, and the WebShop analysis finds generated reflections often generic, leaving the agent prone to local minima.
2310.04406.fits: Stage 2, Prompt & Program Optimization group: search over natural-language action sequences rather than prompts — no weight update, improvement entirely at inference time — the guide's contrast to stage 4's persistent methods. Pairs with TextGrad (2406.07496) and DSPy (2310.03714) as text-space optimizers, OPRO (2309.03409) and Promptbreeder (2309.16797) as prompt-only ancestors, Reflexion (2303.11366) for its reflection signal.
2310.04406.reading: Read §3.2–4 for MCTS setup, the six operations and Eq. 2's value function; §5.1–5.4 with Tables 2–10 for numbers and ablations; §6 plus Appendix B for limitations. Skim Appendix A for pseudocode and the n=5, w=1, λ defaults.

2303.17651.tldr: Self-Refine: one frozen LLM generates an output, critiques it, then rewrites it from that critique, iterating with no training, extra data, or reward model — improving 7 tasks by ~20% absolute on average.
2303.17651.method: Training-free, inference-only loop on a single frozen model M with three few-shot prompts. (1) Generate y0 = M(pgen || x). (2) FEEDBACK: fb_t = M(pfb || x || y_t), where pfb carries input-output-feedback triples whose feedback must be 'actionable' (names a concrete fix) and 'specific' (names the phrase or loop to change).
