(3) Stop check: stop(fb_t, t) either fires after a fixed timestep or reads a scalar stop score the model emits in pfb; otherwise (4) REFINE: y_{t+1} = M(prefine || x || y0 || fb0 || ... || y_t || fb_t) — the full output/feedback history is retained so the model does not repeat past mistakes. Iterate to at most 4 rounds; return the last refinement. Greedy decoding, temperature 0.7, no weight updates.
results: Table 1, 7 tasks x 3 base LLMs, the same model with vs without the loop: Constrained Generation GPT-4 15.0 -> 45.0 and ChatGPT 44.0 -> 67.0 coverage; Dialogue Response GPT-4 25.4 -> 74.6 and GPT-3.5 36.4 -> 63.6 preference; Sentiment Reversal GPT-4 3.8 -> 36.2, ChatGPT 11.4 -> 43.2; Code Optimization GPT-4 27.3 -> 36.0, GPT-3.5 14.8 -> 23.0; Code Readability GPT-4 27.4 -> 56.2; Acronym Generation GPT-3.5 41.6 -> 56.4.

Math Reasoning is the flat case (Table 1): GPT-3.5 64.1 -> 64.1 (0), ChatGPT 74.8 -> 75.0, GPT-4 92.9 -> 93.1 — the authors trace it to the model feeding back 'everything looks good' for 94% of ChatGPT instances.

Iterations help but saturate (Figure 4 left, averaged over the three models): Code Optimization 22.0 (y0) -> 27.0 -> 27.9 -> 28.8 (y3); Sentiment Reversal 33.9 -> 36.8; Constrained Generation 29.0 -> 49.7 at y3, with marginal gain shrinking each round.

Feedback quality is the causal lever (Table 2, actionable vs generic vs no feedback): Code Optimization 27.5 / 26.0 / 24.8, Sentiment Reversal 43.2 / 31.2 / 0, Acronym Generation 56.4 / 54.0 / 48.0 — the model may still iterate without feedback, and the task then fails outright.

Against fine-tuned and sampled baselines on the PIE code-optimization benchmark (Table 8, %OPT): Self-Refine with GPT-4 36.0 using at most 4 samples, vs PIE-16B best@32 26.6, PIE-few-shot best@32 38.3, and human references 12.6 / 19.6. With an oracle correctness signal on math the gains reappear (Table 9): GPT-3.5 64.06 -> 68.9, ChatGPT 74.8 -> 76.2, GPT-4 92.9 -> 93.8.
advantages: Trains nothing: no supervised refinement data, reward model, RL, or separate refiner — one model plays generator, feedback provider and refiner, and only the three few-shot prompts change across 7 heterogeneous tasks (dialogue, code optimization, code readability, math, sentiment reversal, acronyms, constrained generation).

Shows refinement beats spending the same budget on sampling: in a 1-vs-k human evaluation, Self-Refine's output was preferred over all k = 4 plain ChatGPT samples, so the gain is the feedback-conditioned revision, not extra generations.

Quantifies the mechanism rather than asserting it — the feedback ablation (Table 2) shows actionable, specific feedback is what carries the improvement, and the manual analysis of 70 cases found 61% of failures were bad fixes suggested by feedback and only 6% were the refiner misimplementing good feedback.

Establishes the reference template for test-time self-improvement — generate, critique, refine, retain history, stop on a scored signal — and reports Wilson confidence intervals (Table 13) showing nearly all GPT-4 gains significant, ChatGPT 4/7 and GPT-3.5 3/7.
limitations: Requires a strong instruction-following base model. Vicuna-13B could not reliably emit feedback in the required format, and even given oracle or hard-coded feedback it repeated its output or hallucinated dialogue instead of refining (Appendix G) — though Vicuna-13b initialized at 24.18% on math did reach 40.5% when ChatGPT supplied the feedback and refinement.

Feedback is the bottleneck and it is self-generated: on math the model declares the answer fine in 94% of ChatGPT cases, and in the audited failures 33% of errors came from feedback mislocating the bug and 61% from feedback proposing an inappropriate fix.

All base LLMs are closed (text-davinci-003, gpt-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, code-davinci-002) with undisclosed pretraining data, sizes and biases, and are paid to use; the paper's own limitation section also notes the evaluation is English-only with no guard against prompting a model toward toxic or harmful text.

The stopping rule is essentially a fixed budget of up to 4 FEEDBACK-REFINE rounds or a prompted per-task scalar score rather than a learned criterion, and gains are already diminishing after the first iteration.
2303.17651.fits: Stage 3's founding inference-time loop and the minimal self-improvement primitive — one frozen model as both solver and critic — that CRITIC, Reflexion and later harness-level work extend. Read as the positive counterpart to the stage's negative control, Huang et al. 2310.01798, whose oracle-label and prompt-symmetry critiques land directly on these numbers.
2303.17651.reading: Read §2 (Algorithm 1, the feedback/refine equations) and §4 (Table 2 feedback-quality ablation, Figure 4 iterations), then §6 Limitations plus Appendix G (Vicuna-13b), H.1 (oracle math) and J (confidence intervals).

2309.11495.tldr: Chain-of-Verification (CoVe): draft an answer, plan verification questions about its factual claims, answer those questions without the draft in context, then regenerate. Wikidata list precision 0.17 -> 0.36 and biography FactScore 55.9 -> 71.4, with no tools or retraining.
2309.11495.method: Four prompted steps on one frozen base LLM (Llama 65B, 3 few-shot examples, greedy decoding): (1) generate a baseline response; (2) plan verification questions covering the draft's factual claims, freely phrased by the model rather than templated; (3) execute those verifications; (4) generate the final verified response conditioned on the question-answer pairs. Step 3 has four variants differing in what may attend to what: joint (plan and answer in one prompt, so answers still see the draft), 2-step (questions answered with the draft removed from context), factored (each question answered in its own prompt, so no draft and no cross-question interference, and prompts batch in parallel), and factor+revise (adds one cross-check prompt per question emitting CONSISTENT / INCONSISTENT / PARTIALLY CONSISTENT). The final prompt presents the verification answers as coming from "another source".
results: Wikidata list questions (micro precision, Llama 65B few-shot): 0.17 -> 0.36 with 2-step CoVe, driven by hallucinations collapsing (negatives 2.95 -> 0.68) while correct entities dip only slightly (0.59 -> 0.38).
Harder Wiki-Category list task: precision 0.12 -> 0.22 with factored CoVe (negatives 4.05 -> 1.52); factored beats joint on every task.
Closed-book MultiSpanQA: F1 0.39 -> 0.48 (factored), a 23% gain from both precision (0.40 -> 0.50) and recall (0.38 -> 0.46).

Biography generation (FactScore, Min et al. metric): 55.9 -> 71.4 with factor+revise, +28%, at 16.6 -> 12.3 average facts; this beats ChatGPT 58.7 and retrieval-augmented PerplexityAI 61.6 using only the base model (joint 60.8, factored 63.7).

Diagnostics: only ~17% of the few-shot baseline's list entities are correct, yet ~70% of those same facts are answered correctly when queried individually; question form matters (Table 4, Wiki-Category) - LLM-written open questions (factored 0.22) beat yes/no (0.19) and templated rule-based (0.16); and neither instruction tuning nor CoT helps (Llama 2 70B Chat zero-shot F1 0.20 vs few-shot Llama 65B 0.39).
advantages: Reduces hallucination with no retrieval, no tools and no weight updates - purely inference-time deliberation on a frozen model - yet still out-fact-scores ChatGPT and a retrieval-augmented system on biographies.

Isolates attention control as the causal mechanism rather than crediting 'more compute': joint < 2-step < factored across tasks shows the gain comes from stopping verification from attending to the hallucinated draft, and Table 4 shows generated questions beat templated heuristics.

Is not precision bought with recall: hallucinated entities fall 2.95 -> 0.68 while correct ones only dip 0.59 -> 0.38, and since FactScore is normalized, producing fewer facts is not the explanation (clipping Llama 2 to 10 sentences only moved 41.3 -> 42.7).

Supplies the reusable design pattern for self-checking - decompose the check into short, independently answerable questions and keep each one blind to the text being checked - which later verification and memory-evolution loops inherit.
limitations: CoVe does not remove hallucinations, only reduces them; the paper's own Section 6 concedes it can still produce incorrect or misleading output.
Scope is directly stated factual inaccuracies (and, on Wikidata/Wiki-Category, listed entities) - not errors inside reasoning steps and not opinions.

The ceiling is the base model's own knowledge, since verification is performed by the same weights: Figure 2 shows retrieval-augmented PerplexityAI still wins on very rare facts, and the paper names tool use as the obvious extension.
Extra cost: more generated tokens, like chain-of-thought, and factored CoVe runs many more prompts (batchable, but no cost analysis or variance/error bars are reported across the four tasks).
2309.11495.fits: Stage 3, self-verification - the positive counterpart to the stage's negative result. CoVe works where intrinsic self-correction fails because verification is decomposed into short, independent, more-answerable questions instead of asking the model to judge its own reasoning. Pairs with Self-Refine (the loop it disagrees with), CRITIC (the tool-grounded version of step 3) and Self-Consistency.
2309.11495.reading: Section 3 for the four steps and the joint / 2-step / factored / factor+revise variants; Tables 1-3 for the numbers; Table 4 and Section 9 with Section 6 for question form and limits.

2305.11738.tldr: CRITIC: a frozen LLM proposes an answer, critiques it by actually querying external tools (Google, a Python interpreter, Perspective API), then revises against that evidence — the tool feedback is what makes self-correction work; the model's own critique is not.
2305.11738.method: No training or weight updates — few-shot prompts only. Each tool is wrapped as a text-to-text function and interleaved in ReAct-style demonstrations. An initial answer (CoT for QA, program-of-thought for math) is verified by asking "What's the problem with the above answer?": for QA the model issues a Google query whose top-1 page is scraped and fuzzy-matched to at most 400 characters; for math a Python interpreter returns "Execution: {error message}" plus the value of the variable answer; for detoxification Perspective API returns overall plus six fine-grained attribute scores, rendered as "The text has {score} toxicity of {attribute}". Critiques are concatenated with input and previous output to regenerate. Algorithm 1 loops verify-then-correct, stopping when the critique reports correctness, when the answer is unchanged twice, or at n rounds (QA n=3, math n=4, toxicity n=4 or toxicity below 10%). CRITIC* is the oracle arm; search results are cached (9GB).
results: QA (Table 1, ChatGPT, 500 sampled validation examples, EM/F1): CoT to CRITIC lifts AmbigNQ 51.8/64.3 to 62.0/74.9, TriviaQA 72.9/79.2 to 75.1/81.7, HotpotQA 32.7/42.8 to 40.3/52.9 — average +7.7 F1 (text-davinci-003 +5.6); oracle CRITIC* reaches 69.6/80.9/44.3 EM.

Math program synthesis (Table 2, solve rate): ChatGPT PoT to CRITIC moves GSM8K 72.5 to 78.2, SVAMP 82.0 to 83.3, TabMWP 75.0 to 89.0 (+7.0 average); CRITIC* 83.9/89.0/94.0. Gains scale with the base model — LLaMA-2 TabMWP +4.7/+9.4/+16.0 at 7B/13B/70B (59.0 to 75.0 at 70B).

Toxicity (Table 3, 1k RealToxicityPrompts, ChatGPT): max toxicity 0.325 to 0.173 and toxicity probability 0.192 to 0.040 (79.2% reduction), at perplexity 14.54 to 15.66 and dist-2 0.77 to 0.78 — matching trained GPT-2 Self-Correct (0.171/0.026) with zero training.

Tool ablation is the paper's central evidence: CRITIC w/o Tool averages -0.03 F1 (text-davinci-003) and +2.33 (ChatGPT) against CRITIC's +5.6/+7.7 on the same tasks, and text-davinci-003 GSM8K falls 70.1 to 68.3; on Codex, Self-Refine drops PAL 71.3 to 26.7.

Self-verification (Table 5): CRITIC's AUROC for spotting hallucinated QA answers is 0.810/0.818/0.831 (AmbigNQ/TriviaQA/HotpotQA) vs Self-Eval 0.668/0.731/0.713 and best intrinsic Self-Con 0.760 on AmbigNQ; Self-Eval accuracy on HotpotQA is 0.540, near chance.
advantages: Isolates the active ingredient instead of asserting one: the oracle arm, the w/o-Tool arm and the uncertainty study (Table 5) jointly show tool feedback — not self-critique — drives every gain, and that intrinsic self-correction is unreliable. The critiques are interpretable (retrieved snippets, interpreter errors) and double as a hallucination detector.

Black-box and training-free: identical prompts across ChatGPT, text-davinci-003 and LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B, requiring only text-to-text tool APIs plus a few-shot demonstration — no annotations, no separate corrector model.

Gains compound with scale and compose with retrieval: LLaMA-2 TabMWP improves +4.7/+9.4/+16.0 from 7B to 70B, and ReAct-then-CRITIC beats plain ReAct on most QA settings (ChatGPT AmbigNQ F1 64.8 to 72.2).
Beats best-of-N at comparable sampling: on AmbigNQ, CRITIC* EM 69.6 vs rejection sampling 60.9 (ChatGPT) — regenerating conditioned on critiques beats regenerating from scratch.
limitations: Corrections can destroy correct answers: on GSM8K's 1319-item test set CRITIC lowers accuracy on originally correct outputs by 4.3%, 14.3% of post-correction errors are wrong corrections, and text-davinci-003 SVAMP regresses 84.0 to 80.7.

Coverage is bounded by the tool: only 26.7% of GSM8K intrinsic reasoning errors get fixed (vs 57.4% of unreasonable outputs, 35.3% of syntax errors); HotpotQA refusal to answer rises 2% to 12%; QA evidence is a single top-1 page truncated to 400 characters.

Tools are pre-specified per task behind hand-built ReAct-style demonstrations; the paper flags prompt-construction sensitivity as a caveat and leaves automatic tool selection to future work. Latency grows linearly with iterations (roughly 2x PoT for two corrections).

Nothing persists — weights never change — and scope is three text tasks with 500-example QA samples. On LLaMA-2-70B, rejection sampling wins 5 of 6 QA metric columns against CRITIC (HotpotQA F1 58.1 vs 49.6).
2305.11738.fits: Stage 3's external-feedback hinge. Self-Refine's loop minus tools is exactly CRITIC w/o Tool, where the gains vanish — the negative result Huang et al. (2310.01798) later confirms. CRITIC supplies the fix, and its critiques-as-signal framing feeds stage 4 (Reflexion-style memory) and tool-using harnesses.
2305.11738.reading: Section 3 with Algorithm 1 (especially 3.3 verification, 3.4 correction), then 4.1-4.3 with Tables 1-3; Appendix D.1/Table 5 for self-verification reliability and Tables 6-7 for error modes. Appendix E case studies are skippable.

2203.11171.tldr: Sampling many diverse chain-of-thought paths and taking a majority vote over their final answers lifts accuracy by roughly 3-24 points over greedy CoT, with no training, no verifier and no extra data.
2203.11171.method: Prompt the LM with the same few-shot chain-of-thought exemplars as Wei et al. (8 for arithmetic, 4-7 for commonsense), then replace greedy decoding with "sample-and-marginalize". Sample m reasoning paths (r_i, a_i) independently - T=0.5 with top-k=40 for UL2-20B and LaMDA-137B, T=0.7, k=40 for PaLM-540B, T=0.7 with no top-k for GPT-3 - and parse each final answer a_i after "The answer is". Marginalize out the latent paths by majority vote, argmax_a sum_i 1(a_i=a); main results average 10 runs of 40 paths. No training, verifier, re-ranker or annotation - a "self-ensemble" over a single model. Aggregation was ablated: unweighted majority vote (74.4 GSM8K) matches length-normalized probability weighting (74.1), because normalized path probabilities are too close to discriminate; unnormalized weighting collapses to 59.9.
results: GPT-3 code-davinci-002: GSM8K 60.1 -> 78.0 (+17.9), SVAMP 75.8 -> 86.8 (+11.0), AQuA 39.8 -> 52.0 (+12.2), MultiArith 96.2 -> 100.0, CSQA 79.0 -> 81.5 - new SoTA without any supervised fine-tuning.
Gains scale with model size: UL2-20B only +3.2 to +6.8 points (GSM8K 4.1 -> 7.3) vs LaMDA-137B +9.1 to +23.9 (MultiArith 51.8 -> 75.7, GSM8K 17.1 -> 27.7), and GPT-3 code-davinci-001 +6.7 to +23.2.

Beats other uses of the same compute at matched budget: vs beam search on UL2-20B AQuA (beam-40 = 10.2, beam-1 = 23.6 vs self-consistency 26.9 +/- 0.5 over 40 sampled paths); vs prompt ensembles on LaMDA-137B GSM8K (3 prompt sets 18.6, 40 prompt permutations 19.2 vs 27.7); vs multi-model ensembles (LaMDA-137B + PaLM-540B = 36.9 vs 74.4 for PaLM-540B alone).

Robust and re-usable elsewhere: holds across three prompt sets (PaLM GSM8K 74.4 / 72.1 / 70.4), across sampling parameters (T, top-k, nucleus p), on imperfect CoT prompts (LaMDA-137B GSM8K 14.9 -> 23.4, above the 17.1 of a correct prompt with greedy decode), equation-only rationales, and zero-shot CoT (PaLM 43.0 -> 69.2).
advantages: Establishes inference-time diversity plus answer agreement as a training-free accuracy lever: new SoTA on GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA and StrategyQA with no additional training, annotation or auxiliary model - beating prior work that required fine-tuning on 7.5k examples plus a second 175B verifier (GSM8K 55 vs 74.4).

Shows the gain comes from diversity of reasoning paths, not merely from more samples: it dominates beam search (which degrades as beams grow, 23.6 -> 10.2 AQuA), sample-and-rank, prompt-order and multi-prompt ensembles, and cross-model ensembles, at equal sample count.

Turns agreement into a usable uncertainty signal: the share of decodes agreeing with the majority answer correlates strongly with accuracy, giving a calibration / "know when it doesn't know" estimate for free.

The primitive is portable and cheap: compatible with any sampling scheme, with zero-shot CoT and with non-natural-language rationales (equations); majority-vote-over-self-samples is the mechanism later RSI pipelines inherit for aggregating debate (stage 6) and for filtering self-generated data.
limitations: Cost multiplies with the number of paths (40 in the main results) for one final answer; the paper's own advice is to start with 5-10 paths, since the accuracy curve saturates quickly.
It only applies where the final answer comes from a fixed answer set that can be parsed and counted; open-ended generation needs an externally defined consistency metric.

The model cannot distinguish good reasoning from bad: normalized path probabilities cluster closely enough that probability weighting adds nothing over vote counting, and the paper notes models still emit incorrect or nonsensical rationales (the StrategyQA population figures in Table 4), leaving rationale grounding to future work.

No correctness guarantee - agreement is only a proxy, and the premise that correct reasoning is more consistent than incorrect reasoning is argued by intuition rather than proved, so a confidently wrong majority survives the vote.
2203.11171.fits: Stage 3's founding inference-time result and the baseline the stage's papers argue against: nothing is revised, reliability comes from aggregating diverse samples of one frozen model. Debate aggregation (stage 6) and consistency filtering of self-generated data inherit the primitive. Pairs with Self-Refine; the negative result targets revision, not voting.
2203.11171.reading: §2 (sample-and-marginalize and why majority vote matches probability weighting - Table 1) and §3.2 Table 2 for the headline numbers; §3.4 Tables 6-7 for the beam-search and ensemble baselines. Skim §4 and the appendix figures.

2305.20050.tldr: Process supervision — human labels on every reasoning step — trains reward models that beat outcome supervision on MATH: the PRM solves 78.2% best-of-1860 vs 72.4% for the ORM, and active learning makes step-level labelling 2.6x more data-efficient.
2305.20050.method: Humans label generator-produced MATH solutions step by step as positive, negative, or neutral (neutral = reasonable but non-progressing), and labelling stops at the first mistake so the cost matches outcome labelling. A PRM is the MathMix-finetuned base model trained to emit that label token after each step; at test time a single forward pass gives per-step probabilities, and the solution score is their product. Data collection is active: a small PRM_selector ranks 1000 samples per problem and 80% of surfaced solutions are its highest-scoring wrong-answer ones (20% other convincing samples), with the PRM retrained between generations. The ORM baseline instead predicts solution correctness at the final token. The generator itself is never RL-trained; only the reward models are compared, judged by best-of-N search over uniformly sampled solutions.
results: MATH, 500 held-out problems, best-of-1860 over generator samples: PRM 78.2% vs ORM 72.4% vs majority voting 69.6% (Fig. 3). The PRM leads at every N and the gap widens as N grows, while majority voting is a strong but beaten baseline.

Scoring-strategy sweep (Table 4, best-of-1860): product of step scores with neutrals counted positive 78.2%, product with neutrals negative 77.4%, minimum reduction 77.6% / 77.8% — all within 0.8 points, so the win is not an artifact of the reduction rule.

Controlled small-scale comparison on identical data (1-200 samples per problem, Fig. 4): process supervision beat both outcome-supervision forms at every data scale, and PRM_large-scored outcome supervision beat final-answer-checked outcome supervision — the gap is exactly the right-answer/wrong-reasoning false positives.

Active learning (80% convincing wrong-answer + 20% other convincing samples) is ~2.6x more data-efficient than uniform labelling, estimated from the slopes of the best-of-500 fit; gains flatten at 200 samples/problem because that is already a large fraction of the 1000-sample selection pool.

Out-of-distribution held-out AP Calculus/Chemistry/Physics + AMC10/12 set, best-of-100 (Table 1): aggregate PRM 72.9% vs ORM 63.8% vs majority 61.3%; AMC10/12 53.2% vs 49.1% vs 32.8%. PRM800K is released: 800K step-level labels over 75K solutions and 12K problems (phase 1 is ~5% of it, ~40K labels).
advantages: A negative alignment tax: unlike most safety-motivated methods, process supervision improves reliability and capability at the same time, so adopting it does not cost accuracy — the authors argue this should raise its adoption and its alignment side-effects.

Precise credit assignment is the named mechanism: an outcome label says only that a solution is wrong, while step labels say which prefix was right and where the first error is, and the difficulty-quintile breakdown shows the PRM stays robust (and gap persists) across all five quintiles while the ORM degrades on the easiest one as N grows.

Active learning plus the released PRM800K removes the main barrier to entry — human step-level labelling — and PRM_large is shown to work as a cheap labelling oracle, making large data-collection ablations feasible at small scale.
The result holds under distribution shift: on fresh, post-pretraining AP/AMC exams the PRM beats both the ORM and majority voting, so the advantage is not only an in-distribution artifact.
limitations: The large-scale head-to-head is confounded by construction: the ORM trains on 100 uniformly sampled solutions per problem while the PRM trains on an active-learning-biased, order-of-magnitude smaller PRM800K, so Section 3 is not apples-to-apples — the controlled Section 4 comparison is the real evidence.

Scope is mathematical reasoning only, and the generator is deliberately never RL-trained; the paper makes no claim about process reward models inside an RLHF or self-improvement loop, which it calls a natural next step but explicitly out of scope.

MATH test-set contamination cannot be ruled out: the test problems appear online and string-matching was not a guarantee, so some inflation is possible (though the authors argue it would hit all methods similarly, and the uncontaminated OOD results support that).

Active learning underperforms its own trend at 200 samples/problem, and iteratively retraining PRM_selector between generations was unstable with no performance gain — the authors call iterative retraining compelling but unsupported.
2305.20050.fits: Stage 3 (Harness-level RSI / Self-Verification & Self-Correction): it makes the verifier itself a trainable artifact and shows that where feedback is placed decides reliability. Pairs with CRITIC (2305.11738, the external-feedback hinge), Self-Refine (2303.17651), the negative result 2310.01798, self-consistency (2203.11171), and verifier-training descendants like SWE-Gym (2412.21139).
2305.20050.reading: §2 (ORM vs PRM training, step scoring), §3 Fig. 3 for the 78.2/72.4/69.6 headline, §4.1-4.2 for the controlled comparison and 2.6x active learning, §5 Table 1 for OOD, §6.3 contamination, Appendix F.2 Table 4 scoring.

2310.01798.tldr: The counterweight: LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning without external feedback. Intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy on GSM8K, CommonSenseQA and HotpotQA across GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2, and multi-agent debate loses to self-consistency at equal inference cost.
2310.01798.method: A measurement protocol, not a method. Each trial uses a three-step prompt: (1) initial generation, (2) review that answer and emit feedback, (3) re-answer the question conditioned on the feedback — capped at two correction rounds. Two conditions are contrasted: oracle-guided, where a ground-truth stop check prevents the model from altering an already-correct answer, and intrinsic, where the model alone decides whether to revise. Benchmarks: GSM8K (1,319 problems), CommonSenseQA dev (1,221), HotpotQA closed-book exact match (100). Models: GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 and GPT-4 (temperature 1), GPT-4-Turbo-1106 and Llama-2-70b-chat (temperature 0). Two follow-up controls: replicating multi-agent debate (3 agents, 2 rounds, gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, Du et al.'s own prompts) against self-consistency at matched response counts, and re-running Self-Refine's constrained-generation setup with the task constraint moved into the initial prompt.
results: Oracle labels are what made prior work look good (Table 2): GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0; GPT-4 95.5 -> 97.5, 82.0 -> 85.5, 49.0 -> 59.0.

Intrinsic self-correction degrades every model (Tables 3-4). GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0 and 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0 and 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo: 91.5 -> 88.0 -> 90.0 (GSM8K), 84.0 -> 81.5 -> 83.0 (CSQA). Llama-2-70b-chat collapses: 62.0 -> 43.5 -> 36.5 and 64.0 -> 37.5 -> 36.5. Three alternative feedback prompts do not rescue it (Tables 5-6): every variant still ends below its single-call baseline (GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 -> 88.0/90.0/91.0; Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 -> down to 30.5-58.0).

Multi-agent debate is self-consistency in disguise (Table 7, GSM8K): standard prompting 76.7 (1 response); debate 82.5 at 3 responses vs self-consistency 83.2; debate 83.0 at 9 responses vs self-consistency 88.2 — debate loses outright once response counts are matched.

The Self-Refine gain was a bad initial prompt (Table 8, CommonGen-Hard concept coverage): Madaan et al. standard 44.0 -> 67.0 with 7 calls, but adding 'includes *ALL* of the above concepts' to the initial prompt gives 81.8 with 1 call — and self-correction on top of that drops it to 75.1.

Why it degrades (Section 3.3, Figure 1): GPT-3.5 keeps its GSM8K answer unchanged 74.7% of the time, and among the rest, correct -> incorrect flips outnumber incorrect -> correct fixes; GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo retain their initial answers more often than the weaker models.
advantages: Isolates the label leak that inflated the whole self-correction literature: it reproduces RCI's and Reflexion's reported gains, then shows they vanish the moment the oracle correctness label used as a stopping criterion is removed (Table 1 gives the per-paper taxonomy).

Establishes the equal-inference-cost baseline as a norm — self-consistency at the same number of responses — and shows multi-agent debate only matches it at 3 responses and falls 5.2 points behind at 9, so the improvement is selection, not correction.

Falsifies the Self-Refine improvement by construction rather than argument: folding the feedback prompt's missing constraint into the initial prompt beats 7 self-correction calls using 1 call, identifying prompt asymmetry as the source of the claimed gain.
The negative result is not a sampling artifact of one model or decoding scheme: it replicates across four models, two temperatures (0 and 1), three benchmarks, and four different feedback prompts.
limitations: The paper's own Section 7 scope limit: this evaluates reasoning only, and the authors expect self-correction to remain useful where the model can actually assess the response, e.g. preference, style or safety alignment — the failure is specific to judging reasoning correctness.

Coverage is a fixed menu: four 2023-2024 models, at most two correction rounds, one three-step prompt template family, and 200 sampled questions per dataset for every model except GPT-3.5 (HotpotQA only 100, a size the authors themselves call too small for the Section 3.3 answer-change statistics, footnote 1). No variance or significance is reported anywhere.

The Section 4 debate replication is a re-implementation: same prompts but gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 on the full 1,319-question test set instead of the original's 100 examples, so the head-to-head is not bit-identical to Du et al.
Aim is measurement, not repair: it names external feedback (code executors, search, trained verifiers, humans) as the escape route but proposes and evaluates no new self-correction method of its own.
2310.01798.fits: Stage-3 negative control — the measurement discipline every self-correction claim in this catalog has to survive. Pairs directly with Reflexion and RCI (whose gains it traces to oracle labels), Self-Refine (its prompt-design critique), Du et al. multi-agent debate (the equal-cost baseline), and stage-4 verifier work, which is the external-feedback escape route it recommends.
2310.01798.reading: Read Section 3 (Tables 2-4 plus Figure 1's answer-change analysis), Section 4 (Table 7, debate vs self-consistency), Section 5 (Table 8, prompt design), and Section 7. Appendix A has the verbatim prompts.

2308.10144.tldr: ExpeL learns without gradients: it retries training tasks via Reflexion, distills same-task fail/success pairs and success batches into an editable natural-language insight list, and at test time concatenates those insights plus the k most task-similar past successes to a ReAct agent.
2308.10144.method: Three stages over a ReAct base, zero weight updates. (1) Gather: each training task is retried at most Z=3 times via Reflexion; every trajectory enters experience pool B (Faiss kNN + all-mpnet-base-v2, seeded with the manual fewshots) and each failure emits a self-reflection concatenated into the next attempt, so B holds successes and same-task fail/success pairs. (2) Extract: gpt-4-0613 (LLM_insights) is fed either a fail/success pair or a chunk of L successes (L=8 HotpotQA/ALFWorld, 4 WebShop) sampled without replacement, and rewrites the growing insight list through ADD / EDIT / UPVOTE / DOWNVOTE; a new insight starts at importance count 2, gains 1 on upvote or edit, loses 1 on downvote, and is deleted at 0. (3) Infer: one attempt per unseen task, task spec augmented with all of insights plus top-k task-similar successful trajectories (k=6 HotpotQA, 2 ALFWorld/WebShop).
results: HotpotQA (Table 3): ReAct 28.0 ± 1.4 → ExpeL 39.0 ± 1.7; ablations 32.0 ± 1.1 (human-crafted insights), 32.0 ± 0.4 (gpt-3.5-turbo as insight LLM), 29.0 ± 0.4 (reflections added to insight extraction).

ALFWorld (Table 3, retrieval ablation): ReAct 40.0 ± 0.3 → ExpeL 59.0 ± 0.3, with reason-similarity retrieval 48.5 ± 2.1 and random retrieval 42.5 ± 0.8. Per-category (Table 5), ExpeL vs ReAct: put 83 vs 50, look 39 vs 0, heat 43 vs 13.
WebShop (Table 5): mean environment reward ExpeL 0.701 vs ReAct 0.665 and Act 0.666; single-mode variants sit at 0.675 (insights-only) and 0.67 (retrieve-only), whose success rates are 37% / 38%.

The two learning modes are complementary and domain-specific: restricting to one gives HotpotQA 36% / 31% (insights / retrieve) and ALFWorld 50% / 55%, and an agent extracting insights from fewshots alone shows no gain over ReAct.

Transfer HotpotQA → FEVER (Table 1): Act 58 ± 0.0, ReAct 63 ± 0.4, ExpeL Transfer without task demos 65 ± 1.7, ExpeL Transfer 70 ± 0.7. Adding Reflexion retries on ALFWorld (Table 2): ExpeL 59.0 → 64.2 across R0–R3 vs ReAct+Reflexion 40.3 → 54.4.
advantages: Inter-task learning that pays off without retries at deployment: ExpeL's single-attempt ALFWorld 59.0 beats Reflexion's R3 54.4, so it improves where reattempts are unavailable, and it never needs model weights, making it usable with closed API models (GPT-4/Claude).

The ablations show each stage is load-bearing and not interchangeable: insights dominate HotpotQA (36 vs 31) while retrieved trajectories dominate ALFWorld (55 vs 50), and task-similarity ranking clearly beats reason-similarity (48.5) and random (42.5) retrieval.

Every artifact stays in natural language - insights and trajectories are inspectable, editable, deletable, and expert insights can be inserted - and autonomously learned insights beat hand-crafted ones (39.0 vs 32.0), with a stronger insight LLM lifting the ceiling (gpt-4 vs gpt-3.5: 39.0 vs 32.0).
Knowledge transfers across distributions with only a few target demonstrations: adapting HotpotQA insights with FEVER fewshots raises 63 ± 0.4 to 70 ± 0.7 without any target-task experience pool.
limitations: Text-only observations, by the authors' own account: image observations (via VLMs or captioning models) are left to future work, so the results do not cover real-world embodied settings.

All experiments use closed-source API LLMs (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 for policy/reflection, gpt-4-0613 for insights); open-source LLMs are named as untested future work, which the authors flag as off-limits in some applications.
The insight list is assumed to fit the context window; truly lifelong agents would need a retrieval step over insights to bound context, which is proposed but not implemented or evaluated.

Prompting lacks the theoretical grounding of RL (no optimality guarantee), and the paper concedes WebShop stays on the lower side of Reflexion's success range; reflections added to insight extraction hurt (29.0 vs 39.0) because they hallucinate.
2308.10144.fits: Stage 4's core experience-learning card: it converts Reflexion's intra-task trial-and-error into inter-task, no-gradient learning by distilling an editable insight list plus a retrieval pool. Pairs with Reflexion (the gathering loop it reuses), Voyager (skill library), ACE (context as the evolving artifact), EvolveR (experience into RL), A-MEM / MemoryBank (where the store itself becomes agentic), and stage-4 skill-evolution work.
2308.10144.reading: Read §4.1–4.3 (gathering, insight operators, task inference) with Algorithms 1–3 and Table 4's hyperparameters, then §5.2–5.6 for main results, transfer, retries and ablations, plus §6 limitations and Appendix H's real extracted insights.

2502.12110.tldr: A-MEM turns agent memory into a self-organizing Zettelkasten: each interaction becomes an LLM-annotated note (keywords, tags, context, embedding), new notes link to nearest neighbours and rewrite them, beating MemGPT/MemoryBank on LoCoMo while using ~1,200 tokens per operation.
2502.12110.method: Each interaction becomes one atomic note m = {content, timestamp, LLM keywords K, LLM tags G, LLM context X, embedding e, links L}. A note-construction prompt (Appendix B.1) makes a structured LLM call returning keywords/tags/context as JSON; e = encoder(concat(c,K,G,X)) with all-minilm-l6-v2. On write, cosine similarity against every stored note selects top-k neighbours (k=10 by default, tuned 10-50 per model and category, Table 8). A second LLM call then returns structured JSON - should_evolve, actions (strengthen, update_neighbor), suggested_connections, tags_to_update, new_context_neighborhood - which establishes the links and rewrites the neighbours' context and tags in place, so existing notes change as new ones arrive. Retrieval embeds the query, takes top-k by cosine, and (per Figure 2) co-accesses notes linked in the same 'box'. No weights are trained: all structure is inference-time LLM calls over a growing note store.
results: LoCoMo across six frozen models (Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Qwen2.5 1.5B/3B, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini): A-MEM takes the best average rank in every model (1.0-1.6) while no baseline ranks better than 2.0; it beats every baseline in every category for the non-GPT models, and on GPT models is 'at least two times better' on Multi-Hop (GPT-4o-mini: ROUGE-L 44.27 vs LoCoMo 18.09, METEOR 23.43 vs 7.61, SBERT 70.49 vs 52.30).

DialSim (Table 2, A-MEM vs LoCoMo vs MemGPT): F1 3.45 vs 2.55 vs 1.18 (+35% over LoCoMo, +192% over MemGPT), BLEU-1 3.37 vs 3.13 vs 1.07, ROUGE-L 3.54 vs 2.75 vs 0.96, ROUGE-2 3.60 vs 0.90 vs 0.42, METEOR 2.05 vs 1.64 vs 0.95, SBERT 19.51 vs 15.76 vs 8.54.

Ablation on GPT-4o-mini (Table 3), no link generation or evolution -> link generation only -> full A-MEM: Multi-Hop F1 9.65 -> 21.35 -> 27.02; Temporal 24.55 -> 31.24 -> 45.85; Single Hop 13.28 -> 39.17 -> 44.65; Adversarial 15.32 -> 44.16 -> 50.03; Open Domain 7.77 -> 10.13 -> 12.14.

Cost: roughly 1,200 tokens per memory operation (1,200-2,500 depending on model) against 16,900 for LoCoMo and MemGPT, an 85-93% reduction, under $0.0003 per operation; 5.4 s average per operation on GPT-4o-mini and 1.1 s on locally hosted Llama 3.2 1B.

Scaling (Table 4): retrieval latency 0.31 us at 1,000 notes, 0.38 at 10,000, 1.40 at 100,000, 3.70 at 1,000,000, versus ReadAgent's 43.62 / 484.45 / 6,682.22 / 120,069.68 us; storage is identical linear O(N) for A-MEM, MemoryBank and ReadAgent (1.46 MB at 1,000 notes rising to 1,464.84 MB at 1M).
advantages: The agency is in storage, not retrieval: A-MEM's second LLM call rewrites both the link graph and the text of existing notes, whereas agentic RAG (§2.2's own contrast) keeps a static knowledge base and only decides when/what to fetch. Nothing is pre-specified - no schema, no write points in the workflow, no fixed topology.

The ablation isolates both mechanisms with the right ordering: dropping link generation and evolution collapses Multi-Hop to 9.65 F1 and Adversarial to 15.32, restoring linking alone reaches 21.35 / 44.16, and evolution adds the rest - so the graph is load-bearing, not decoration.

It wins while being cheaper and scalable: ~1/10 the tokens of LoCoMo and MemGPT per operation, sub-microsecond retrieval that grows only ~12x from 1K to 1M notes (3.70 us, vs ReadAgent's 120,069 us), and no storage overhead over plain vector baselines.

Model-agnostic and released: works over six frozen backbones from 1B local (Ollama, LiteLLM structured output) to GPT-4o with zero weight updates, and both the benchmark code and a production memory service are public.
limitations: The paper's own first limitation: organization quality is bounded by the underlying LLM - different models generate different contexts and links, so the memory inherits the backbone's capability and variance.
The paper's own second limitation: text only. Multimodal memories (images, audio) are left as future work, and the whole note schema assumes textual interaction turns.

Memory only grows: the evolution prompt can name 'merge' and 'prune' actions, but §3.3 implements only in-place context/keyword/tag rewrites - there is no dedup, deletion or forgetting, and no audit of evolved-note quality or of how many generated links are wrong.

Evidence is conversational QA only (LoCoMo, DialSim) scored by F1/BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/SBERT, with k tuned per category and model against those same evaluation categories (Table 8); no downstream agent task, and no test of whether the shipped links survive beyond the benchmark.
2502.12110.fits: Stage 4's memory-organization centre: it lifts the Reflexion/ExpeL/ACE line from append-and-retrieve to self-linking, self-rewriting notes. Pairs with MemoryBank (a fixed decay curve where A-MEM has agentic reorganization), MemEvolve (which evolves the memory system itself and uses A-MEM as a baseline), EvolveR (experience into RL), and ACE (context as the evolving artifact).
2502.12110.reading: §3.1-3.4 for note construction, link generation, evolution and retrieval, with the Appendix B.1-B.3 prompt templates; §4.3 Table 3 ablation, §4.6 Table 4 scaling, §6 limitations. Read Table 1 on the page image - pdftotext scrambles its columns.

2305.10250.tldr: MemoryBank adds persistent long-term memory to frozen LLMs: timestamped dialogue logs with LLM-written event summaries and user portraits, FAISS dense retrieval, and an Ebbinghaus forgetting curve that decays unreinforced memories — demonstrated in SiliconFriend, an empathetic companion chatbot.
2305.10250.method: Storage has three tiers: timestamped multi-turn dialogue logs; LLM-generated daily event summaries rolled up into a global summary; and daily personality insights aggregated into a global user portrait (fixed prompts, e.g. "Summarize the events and key information in the content [dialog/events]"). Each dialogue turn and summary is a memory piece, embedded (MiniLM for English, Text2vec for Chinese) and indexed in FAISS via LangChain, DPR-style dual-tower retrieval. At interaction time the current conversation is the query; retrieved memories plus the global portrait and event summary are packed into the prompt. Updating applies the Ebbinghaus curve R = e^(−t/S): retention R decays with elapsed time t; strength S starts at 1 on first mention, and each recall increments S by 1 and resets t to 0, so re-accessed memories persist longer. Open-source variants add LoRA tuning (rank 16, 3 epochs, one A100) on 38k psychological dialogues.
results: Quantitative eval: 194 hand-written probing questions (97 English, 97 Chinese) over a simulated 10-day memory store of 15 ChatGPT-role-played users; human annotators scored retrieval accuracy, response correctness, coherence, and ranking (s = 1/rank).
SiliconFriend_ChatGPT is best overall: English retrieval 0.763, correctness 0.716, coherence 0.912, ranking 0.818 (Chinese: 0.711 / 0.655 / 0.675 / 0.758).

Open-source variants match or beat retrieval (BELLE 0.814 EN / 0.856 ZH; ChatGLM 0.809 / 0.84) but lag sharply on correctness (0.418–0.603) and coherence — attributed to weaker base models, not the memory layer.

Qualitatively, an online SiliconFriend platform collected real user conversations; the paper shows it recalling a recommended book and a quicksort request days later and correctly denying an undiscussed heap-sort session.
The forgetting curve itself is never quantified: no ablation or number isolates its effect, and the paper flags the model as exploratory.
advantages: Early (May 2023) mechanism giving both closed-source (ChatGPT) and open-source (ChatGLM 6.2B, BELLE 7B) LLMs persistent, evolving memory with no weight changes — the memory layer alone, plus optional LoRA for empathy tuning.
Forgetting-as-feature: time-decayed retention with reinforcement on recall (spacing effect) replaces append-only logs or fixed-window truncation with an anthropomorphic update policy.
Memory is more than retrieval: hierarchical daily-to-global summaries plus a user portrait let the bot adapt to personality, not just look up facts.
Practical and bilingual: swappable embedders and backbones, released as working SiliconFriend code.
limitations: The paper itself calls the Ebbinghaus update "exploratory and highly simplified": S is a bare integer counter, and no experiment measures whether forgetting helps or hurts.
Quantitative evaluation is fully simulated — ChatGPT role-plays all 15 users and generates the dialog history — with only 194 probing questions scored by annotators.
Summary-based storage discards detail: correctness for open-source backbones falls to 0.42–0.60, so specific recall is unreliable even when retrieval succeeds.
Scoped to companion/counseling interactions of 10 simulated days; far shorter than real long-horizon deployment.
2305.10250.fits: Stage 4's "memory as database with decay" baseline: an external store passively written, densely retrieved, and decayed by a hand-set curve — the update policy is fixed by design, never learned. A-MEM makes memory agentic (LLM organizes and links notes into a graph); MemEvolve evolves the memory system's own architecture.
2305.10250.reading: §2 covers the three components (storage 2.1, FAISS retrieval 2.2, Ebbinghaus update 2.3 — the R = e^(−t/S) rules); §3.1 for the 38k-dialogue LoRA tuning; Table 2 for all numbers. §4.1 examples are skippable.

2604.15097.tldr: Across 4,590 trials on 45 scientific code tasks, a compact ~230-token "strategy gene" beats documentation-heavy skill packages for test-time control (54.0% vs 49.9% avg) and carries evolved failure experience better.
2604.15097.method: A gene is a frozen-model control object injected through systemInstruction: ~230 tokens of signals_match (domain keywords), a one-sentence summary, an ordered strategy list with AVOID cues, and optional constraints/validation hooks, distilled from a skill document, prior trajectories, or a validated capsule. The Gene Evolution Protocol canonicalizes it and updates it through a six-stage loop — SCAN runtime traces and execution failures, SIGNAL (convert raw traces into standardized triggers), INTENT (repair, optimize, or extend), MUTATE (rewrite strategy steps, AVOID cues, or metadata), VALIDATE (sandbox execution against the validation hooks), SOLIDIFY (write the passing asset back into the gene/capsule store and log an immutable event). Genes are the atomic control unit; capsules record validated execution paths; events are the audit log. Base-model weights never change.
results: Headline (Table 1, 4,590 trials): Gene 54.0% average pass rate, +3.0pp over no guidance (51.0%); the full ~2,500-token Skill package scores 49.9% (−1.1pp). Skill lifts Flash 41.8→49.0% but drags Pro 60.1→50.7%; Gene holds Pro at 59.9% and lifts Flash to 48.2%.

Skill's usable signal is sparse (Table 12): Skill-Workflow 52.5% (+1.5pp) is the only clearly helpful section, while Skill-Overview 46.3% (−4.7pp) is the most harmful. Trimmed to Gene's ~230-token budget (Table 13), Skill-Pitfalls-Short reaches 52.0% (+1.0) and Skill-Workflow-Short 51.5% (+0.5) — closer, but still below Gene's 54.0%.

The gain is not brevity (Table 2): keywords-only 53.5% (+2.5pp) already beats keywords+summary at 51.0% (+0.0), and only the full keywords+summary+strategy gene reaches 54.0%. Reattaching documentation dilutes it (Table 3): Gene+API notes 51.5%, Gene+examples 52.0%, both below Gene alone. Naive composition fails (Table 4): two complementary genes 44.9% (−6.1pp), three 50.4%, two conflicting 53.2%, single gene 54.0%.

Structurally robust but content-sensitive (Table 14): inverted priority 52.8%, overconstrained 55.9% and stale paradigm 56.6% stay at or above clean Gene (54.0%), whereas wrong algorithm 48.8% and wrong domain 49.4% collapse it.

Evolution carrier (Tables 5–7): Gene+failure 52.0% beats Skill+failure 47.8% and freeform+failure 49.6%; flattening Gene into prose drops it to 50.5% (−0.5pp); failure-warnings-only reaches 54.4% (+4.6pp), the best condition in that probe, above strategy-only 52.3% and both mixed orderings. On CritPt, Evolver (Gene) 2026-02-16 scores 18.57% vs 9.1% for Gemini 3 Pro Preview (+9.47), and the 2026-03-26 run 27.14% vs 17.7% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (+9.44), at ~$0.81 in observed input/output tokens — the authors' own estimate, ~32.1× below the reported $26 benchmark cost.
advantages: The largest controlled probe of experience representation in this catalog: 4,590 retained trials over 45 scenarios, two fixed models, one shared pipeline (T=0.05, 16,384 max output tokens, control injected through systemInstruction separately from the task in contents, 120s sandbox timeout), so deltas isolate the representation rather than the task set or decoding.

It separates packaging from content twice. Budget-matched ~230-token Skill fragments still lose to Gene, and the same gene flattened into prose loses most of its +3.0pp — so the win is control-oriented schema, not token count. Reattaching the documentation Gene deliberately dropped always loses.

It shows experience accumulation must be selective rather than additive: failure-warnings-only (54.4%, +4.6pp) beats both mixed strategy/failure bundles, and naive composition of nominally complementary genes is the worst condition measured (44.9%, −6.1pp) — a concrete negative result against the bag-of-skills assumption.

GEP is a real protocol rather than a prompt format: typed gene/capsule/event objects, an explicit six-stage loop, an open reference implementation (EvoMap/skill2gep), and a demonstrated end-to-end payoff on CritPt where the base weights never change.
limitations: Scope is 45 scientific code-solving scenarios scored by Python checkpoints under two Gemini 3.1 models; no non-code domain, no second model family, and no seed variance or confidence intervals, so the ~1pp scale of several deltas is not bracketed.
It is a self-described "beta technical report" with no limitations section; capsules and events are "paper-side formalizations" that are never empirically evaluated — only the gene layer is tested.

Reuse has an unresolved scope boundary: naive composition of complementary genes collapses to 44.9% and reattaching documentation always loses, so the paper can demonstrate when Gene fails but not yet how to select or combine genes in practice.

The CritPt evidence is two ~2-day single runs of two successive versions against their own paired base models (+9.47, +9.44), with no seed variance and no ablation of which genes carried the gain across 70 tasks, 210 gene slots and 36 gene IDs; the $0.81 cost figure excludes reasoning tokens by the authors' own caveat, and several perturbations actually beat the clean gene (overconstrained 55.9%, stale paradigm 56.6% vs 54.0%), which the authors explain only post hoc — the mechanism is not fully characterized.
2604.15097.fits: Stage 4's skill-library / context-as-evolving-artifact line: it stress-tests the Voyager–ACE assumption that richer structured experience helps, finding the control signal sparse and packaging-dependent, then bridges to stage 5 with an evolution-ready object. Pairs with SkillOpt (skill doc as trained parameter), ACE's playbook bullets, MetaSkill-Evolve, MemEvolve and EvolveR.
2604.15097.reading: §3.3 for the gene schema and GEP; §4.1–4.3 with Tables 1–7 for the three probes; §4.4/Fig. 5 and Appendix D for the CritPt evolution runs; Appendix A for the six-stage protocol loop.

2602.07755.tldr: ALMA meta-learns the memory design itself: a GPT-5 Meta Agent searches memory designs written as executable Python, reflecting on archived designs and their eval logs, and the discovered designs beat Trajectory Retrieval, ReasoningBank, Dynamic Cheatsheet and G-Memory on all four sequential-decision benchmarks.
2602.07755.method: The Meta Agent (GPT-5) runs open-ended exploration over memory designs expressed as executable Python — code is the search space, so Turing completeness theoretically admits any design. Designs implement two abstract classes: MemoStructure with general_update/general_retrieve orchestrating sub-module layers, and Sub_memo_layer with its own update/retrieve and optional database; layers chain, so one sub-module's output feeds the next. Each step samples up to 5 archived designs without replacement (probability set by success rate and inverse visit count, tau=0.5, alpha=0.5 visit penalty, all probabilities non-zero), reflects on the sampled design's source, success rate and interaction logs to plan, implements a new design in code, trial-runs it (up to 3 debugger reflections on runtime errors), then evaluates and archives it with metrics and logs. 11 steps discover 43 designs. Evaluation is two-phase: memory is collected from memory-free trajectories, then deployment success rate is measured (static mode during learning, dynamic mode for distribution shift).
results: GPT-5-nano agentic system, four benchmarks: overall success 6.1% (no memory) to 12.3% (+6.2) for the best-learned design, above every human baseline (G-Memory 7.7, Trajectory Retrieval 8.6, ReasoningBank 7.5, Dynamic Cheatsheet 7.2); ALFWorld 2.9% to 12.4% (+9.5), Baba Is AI 9.5% to 19.0% (+9.5).

Transferred unchanged to a stronger GPT-5-mini agentic system: overall 41.1% (no memory) to 53.9% (+12.8), again above all human baselines; ALFWorld 67.6% to 87.1% (+19.5). The 12.8 vs 6.2 delta of 6.6% exceeds that of every human-designed memory, i.e. learned designs help stronger models more.

Ablation, greedy search on ALFWorld at the same 43-design budget: best-learned 11.9% (GPT-5-nano) and 77.1% (GPT-5-mini) versus 12.4% and 87.1% from open-ended exploration — the archive's stepping-stone sampling is what buys the gain.

Task distribution shift (memory collected from 70 valid-seen ALFWorld tasks, deployed in dynamic mode on valid unseen, GPT-5-mini): learned design 84.1%, outperforming all human baselines; Fig. 4 shows it also reaches higher success sooner as collection task count grows (better sample efficiency).

Cost (Fig. 6): 53.9% average success at $0.09 end-to-end memory cost, lower than all handcrafted baselines, with 1,319 retrieved tokens per task versus 9,149 (Trajectory Retrieval), 6,095 (G-Memory) and 2,258 (Dynamic Cheatsheet).
advantages: The searched object is the memory architecture itself — which databases exist (embedding, graph, dictionary), what is stored, how it is retrieved and updated — as one evolvable Python file, so it sits a meta-level above this catalog's fixed memory designs (ACE playbooks, G-Memory, Dynamic Cheatsheet) rather than tuning them.

It specializes per domain instead of reusing one recipe: Fig. 3 shows learned ALFWorld/TextWorld designs built on spatial relations, affordance graphs and trajectory schemas, while Baba Is AI and MiniHack designs converge on abstract strategy libraries and plan synthesis.

Open-ended archive search is shown to beat greedy selection at equal exploration budget (Appendix C.2, Fig. 14), and the resulting code plus logs are the artifact — the learned design transfers across evaluator FMs without retuning.

Efficiency falls out without being optimized for: no cost term in the objective, yet the best-learned design is cheaper per memory than every handcrafted baseline, which the authors read as an argument for adding multi-objective Pareto search as future work.
limitations: Memory designs are learned offline against a fixed learning set; the authors deliberately skip online learning of designs because evaluating each candidate needs many rollouts and would blow the compute budget — an adaptive continual learner should discover designs from dynamic data.

Scope is token-level memory only: parametric and latent memory are explicitly out of scope, chosen because explicit token memory evaluates faster without extra model training and is more interpretable and transferable.

Model-generated memory code executes inside the agentic loop, so designs are run in isolated sandboxes and human-inspected for harmful behavior such as prompt injection; the paper calls for systematic inspection as the system scales.

Evidence is four text-based sequential decision-making benchmarks (ALFWorld, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack) with one fixed agentic system per run; each domain needs its own 11-step, 43-design search.
2602.07755.fits: Stage 4 (Harness-level RSI), Context & Memory Evolution: the memory-design-as-search-space counterpart to ACE's context playbooks and MemEvolve's meta-evolution of memory systems — ALMA's related work names MemEvolve as the concurrent work, contrasting open-ended archive search with MemEvolve's handcrafted initializations plus greedy selection. It replaces the fixed memory loops of Reflexion and ExpeL.
2602.07755.reading: §3.1–3.3 (code search space, two-phase evaluation, archive sampling); §4.1–4.4 with Table 1 for the numbers; Appendix A.1 for the MemoStructure/Sub_memo_layer classes, A.6 pseudocode, C.2 greedy ablation, Fig. 6 cost.

2607.14159.tldr: MemoHarness splits an agent harness into six editable control dimensions, searches them from its own executions into a dual-layer experience bank, then retrieves that experience at test time to build a case-specific harness — 0.806 vs Codex's 0.722 on Terminal-Bench.
2607.14159.method: Phase A searches a six-dimensional harness space — D1 context assembly, D2 tool/retrieval, D3 decoding, D4 orchestration topology, D5 cross-call memory, D6 output post-processing — starting from a minimal W0 with all optional components off. Each of T=10 rounds the controller issues a structured query over the bank, retrieves a bounded slice, proposes W_t, runs it on every labeled search case, and writes a per-case entry: case features, configuration delta, trajectory, reward, token cost, and a diagnosis {success, primary failure dimension (D1–D6), secondary dimensions, analysis}. A diagnostic operator maps verifier outcomes, exceptions, timeouts and missing artifacts to a dimension; distillation fires after M=5 new entries or N=3 consecutive failures. W* is selected lexicographically — mean reward first, token cost only as tiebreaker. Phase B freezes W*, retrieves the K nearest successful and failed training cases plus feature-matched patterns, and emits a case-specific W(x) with no labels, feedback or extra search.
results: Terminal-Bench (18-task held-out split, GPT-5.3-Codex): MemoHarness 0.806 vs the strongest baseline Codex 0.722 (+0.084), and +0.250 to +0.445 over Claude Code, OpenCode and Terminus.

Final validation-selected harness beats base on all three benchmarks: 0.722 → 0.806 (Terminal-Bench), 0.900 → 0.967 (LiveCodeBench), 0.600 → 0.767 (FinanceAgent). The shipped harness sits below the in-training peak on two of them — LiveCodeBench touches 1.000 at iteration 3 and Terminal-Bench 0.833 at iteration 4 — and only the long-horizon workload keeps improving across the 10 rounds (FinanceAgent 42.5% → a 65.0% peak near iterations 8–9, versus LiveCodeBench oscillating in a 91.2%–95.0% band).

Cross-model transfer with no retraining: every one of six held-out base models improves on Terminal-Bench, mean +0.098, from +0.038 (GPT-4.1, 0.500 → 0.538) to +0.233 (GLM-5, 0.500 → 0.733). The source model keeps its +0.084.

Cross-dataset transfer is positive but selective (Table 2, shared Codex). The Terminal-Bench-derived harness lifts MMMLU 0.818 → 0.848 and StrongReject 0.879 → 0.909 (+0.030 each) and SWE-Bench Pro 0.706 → 0.765 (+0.059); saturated HumanEvalFix (1.000) and Reasoning-Gym-Easy (0.947) do not move, and LawBench is mixed.

Cost: MemoHarness pulls more input (14.18M tokens) but 13.32M of it is cached, giving $6.89 on the 18-task split vs $10.28 for Codex and $9.51 for Claude Code at higher accuracy; Terminus ($6.68) and OpenCode ($2.34) stay cheaper at substantially lower success.
advantages: Test-time adaptation with no test-time signal at all: the case-specific harness is built from only (instruction, case features) plus the frozen bank — no labels, no feedback, no gradient updates, no extra search rounds. That is what lets simple cases stay lightweight while retrieval-heavy or format-sensitive cases invoke richer orchestration, an axis AFlow/DSPy-style training-time optimizers do not have.

It moves the object of optimization from a narrow artifact to the whole control layer. Prompt optimizers (OPRO, Promptbreeder), pipeline compilers (DSPy, MIPRO, TextGrad) and workflow searchers (AFlow, AutoFlow) each edit one slice; Meta-Harness searches harness code but still ships a single training-time artifact for all cases, which is exactly the gap MemoHarness's Phase B fills.

The bank stores diagnosis, not just a score. Because each entry carries the configuration delta and a dimension-level failure attribution, the paper can run an operation-level transition analysis (Appendix G): newly appearing cat, sed, which and test coincide with reward increases at +59.5, +23.2, +20.2 and +17.3 pp over the ~13.2% all-transition baseline, while curl (−2.1), echo (−2.5) and grep (−7.9) are flat or negative — attribution a scalar score curve cannot supply.

Correctness-first selection keeps search off cheap-but-wrong harnesses: reward ranks candidates and token cost only breaks ties, and dollar cost is computed offline rather than optimized — yet the cacheable retrieved context still lands the system below two commercial baselines in cost.
limitations: The primary evaluation is an 18-task held-out split (80/20 of the 89-task suite, seed 42) reporting point estimates with no confidence intervals or significance tests, so results are evidence under one fixed protocol rather than a statistical characterization (Appendix A).

Not every baseline is a pure scaffold transplant with the same model and runtime surface, and Meta-Harness — the closest prior system — was not run at all, because no public implementation suitable for the evaluation stack existed when experiments were finalized; the comparison is qualitative.

No component ablation: the experience bank, the distilled global patterns and the case-specific test-time adaptation are not separately isolated, so how much of the gain each contributes is unmeasured — the authors name this explicitly as open.

The cost result depends on the observed cacheability of retrieved experience (lower cache reuse would change the profile), transfer is selective rather than uniform (LawBench mixed, saturated suites unmoved), and the controller and diagnostic operators are heuristic instantiations that future work should replace with learned ones.
2607.14159.fits: Stage 5 harness-level RSI at its case-adaptive end: the evolved artifact is the control layer itself, not a prompt or pipeline. Closest neighbours are Meta-Harness (searches harness code but ships one static artifact) and AutoHarness; its no-feedback per-case step complements Continual Harness's reset-free online loop. Pairs with ADAS/AFlow as training-time ancestors and ACE for context-level experience reuse.
2607.14159.reading: §2.2–2.6 for the six dimensions, the dual-layer bank, lexicographic correctness-first selection and the no-feedback adaptation rule; §3.2 with Figure 2, Tables 2–4 for the numbers; Appendix A for the limitations and Appendix G for the operation-level lift analysis.

2607.26784.tldr: SkillRise trains one policy to alternate between solving a task and rewriting a textual skill document it hands to the next task, supervised by decoupled credit assignment over ordered sequences of related tasks (+2.3–8.5 pp over GiGPO).
2607.26784.method: Sequences are built by partitioning instances on environment-provided family metadata, greedily grouping diverse instances, then ordering them simple→complex by task attributes (WebShop: product category, ascending required attributes/options); training uses K=3. One shared policy π_θ plays two roles under role-specific prompts: it solves task x_i conditioned on the textual skill document S_{i-1}, then rewrites that whole document from (S_{i-1}, τ_i, r_i), with S_0=∅ and only S_i crossing to the next task — earlier trajectories never enter a later solving context. N=8 independent trials per sequence each evolve their own document. Credit is decoupled: solving is scored by the current reward r_i, curation by the discounted Σ_{j>i} γ^{j-i} r_j (γ=0.6), and group-relative advantages are computed per sequence position and phase so the two roles never baseline each other; a clipped PPO-style objective then updates both jointly. Curation prompts mandate abstraction, grounding in the observed attempt, pitfalls, and concision.
results: Qwen3-4B Pass@1: 85.9% ALFWorld, 84.4% WebShop, 54.6% ScienceWorld — beating the strongest baseline GiGPO (83.6 / 77.3 / 46.1) by +2.3, +7.1, +8.5 points.

Within-task generalization despite cross-task training (Pass@3, retrying the same held-out task with the carried document): 92.2 / 96.1 / 61.0, ahead of the strongest baseline by 0.8 / 1.6 / 5.5 points and of LaMer — trained explicitly on repeated same-task attempts — by 0.8 / 1.6 / 14.2 points.

Cross-task test-time scaling (ALFWorld, same 128 held-out tasks repartitioned into sequences of length K, each attempted only once): 83.6% at K=2 → 87.5% at K=6, while GRPO, GiGPO and LaMer show no sustained growth; the margin over the strongest baseline widens from 3.9 to 8.6 points.
Backbone scaling on ALFWorld: Qwen3-1.7B 78.1% vs GRPO 75.0 (+3.1 points); Qwen3-4B 85.9% vs 79.7 (+6.2), with SkillRise gaining +7.8 points from 1.7B→4B against +4.7 (GRPO) and +3.3 (LaMer).

Pipeline efficiency: 85.9% ALFWorld average matches RetroAgent (85.9%) and beats SkillRL by 12.5 points while RetroAgent and SkillRL need 6.0× and 4.3× SkillRise's end-to-end runtime under the same 8×H800 configuration.
advantages: Makes the skill artifact itself the supervised object: the document is the sole channel between tasks, so later-task outcomes score curation directly — removing the extraction/retrieval/execution entanglement that makes multi-stage pipelines (RetroAgent's memory buffer plus utility updates, SkillRL's teacher distillation + SkillBank + cold-start SFT + retrieval) hard to attribute.

Shows the learned curation policy transfers outside its training regime: it wins repeated same-task attempts (Pass@2/3) even though trained only across distinct tasks, and yields monotone cross-task test-time scaling where each task gets one attempt — so the gain is reusable procedure, not extra sampling of one instance.

Genuinely compact end-to-end: one policy, no external teacher, no separate memory store or retrieval module (SkillRL's reproduction needs Gemini-2.5-Pro as teacher), and the result is robust to the cross-task discount — γ∈{0.3,0.4,0.6,0.7} converge within roughly one point.

The curation ablation isolates the mechanism: a no-curation variant with the same K=3 related-task sequences and the same interaction budget trails SkillRise by about 3 points and GRPO by more than 6, so sequencing related tasks alone is not enough — the explicit rewrite step carries the improvement.
limitations: Assumes task-family metadata: sequences come from environment-provided family labels plus hand-chosen difficulty attributes (product category, attribute/option counts); automatically discovering relatedness in open-ended task streams is left open (§8).
Narrow evidence base: three text benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld) with verifiable outcome rewards, 128 held-out instances each, and backbones capped at Qwen3-4B for compute reasons.

Training sequences are K=3 while test-time scaling is probed up to K=6, so the longest-horizon behavior is extrapolation; and the no-curation ablation's ~3-point gap suggests the headline gains rest mostly on related-task sequencing plus a modest curation increment.

The document is sequence-local and thrown away per sequence (every trial restarts from S_0=∅), so there is no accumulating lifelong skill library; curation quality is also bounded by the policy's own reflection ability, with the rewrite rules (abstract, ground, extract pitfalls, stay concise) hand-authored per environment.
2607.26784.fits: Stage 4 (Memory, Reflection & Skills), subsection Self-Evolving Agent Frameworks — the bridge from Voyager-style hand-curated skill libraries to agentic RL, showing the curation step itself can be trained. Pairs with LaMer (same-task Meta-RL), the SkillRL/RetroAgent pipelines it undercuts on cost, and stage-5 skill-internalization work (SkillOS, Skill0).
2607.26784.reading: §3.1–3.3 for sequence construction, the two-phase solution/curation rollout, and decoupled credit assignment (Eqs. 3–8); §4.2 Tables 1–2 for headline numbers; §5.1 for cross-task test-time scaling; Appendix A for the verbatim curation prompts.

2512.18746.tldr: MemEvolve treats the agent's memory architecture itself — Encode/Store/Retrieve/Manage — as the evolvable object: an outer loop diagnoses each candidate's failures and redesigns its four modules, lifting Flash-Searcher and SmolAgent by up to 17.06 points on agentic benchmarks.
2512.18746.method: Any memory system is abstracted as a genotype Omega = (Encode, Store, Retrieve, Manage) inside EvolveLab, which re-implements 12 published memories on one BaseMemoryProvider ABC. Each iteration k runs two nested loops. Inner: every candidate Omega_j starts from an empty memory base and populates it over a 60-task batch (40 fresh + 20 reused from the previous iteration), scoring each trajectory into f = (task success, token cost, latency). Outer: summaries F_j = (Perf, -Cost, -Delay) are ranked by non-dominated Pareto sort, ties broken by Perf; the top-K = 1 parent survives, and Diagnose-and-Design replays that parent's own trajectories to emit a structured defect profile across its four modules (retrieval failures, ineffective abstractions, storage inefficiencies), from which an LLM designs S = 3 executable descendants that edit only the permissible implementation sites. Three iterations, seeded from one hand-built memory (AgentKB); the best descendant is then frozen and re-deployed.
results: Flash-Searcher + GPT-5-mini with the TaskCraft-evolved memory, no dataset-specific meta-evolution: GAIA 69.09 -> 73.33 pass@1, xBench-DS 69.0 -> 74.0, WebWalkerQA 71.18 -> 74.71 — a 3.53-5.0 point gain on all three, matching the paper's stated 3.54%~5.0% range.

SmolAgent + GPT-5-mini rises from xBench pass@1 51.0 to 57.0 and pass@3 68.0, and reaches GAIA pass@3 72.12 — comparable to AgentKB's 73.94 while skipping AgentKB's large offline knowledge base. Flash-Searcher + MemEvolve hits GAIA pass@3 80.61, above CK-Pro pass@3 (75.15) and OWL-Workforce (60.61).

Cross-LLM transfer with the GPT-5-mini-evolved memory, no manual adaptation: Kimi K2 goes WebWalkerQA 52.35 -> 69.41 (+17.06 points) and TaskCraft 58.00 -> 68.00 (+10.0); DeepSeek V3.2 goes WebWalkerQA 69.41 -> 72.35.

The seven re-implemented human-designed memories give no consistent gain under the same framework. ExpeL underperforms No-Memory on all three (GAIA 66.06 vs 69.09; xBench 64.00 vs 69.00; WebWalkerQA 69.41 vs 71.18) and DILU costs 2.42 points on GAIA (66.67 vs 69.09).

Gains are not bought with tokens: GAIA API cost per query $0.085 vs $0.086 no-memory, xBench $0.136 vs $0.141, WebWalkerQA cheaper at $0.040 vs $0.048 — but wall-clock latency rises (GAIA 693.33s vs 505.46s).
advantages: Moves the evolvable object one level down: instead of hand-picking a memory schema and only filling it with experience, MemEvolve bilevel-optimizes the schema — inner loop evolves the experience base, outer loop evolves the architecture — with an explicit fitness vector covering quality, cost and latency rather than accuracy alone.

The four-module genotype is what makes architecture search tractable: every descendant must be an executable configuration of (Encode, Store, Retrieve, Manage) inheriting one ABC, so evolved memories stay valid and pluggable instead of degenerating into unparseable prompt soup.

EvolveLab is a reusable artifact in its own right: 12 unified memory re-implementations, online and offline evaluation modes, and LLM-as-Judge or exact-match protocols — a fair arena for comparing memory designs that did not previously exist.

The evolution trace is inspectable and legible: AgentKB's frozen encode/store becomes an Adaptive Decision system (nine skill granularities), then a Meta Memory system (four-level trajectory storage plus an LLM retrieval guardrail), then Riva, then Cerebra — which distills reusable tools and adds periodic database maintenance.
limitations: The search is a shallow local hill-climb, not open-ended evolution: 3 iterations, survivor budget K = 1, S = 3 descendants per round, 60 trajectories per evaluation, and a single fixed seed architecture (AgentKB). No ablation isolates how much of the gain comes from the architecture versus from merely having richer retrieval context.

Gains are bounded by the host framework, on the authors' own account — "memory is not a panacea and remains bounded by the capabilities of the underlying agentic framework." On GAIA, MemEvolve on SmolAgent only matches AgentKB (72.12 vs 73.94 pass@3).

The cost of meta-evolution itself is never reported: three rounds x three candidates x 60 deep-research rollouts of search overhead, in dollars and wall-clock, is unaccounted for against the per-task cost table.

Transfer is intra-regime. The authors concede memories evolved on TaskCraft are unlikely to transfer to fundamentally different task families (e.g. embodied action) where environments, action spaces and tool sets differ substantially — cross-task generalization is demonstrated only among web/deep-research benchmarks.
2512.18746.fits: Stage 4 (Memory, Reflection & Skills), advancing the memory line from fixed substrates to the memory architecture as the search object. Pairs with the fixed memories it re-implements and beats (ExpeL, AgentKB, Dynamic Cheatsheet) and with stage-5 scaffold search (ADAS, DGM), which evolves the agent rather than its memory.
2512.18746.reading: Read §3.2 for the (Encode, Store, Retrieve, Manage) abstraction, §4.2 for Diagnose-and-Design (Pareto ranking, defect profile, S=3 descendants), §5.3 Table 3 for the memory bake-off, and §5.4 with Figure 6 for the AgentKB->Riva->Cerebra path.

2607.05297.tldr: MetaSkill-Evolve makes skill self-improvement recursive: every branch carries a task skill plus a meta-skill m=(ψ,σ,α,π,ε) that parameterises the Analyzer/Retriever/Allocator/Proposer/Evolver pipeline, updated on a slower loop by that same pipeline. Frozen Gemma-4 31B gains +23.54/+16.09/+1.92 on OfficeQA/SealQA/ALFWorld.
2607.05297.method: Each branch state b=(s,m,h) pairs a Markdown task skill s, a branch-local meta-skill m=(ψ,σ,α,π,ε) — one SKILL.md per pipeline agent (Analyzer, Retriever, Allocator, Proposer, Evolver) — and iteration history. Fast loop: restore the branch snapshot from a SQLite DAG, score s on Dtrain, take the worst example, then Analyzer(ψ) emits a ≤15-word failure tag plus diagnosis, Retriever(σ) pulls same-/cross-branch inspirations by tag match (3× over-fetch, LLM re-rank), Allocator(α) sets child budget K∈[1,3], and K Proposer/Evolver children are written to disk, scored on Dval, and committed to the archive only when ΔU>0. Every H=2 iterations the slow loop folds the window's mean ΔU into a synthetic meta-failure trace and reruns the same five agents over the meta-skill files themselves — all five co-edited per round, Proposer sequential, Evolvers parallel. Parents are chosen by η1U+η2P̂+η3N.
results: Held-out test accuracy with a single frozen Gemma-4 31B shared by all five pipeline agents: 55.32% OfficeQA, 45.26% SealQA, 94.23% ALFWorld — +23.54 / +16.09 / +1.92 over the No-Skill backbone (31.78 / 29.17 / 92.31).

The progression is monotonic on both QA benchmarks: Static skill 36.09 / 29.41 (+4.31 / +0.24 over No-Skill), Single-Level Evolution 48.94 / 37.21 (+12.85 / +7.80 over static), full system 55.32 / 45.26 — so the slow loop alone contributes +6.38 / +8.05 points over the identical fast loop with the meta-skill frozen.
ALFWorld is near ceiling (No-Skill 92.31%): the static skill regresses to 90.38, single-level evolution recovers exactly to 92.31, and the whole +1.92 comes from meta-skill updates.

Component ablation (§4.3, Table 3): −α (Allocator frozen at K=2) costs 19.7 points on OfficeQA (55.32→35.58) and −π 17.7 (→37.59), but on SealQA the dominant component flips to π (45.26→36.84), and on ALFWorld π again (94.23→86.54) — no single ablation matches the full system.

Horizon sweep with three meta-updates held fixed: H=2 beats H=8 everywhere (OfficeQA 48.94→41.35→39.84, SealQA 44.14 / 44.14 / 43.24, ALFWorld 90.38 / 90.38 / 88.46), and removing only cross-branch retrieval returns ALFWorld exactly to the Single-Level 92.31.
advantages: Names and optimises the quantity fixed-meta evolution ignores: meta-productivity P(m|s) = expected per-child ΔU over K proposals, estimated as the mean ΔU of a node's children, balanced against utility and novelty in the frontier score η1U+η2P̂+η3N with N=1/(1+times_selected). Each η=0 ablation exposes a distinct failure mode (locked high-utility nodes, single-lineage collapse, noisy single-child gains), so frontier selection is the interpretable lever rather than a hidden heuristic.

The recursion costs nothing architecturally: every meta-skill component is a Markdown SKILL.md in the same format the pipeline already consumes, so the identical five agents improve m with no extra model, no fine-tuning and no new objective — a bounded, one-level reflexive application of the improvement operator to itself.

Two typed stages beyond the standard analyze→propose→evolve loop: a Retriever for cross-branch sharing (p_cross=0.2, L_same=3, L_cross=2, plus inspiration edges in the graph) and an Allocator whose adaptive child budget widens after stagnation — the OfficeQA result says the widening is what produces a successful child at all.

Full provenance in a persistent SQLite DAG: lineage and inspiration edges, failed children (ΔU≤0) retained as inspiration even though ineligible as parents, and branch state restored from the node record before each iteration so lineages cannot leak into each other and previously deprioritised branches can be revisited.
limitations: The recursion is bounded and one-level: the five-agent pipeline's roles and wiring are themselves fixed — only the meta-skill files evolve, a limitation the paper states explicitly.
Evidence covers three curated benchmarks with verifiable rewards; transfer to open-ended, long-horizon real-world tasks with noisier feedback is untested (paper's own limitation).

The meta-update horizon H is a fixed hyperparameter, not adaptively scheduled: defaulting to H=2 and sweeping to H=8 costs 9.1 points on OfficeQA, so results are coupled to a hand-tuned stability/reactivity trade-off.

The budget is small and the splits are thin — the default run is 5 fast iterations with two meta-updates scored on roughly 87–107 test items — and on saturated ALFWorld a small validation split starves the loop of failures (enlarging val 0.10→0.25 at tr=0.15 lifts 90.57→93.02).
2607.05297.fits: Stage 4 (Memory, Reflection & Skills) / harness-level scaffold evolution — the definitional RSI move applied to skills: the improver is itself improved, on its own timescale. Pairs with DGM/HyperAgents (self-modifying scaffolds), GEPA and prompt evolution, and the skill-library line (SkillWeaver, AutoSkill, EvoSkill); the minimal template for meta-level recursion without code-level self-modification.
2607.05297.reading: §3.2–3.5 for the meta-skill tuple, the SQLite evolution graph with P̂/N frontier scoring, and Algorithms 1–2; §4.2 Table 1 for main results; §4.3 Table 3 for ablations; App. D for defaults (η1=1.0, η2=0.5, η3=0.25, H=2, Kmax=3).

2604.25850.tldr: Harness engineering is manual; AHE automates it with three observability pillars — components as files, trajectories distilled into a layered evidence corpus, each edit bound to a falsifiable prediction. Ten iterations lift Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 from 69.7% to 77.0%, past Codex and prompt-only self-evolution.
2604.25850.method: A closed loop over a decoupled NexAU harness whose seven component types — system prompt, tool description, tool implementation, middleware, skill, sub-agent config, long-term memory — each live in a workspace file, so one edit is one git commit.
