2403.08715.reading: §2.1 (SOTOPIA-EVAL dimensions), §3 (pipeline + filtering), §5 with Fig 4 and Tables 1-2, §6 (safety, MMLU); Appendix B.2 for exact filtering rules and Table 5 for full per-dimension numbers.

2412.21139.tldr: SWE-Gym: the first executable training environment for SWE agents — 2,438 Python task instances from 11 repos — on which rejection-sampling fine-tuning plus a trained verifier lift a 32B open model to 32.0% on SWE-Bench Verified.
2412.21139.method: SWE-Gym is built from 358 filtered Python repos (>500 stars, >500 PRs, created before July 2022): 64,689 SWE-Bench-style instances (SWE-Gym Raw), of which 11 repos get semi-manually installed dependencies and gold-patch unit-test validation, yielding 2,438 executable instances (plus a 230-instance SWE-Gym Lite) and 6 TB of Docker images. Agents (OpenHands CodeAct, MoatlessTools) roll out against that runtime, whose expert tests supply the reward. Policy training is rejection-sampling fine-tuning (filtered behavior cloning) on 491 off-policy success trajectories from GPT-4o-2024-08-06 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (~19 turns, ~19k tokens each), full-parameter FT of Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 7B/14B/32B (lr 1e-4, <=5 epochs, 32k context). The verifier is an outcome-supervised reward model: the same 32B model fine-tuned to emit <YES>/<NO> over 1,318 success + 1,318 failure trajectories (2,636 total), scoring r = exp(l_YES)/(exp(l_YES)+exp(l_NO)) from SGLang logprobs to rerank k rollouts.
results: OpenHands + Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct-32B fine-tuned on only 491 SWE-Gym trajectories: SWE-Bench Lite 3.0% -> 15.3% (+12.3) and Verified 7.0% -> 20.6% (+13.6); the 7B model goes 1.0% -> 10.0% (Lite) and 1.8% -> 10.6% (Verified) (Table 3).

Training fixes agentic behavior, not just patches: stuck-in-loop rate falls 4.6-18.6 points (7B on Verified 39.6% -> 21.0%; 32B Verified 29.4% -> 23.8%), with empty-patch rate dropping in parallel (7B Lite 40.3% -> 29.7%).

Verifier reranking on SWE-Bench Verified (32B agent + 32B verifier, OpenHands): Best@k 20.6@1 -> 29.8@8 -> 32.0@16, while Pass@k reaches 37.8@8 and 42.8@16; a LoRA verifier beats full-parameter fine-tuning (29.8@8 vs 27.2@8). This 32.0/26.0 is the best open-weight result in the paper's comparison.

The same recipe transfers scaffolds: MoatlessTools verifiers on SWE-Bench Lite move the 7B policy 10% -> 13.3% and the 32B policy 19.7% -> 26.3% at k=8 (t=0.5); the 7B verifier plateaus after k=4 while the 32B one still improves at k=8.

Verifier training data matters: mixing on- and off-policy trajectories reaches 27@8, whereas off-policy-only training plateaus around 22%; MoatlessTools self-improvement moves the 7B model 7.0% -> 9.0% -> 10.0% over two rejection-sampling iterations, and 32B only 19.0% -> 19.7% then flat.
advantages: First executable SWE training environment: unlike SWE-Bench's train split (solutions as patches only, no runtime) or isolated/synthetic sets (HumanEval, APPS, R2E), it ships repo-level tasks with pre-installed dependencies and expert-test reward signals, and releases everything — 6 TB of Docker images, model weights, trajectories and the training pipeline. In its comparison table it is the only row with both model and environment open.

Shows SWE capability is trainable from very little data: 491 trajectories buy double-digit absolute gains, and performance keeps improving as training trajectories scale 25% -> 50% -> 100% with no saturation at the sampling limit — including when deduplicated by instance or by repository — so the bottleneck is sampling compute rather than SWE-Gym's size or repo diversity.

The trajectory data teaches the agentic loop itself: fine-tuning markedly reduces stuck-in-loop and empty-patch rates, addressing the failure mode that most limits open-weight models under general-purpose prompting.
A trained verifier makes inference-time compute pay: Best@k rises roughly log-linearly with rollouts to 32.0% on Verified and 26.0% on Lite, reaching open-weight SOTA with a 32B model.
limitations: Self-improvement largely fails with this recipe: MoatlessTools rejection sampling gains only 7.0% -> 10.0% (7B) and 19.0% -> 19.7% (32B, then flat), and mixing 868 on-policy with 491 off-policy trajectories on OpenHands regressed SWE-Bench Lite 15.3% -> 8.7%. The authors attribute this to filtered-BC and suggest PPO or a stronger base model.

Environment diversity is narrow: only 11 Python repositories with a long tail (pandas ~one third of instances, bokeh ~1%) and hand-configured dependencies; the authors name automated environment synthesis (environment creation, test-case generation, task generation) and broader language/task coverage as the critical next step.

The verifier is the ceiling on inference-time scaling: Best@k trails Pass@k by 10.8 points at k=16 (32.0% vs 42.8%), dropping to ~22% when trained on off-policy data alone, and the 7B verifier stops improving after k=4.

No reinforcement learning and no human-in-the-loop evaluation; the paper's own comparison notes a concurrent 72B system trained on 80,036 trajectories reaches about 40% on SWE-Bench Verified, so scale still buys accuracy beyond what this 32B setup achieves.
2412.21139.fits: Stage 7 (Self-Modifying Coding), 'Iterative Repair & Training' branch: it converts the test-time repair loops of Self-Debug (2304.05128) and AgentCoder into weights by supplying the missing executable environment and test-based reward. Pairs with Self-Debug, AgentCoder, and SICA/DGM, which point the same edit->test->verify gate at the agent's own code.
2412.21139.reading: §3 and Table 2 (environment construction, task statistics), §4.2 + Table 3 (fine-tuning gains, stuck-in-loop), §5.1 (verifier data mixture, Best@k vs Pass@k), §5.2 (data scaling), Appendix A (concurrent 72B comparison).

2304.05128.tldr: Self-Debugging teaches an LLM via few-shot prompts to debug its own code by explaining it line-by-line (rubber duck debugging) — no training, no human feedback — lifting Spider 81.3→84.1 and TransCoder baseline by up to 12%.
2304.05128.method: No finetuning: few-shot prompts only, on Codex (code-davinci-002), gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4, StarCoder-15.5B. One debugging turn has three steps — Generation (predict program; greedy at τ=0, or τ=0.7 for multiple samples, then execution-based majority vote over non-erroring programs, discarding programs that fail provided unit tests), Explanation (model explains the code in natural language, or writes a line-by-line execution trace of a sample input), Feedback (a correctness message from the model itself, or from unit-test execution). Four feedback formats: Simple (bare "correct"/"wrong" sentence, skipping Explanation), Unit Test (UT; execution results of failed tests in the message), Code Explanation (Expl; rubber-duck line-by-line explanation), Execution Trace (Trace; model-simulated intermediate steps, needing no real execution states). Loop ends when feedback says the code is correct or max 10 turns (successful runs end within 3). For Spider, step 3 compares the inferred question return type against the SQL explanation to emit correctness feedback.
results: Spider dev (no unit tests), Codex: baseline 81.3 → +Expl. 84.1, beating prompting-only rerankers Coder-Reviewer 74.5 and MBR-Exec 75.2, and the trained T5-3B + N-best Reranking 80.6 and LEVER 81.9 (Table 1a); Simple feedback alone gives 81.3, i.e. zero gain (Table 2a).

TransCoder C++→Python pass@1, Codex: 80.4 baseline → 89.3 (Simple) → 91.6 (UT) → 92.5 (UT+Expl.), vs 44.5 TransCoder, 51.8 PaLM, 55.1 PaLM-Coder without debugging (Tables 2b, 6). Trace feedback is worse than UT+Expl. here (87.9).

MBPP, Codex: 61.4 → 68.2 (Simple) → 69.4 (UT) → 69.8 (UT+Expl.) → 70.8 (+Trace), vs MBR-Exec 63.0 at n=25, Reviewer 66.9 at n=25, LEVER 68.9 at n=100 — Self-Debugging reaches 72.2 with n=10 samples (Tables 1b, 2c).

Sample efficiency (Spider, Codex): Self-Debugging on greedy decoding matches the baseline using 16 samples, and from 8 samples outperforms the 32-sample baseline; one debugging turn captures nearly all the gain (improvement after turn 1 within 0.1%) (Fig. 6a, §5.2.1).

Ablations: +9% on Spider extra-hard problems (Fig. 6b), the largest fixed-error classes being wrong WHERE conditions 25.7% and missing DISTINCT 17.1% (Table 4); without unit-test execution (Table 3) Codex still gains on TransCoder (80.4 → 83.9 with Expl.) but regresses on MBPP under Simple feedback (61.4 → 57.6, recovering to 66.2 with Trace), while GPT-4 MBPP improves 72.8 → 76.4.
advantages: Establishes that self-debugging needs no training and no human feedback: a few-shot prompt makes the model emit its own explanations and correctness verdicts, and this alone beats trained rerankers on Spider (84.1 vs LEVER 81.9) and trained code-repair models.

Isolates *why* it works: on Spider, where no oracle exists, bare Simple feedback yields literally no improvement (81.3 → 81.3) because the model cannot tell correct from incorrect SQL; adding line-by-line code explanation is what supplies the signal. Explanation, not the iterate-again loop, does the work.

Improves sample efficiency rather than just peak accuracy: debugging from 8 samples beats sampling 32 without debugging, so the same accuracy is bought with ~4× fewer samples — a direct compute-efficiency argument for iterative repair over naive reranking.

Execution Trace feedback is generated by the model, not the interpreter, so it needs no access to intermediate execution states — a cheap stand-in for real traces that still helps. And the method transfers to an open 15.5B model: StarCoder gains ~6% on MBPP with trace feedback (47.2 → 53.2).
limitations: Execution is load-bearing, and removing it can make things worse: on MBPP with Codex, no-execution Simple feedback *drops* accuracy from 61.4 to 57.6, and the paper reports GPT-3.5/GPT-4 are "overconfident in their own initial predictions" without unit-test execution, with few-shot prompting not notably helping their self-debugging.

Richer feedback is not monotonically better and is budget-constrained: Trace underperforms UT+Expl. on TransCoder (87.9 vs 92.5 vs 91.6 for plain UT), and adding explanations shrinks the prompt to 3 exemplars vs 6 for simple/UT feedback, which the paper gives as a reason explanation helps less on MBPP.

Explanation helps least exactly where it would matter most — the paper notes it "plays a smaller role when the initial predicted code is far from the correct solution," where the model just rewrites from scratch. Scope is single-function/query tasks (Spider dev, MBPP, TransCoder) and per-turn generation cost is never quantified.

The paper has no limitations or broader-impact section (§7 gives only future work, and notes preliminary results that model-generated *semantic-error* feedback adds nothing over line-by-line explanation). It is also prompt-format sensitive: GPT-4, far stronger than Codex generally, scores only 73.2 on Spider few-shot vs Codex 81.3, both before and after debugging.
2304.05128.fits: Stage 7 'Iterative Repair & Training' — the code-domain instantiation of Self-Refine (2303.17651): same generate→critique→revise loop, but the critique is a rubber-duck explanation plus an execution oracle. Read as the single-agent ancestor of AgentCoder (role-split repair against generated tests) and of the execution-gated self-modification loops in DGM/SICA, where the same edit→execute→verify gate is turned on the agent's own code.
2304.05128.reading: §3 (the Generation/Explanation/Feedback turn and the four feedback formats) and §5.1–5.2 (Tables 1–4, Figs. 6/8) for numbers; §5.2.2 (Table 3) for what breaks without execution; Appendix C on why explanation helps less on MBPP.

2312.13010.tldr: AgentCoder splits code generation into three roles — a Chain-of-Thought programmer, a test designer that writes basic/edge/large-scale tests without seeing the code, and a Python test-executor — looping until tests pass. GPT-4 reaches 96.3% HumanEval pass@1 at 56.9K tokens.
2312.13010.method: Input is only the task description/stub. The programmer agent (LLM) emits code after a four-step Chain-of-Thought (understand and clarify, select algorithm, write pseudocode, generate code). The test designer agent (LLM, separate call) emits test cases independently — it sees the prompt stub but never the generated code, so its oracles cannot be biased by the bugs it is meant to catch — and is prompted for basic, edge, and large-scale inputs. The test executor agent is a Python script, not an LLM: agents must wrap output in ```py[Code]```/```py[TestCases]``` blocks, which it extracts, runs in a local terminal, and inspects for assertion/runtime errors. All tests pass → return code; otherwise the traceback is fed to the programmer, which regenerates. Loop ends on success or at an iteration budget (5 in experiments). Nothing is trained — all improvement is in-context repair.
results: GPT-4: 96.3% HumanEval / 91.8% MBPP pass@1 at 56.9K/66.3K response tokens, vs MetaGPT 85.9/87.7 at 138.2K/206.5K, ChatDev 84.1/79.8 at 183.7K/259.3K, AgentVerse 89.0/73.5 at 149.2K/193.6K, Self-Collaboration 90.2/78.9 at 74.3K/89.2K (Tab. 9).

GPT-3.5-turbo: HumanEval 57.3% zero-shot → 79.9% with AgentCoder; MBPP-ET 89.1% vs 63.0% for CodeCoT. Mean pass@1 across the four datasets is 84.1% (GPT-3.5) and 91.5% (GPT-4) against 75.3% and 86.8% for the best baselines, and it holds up on the harder enhanced sets (77.4/89.1) where base models collapse.

Ablation (Tab. 2): programmer alone 61.0/47.9 (HumanEval/MBPP) → +test designer 64.0/62.3 → programmer+executor 64.6/69.3 → full AgentCoder 79.9/89.9; both generated tests and real execution feedback are needed.

Test quality: designer-test accuracy 87.8/89.9 (GPT-3.5) and 89.6/91.4 (GPT-4), against MetaGPT (GPT-4) 79.3/84.4, CodeCoT 67.1/79.0, and plain GPT-3.5 47.0/57.2; line coverage 91.7/92.3 (GPT-4) vs MetaGPT 81.7/80.5 and CodeCoT 77.2/82.9.

Iterations 1→5 (GPT-3.5) raise pass@1 74.4→79.9 (HumanEval), 84.1→89.9 (MBPP), 80.3→89.1 (MBPP-ET); one agent doing both jobs is worse than two (test accuracy 61.0/51.8 vs 87.8/89.9, pass@1 71.3/79.4 vs 79.9/89.9).
advantages: Isolates why multi-agent code generation works: the win comes from a *non-oracle-biased test designer* plus a *real execution gate*, not from adding more agents — the executor is a plain Python script, so only two LLM calls are in the loop.

Cheapest of the measured multi-agent frameworks and the most accurate: 56.9K/66.3K tokens vs 138.2K+ for MetaGPT/ChatDev/AgentVerse, i.e. the paper's efficiency claim is bought by removing coordination chatter rather than by skimping on testing.

Ablations separate the contributions cleanly (Tab. 2, Tab. 6–8): a single agent asked to write code then tests loses ~27 points of test accuracy, quantifying the self-confirmation bias in code-then-test prompting.

Robustness under stricter tests: near-flat performance on HumanEval-ET/MBPP-ET is direct evidence the generated code is actually correct rather than tuned to the base datasets' two-or-three weak tests.
limitations: The paper has no limitations or broader-impact section: §5 says they are discussed in the Appendix, but Appendix A.1–A.6 contains only output-format setup, overhead, and case studies.
Scope is single-function generation on HumanEval/MBPP with ground-truth oracles; nothing is repository-scale, and no weights change, so every gain is in-context and evaporates at the end of the task.
The loop stops on 'all tests pass' or a fixed budget of 5 iterations: wrong designer oracles stall or misdirect the repair, and there is no mechanism to detect or discard a bad test.

Cost accounting counts response tokens only (no coordination/latency analysis of the failed iterations), and the abstract pairs the SOTA pass@1 (90.2/78.9, Self-Collaboration) with MetaGPT's token counts (138.2K/206.5K), misattributing the baseline comparison.
2312.13010.fits: Stage 7 'Iterative Repair & Training': the test-time repair loop Self-Debug (2304.05128) runs single-agent, here split into roles against an executed test oracle. It isolates the ingredients — generated tests, real execution, agent division — that SWE-Gym (2412.21139) later trains into weights and DGM/ASI (2505.22954, 2504.15228) turn on the agent's own code.
2312.13010.reading: §3 for the three agents (3.1 programmer CoT, 3.2 the test-designer prompt, 3.3 the executor script); §4.3–4.7 for the ablations (Tables 2–9). Appendix A.1–A.3 has the verbatim prompts and the ```py``` output-format contract.

2601.14525.tldr: Three-part automated executor (Implementer/Scheduler/Worker) turns natural-language ideas into real GPU experiments on nanoGPT pre-training and GRPO post-training, then feeds results back as reward: execution-guided evolutionary search beats baselines within ten epochs; GRPO RL lifts average reward but collapses diversity and never raises the maximum.
2601.14525.method: Two environments, each a baseline codebase with fixed data, benchmark and metric: nanoGPT speedrun (train 124M GPT-2 on FineWeb toward validation loss 3.28 on 8 H100s, proxied during search as 1/loss under a fixed 25-minute budget) and GRPO (finetune Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on MATH; metric is max MATH validation accuracy; validation code sits in a file the executor cannot touch). Three executor blocks: Implementer prompts a code-LLM with idea plus baseline to sample 10 code diffs in parallel, self-revising unappliable patches up to twice and returning the first that applies; Scheduler pulls codebases on a fixed clock and sizes each job to the environment's GPU requirement; Worker runs the job and uploads logs, metadata and metrics to wandb. The ideator reads back each idea's measured result. Search mixes exploitation (variants of ideas beating baseline beta) with exploration, annealed from 50/50; RL finetunes Qwen3-30B-A3B with GRPO on the same executed reward.
results: Execution is feasible at scale: self-execution completion rate is 84% for Claude-4.5-Sonnet on GRPO and 90% on nanoGPT, falling to 42% and 78% when GPT-5 executes Sonnet's ideas; with GPT-5 fixed as executor every ideator lands between 42% and 78%, and best-of-N (N=50) still beats baseline - Claude-4.5-Sonnet reaches max accuracy 60.4% vs the 48.0% GRPO baseline, Claude-4.5-Opus min loss 3.237 vs the 3.255 nanoGPT baseline, Qwen3-235B 50.2% and 3.238.

Execution-guided search wins: within ten epochs Claude-4.5-Sonnet hits 69.4% on GRPO at epoch 2 (baseline 48.0%), beating the best Stanford CS336 student solution at 68.8%; Claude-4.5-Opus reaches min validation loss 3.1407 at epoch 9, and rerun on 8 H100s that recipe reaches the 3.28 target in 19.7 minutes vs 35.9 minutes for the baseline codebase (human speedrun record: 2.1 minutes).

The feedback is load-bearing, not resampling: under an identical sampling budget (N=80 per epoch) GPT-5's execution-guided search beats best-of-N at N in {80, 160, 240} from epoch 1 onward, starting from the same epoch-0 performance.

RL from execution reward raises the mean but not the ceiling: average accuracy on GRPO goes 0.253 to 0.343 over 40 training epochs, and average reward on nanoGPT goes 0.194 to 0.246 over 68 epochs (average validation loss 5.150 to 4.066) - while the max reward per epoch fluctuates with no clear upward trend.

Mode collapse is diagnosed, not just noted: two common ideas (replace RMSNorm with LayerNorm; EMA over intermediate checkpoints) account for 51 of 128 sampled ideas at epoch 0 and 119 of 128 at epoch 68; thinking traces shrink over training, and ideas with the longest thinking traces consistently have the lowest execution rate.
advantages: First realistic-scale demonstration that fully open-ended ideas - no constraint on ideation scope, from hyper-parameter tuning to new architectures and objectives - can be implemented, run on real GPUs and scored automatically, with execution rate measured per model rather than assumed.

The search scaffold is genuinely sample-efficient: ten epochs of 50 (GRPO) or 80 (nanoGPT) ideas per epoch beat both provided baselines, match or beat the best human expert on the GRPO environment, and beat best-of-N at equal sampling budget - so prior execution trajectories, not sample count, are doing the work.

The negative RL result is reported at full strength and mechanistically explained: separating average reward (rises) from max reward (does not) is exactly the distinction that matters for scientific discovery, and the paper grounds it in thinking-length dynamics and per-epoch idea-frequency counts rather than attributing it to noise.

Evaluation is defended against reward hacking in a way worth copying: evaluation hyper-parameters are frozen and a token-by-token inference function blocks attention modifications that leak future tokens, an exploit the authors say occurred repeatedly during development and would otherwise have manufactured fake speedup.
limitations: The paper's own first limitation: generalizability is untested. Both environments are single small scales (a 124M and a 1.5B model, one dataset each), and the best-scoring ideas at that scale may not transfer to larger models or other data; the authors note this could be folded into the optimization objective itself.

The reward signal is execution-biased. Failed patch generation earns reward 0, so RL is pushed toward simple, reliably-implementable ideas; the authors attribute the diversity collapse to exactly this, noting the executor's capability bounds the experiment scope and injects noise into the reward.

RL's ceiling problem is unsolved here: standard GRPO improves average but not upper-bound reward, and all three documented attempts to fix it - appending previous epochs' trajectories to the prompt, a weighted length reward, a weighted similarity penalty - showed no clear gain in early epochs and were early-stopped.

Training rewards only effectiveness. Novelty and interestingness are named as complementary objectives the paper does not attempt to measure or optimize, and the executor itself cannot implement ideas needing new dependencies or external tooling.
2601.14525.fits: Stage 8 (Automated AI R&D): the execution-grounding half that AI Scientist and Agent Laboratory leave to templates or human hands. Pairs with AI Scientist-v2 and autoresearch for the ideate-to-execute arc, MLE-Bench/RE-Bench as the ML-engineering analogue it explicitly distinguishes open-ended research from, and AlphaEvolve/FunSearch (stage 9) as the search scaffold it adapts.
2601.14525.reading: §2.2 for the Implementer/Scheduler/Worker design; §3 with Figure 2 for execution rates; §4.1-4.3 for Algorithm 1 and the best-of-N comparison; §5.2-5.3 with Figures 5-7 for the RL curves and collapse; §8 for limitations.

2608.17906.tldr: Two-stage autonomous-research system: Idea Generation grounds hypotheses in research signals plus domain knowledge through 3-model generation and 3-reviewer cross-validation; Idea Execution grounds conclusions in artifacts through fresh-context verification. RSICD mean Recall 32.84→34.69, with 5 audit-confirmed issue events vs 11–27 for four rival systems.
2608.17906.method: Idea Generation maintains two contexts: external signals harvested from papers, repositories, technical media and fast social platforms (X, Xiaohongshu) with source-aware quality priors, dedup and model-based screening; plus a curated domain knowledge base. Seeds are recast as mechanism-transfer problems H(s,d)={G_m⊕(s,K(d))} where each of M generators may return an explicit no-match instead of forcing a proposal. Idea Forge then runs three frontier models generating and three reviewers scoring, requiring at least two positive reviews on mechanism meaningfulness, methodological simplicity (isolate the effect) and testability, plus freshness and domain-consistency checks, emitting hypothesis h and plan p. Execution compiles p into a task graph over persistent state x_{k+1}=F(x_k,a_k,o_k), dispatches dependency-ready tasks concurrently, and routes non-PASS verdicts from a fresh-context critic (v_k ∈ PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL) into DIAGNOSE, REVISE or RERUN. Claims are admissible only as evidence items e_i=(a_i,o_i,r_i) with a persistent artifact; closure is CONTINUE/REVISE/SCALE/STOP.
results: RSICD bidirectional image–text retrieval: the Idea Forge method, introduced component by component under one fixed protocol, raises mean Recall 32.84 → 33.89 → 34.04 → 34.69 (total +1.85 mR), with each staged contribution remaining measurable.

Audit-confirmed issue events on RSICD: 5 for AutoResearch versus 11 R&D-Agent, 15 AutoResearchClaw, 18 Agent Laboratory, 27 The AI Scientist — the improvement comes with a comparatively reliable execution trace, not just a headline metric.

1024×1024 FP32 matmul under a stated contract (<200 ms, relative error <1e-5 against two numerical references, run-to-run CV <20% over ten wall-clock trials): the pilot met speed and accuracy but failed stability (2/3 gates, CV unstable), triggering a diagnostic sweep over 8 cells that localized a timing bug — CPU time under multi-threaded BLAS conflated with wall-clock; the corrected, rerun baseline is 3.4 ms / 626 GFLOPS at 1024×1024 FP32, ~58× the required margin. AutoResearch logs 4 issue events vs 5 R&D-Agent, 5 Agent Laboratory, 7 AutoResearchClaw, 8 The AI Scientist.

Three Kaggle trajectories with evidence-conditioned closure: Titanic five-fold CV accuracy 0.822 → 0.843 (target ≥0.830) → scale-up; House Prices RMSLE 0.2008 → 0.1251 (target ≤0.120, not reached) → revise; Disaster Tweets F1 0.763 → 0.805 (target ≥0.835) → terminated with the negative result retained rather than searching for a positive one.

Throughput on one server (dual Intel Xeon Platinum 8563C, 98 cores/196 threads, 8× NVIDIA L20, 944 GiB): ~2584 candidate ideas in one week (7×24 h) of continuous operation → ~355 surviving multi-model review and filtering into the experimental queue → ~22 automatically executed experiments → ~14 empirically validated ideas.
advantages: Separates two grounding obligations that agent-scientist systems usually leave implicit: idea grounding (motivation traceable to context, a real transferable mechanism rather than superficial association, a testable central hypothesis) and evidence grounding (Accept(c) ⇒ ∃e∈E with Supports(e,c)=1; claim acceptance requires V(c,E_c,Γ_c)=PASS). The acceptance rule is checkable, which is what makes 'Hallucination Out' operational rather than rhetorical.

The critic is a fresh-context agent that never inherits the producer's reasoning trajectory — it gets only the hypothesis, plan, artifacts and evaluation criteria — so it must reconstruct validity from the research record. This explicit anti-anchoring design is the mechanism behind the low issue counts, and it is what the compared systems lack.

The matmul case is a concrete rejection of a favorable result: a pilot 58× faster than target was refused until its measurement process was independently justified, and the fix was to the measurement (CPU-time vs wall-clock), not to the claim. That is verification of process, not just of output.

Negative and inconclusive outcomes are first-class: termination can record a supported, falsified or inconclusive hypothesis, and Disaster Tweets is stopped below target with the negative result kept — research closure conditioned on accumulated evidence rather than on execution length or a required positive finding.
limitations: The paper's own dependency list is the real boundary: the system still depends on external-signal coverage, the quality of accumulated domain knowledge, and 'the availability of explicit experimental criteria for verification'. Both corrected settings lean on machine-checkable contracts (timing/error/CV gates, Kaggle targets), so domains without such contracts — most open-ended discovery — are untested here.

The recursion is not closed: feeding verified evidence and outcomes back into the knowledge state (K_{t+1}=U(K_t,E_t,Y_t)) is explicitly future work. There is no demonstrated improvement across successive research cycles, so this is an RSI scaffold rather than a demonstrated self-improving research loop.

Evaluation is thin for the strength of the claims: three scenarios with single headline runs against four systems, and reliability is measured by the authors' own audit protocol of 'audit-confirmed issue events' with no multiple seeds, variance or inter-auditor agreement reported.

The front end is extremely lossy and prior-dependent — 2584 candidates → 355 queued → 22 executed → 14 validated — and idea quality is bounded by the curated knowledge base plus source priors the paper names explicitly (researchers and technical creators on X and Xiaohongshu as early signals ahead of literature search).
2608.17906.fits: Stage 8 (Automated AI R&D): the mature generation/execution split with explicit acceptance rules rather than automation for its own sake. Baselines are The AI Scientist, Agent Laboratory, R&D-Agent and AutoResearchClaw; pairs with the autoresearch repo as its minimal industrial-scale counterpart, and with verification-gap surveys. Its future-work knowledge feedback is the RSI hook.
2608.17906.reading: §2.2–2.3 for Idea Forge (3 generators, 3 reviewers, ≥2-review gate, freshness check) and the separate-producer/verifier split; §3.2–3.4 with Figures 2–4 for RSICD, the matmul timing-bug diagnosis, and the continue/revise/stop trajectories. Skim §2.1's formalization.

2607.28568.tldr: Frontis/OpenMLE: an open three-part stack (gym, operator RL, evolutionary search) that post-trains a 35B model as a meta-evolution agent, lifting MLE-Bench Lite Medal Average from 39.39% to 60.61%, and 71.21% with Evo-Max.
2607.28568.method: OpenMLE is a three-layer stack. Gym packages 5,758 quality-gated executable tasks (156 curated anchors, 3,362 Kaggle-dataset tasks, 2,240 competitions) into one contract: public data, hidden evaluator returning a scalar score, sandboxed execution, structured diagnostics. Four atomic operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover) are the shared interface between training and inference. ERL post-trains the base model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) in two stages: budget-adaptive SFT on a 26,259-example corpus (17,245 Draft responses distilled from GLM-4.7/Qwen3 teachers, 9,014 trajectory steps harvested from AIRA-Evo search trees), then GSPO RL with adaptive per-task reward bounds, an entropic advantage concentrating signal on each rollout group's upper tail, asynchronous rollouts, and parent selection by reward, child-reward variance and visit cooling. Evo composes the same trained operators at test time over structured experience cards, three-factor parent selection (quality, improvement, novelty) and on-demand operator-conditioned memory.
results: MLE-Bench Lite (22 tasks, 12 h per task on one RTX 4090 capped at 12 GB VRAM), identical OpenMLE-Evo harness: post-training lifts Frontis-MA1-35B over its Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base from 39.39% to 60.61% Medal Average (Human Rank 0.5828 -> 0.7647, Valid Rate 19.67/22 -> 21.67/22, +21.22 pp); the companion 30B reproduces it, 34.85% -> 53.03% over Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (three-epoch means: 39.39% +/- 5.67% -> 60.61% +/- 7.73%).

With OpenMLE-Evo-Max (MLE-Bench-disjoint cross-task priors plus asynchronous parallel search, same sandbox budget) the 35B system reaches 71.21% / 0.8126 Human Rank / 22.00-of-22 valid, above GPT-5.5 + Codex (63.64% in Table 1; 68.18% final test in Fig. 12) and just below GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 (72.73% each); the 30B reaches 66.67% / 0.8053.

Harness gain at fixed model: against original AIRA-Evo on the same Frontis-MA1-35B, OpenMLE-Evo raises Medal Average 53.03% -> 60.61%, and against general coding scaffolds it moves GLM-5.2 59.09% -> 62.12%, MiniMax M3 54.55% -> 59.09%, Kimi K2.6 59.09% -> 66.67% and MiniMax M2.7 45.50% -> 50.00% (Claude Code / Codex references).

The gains arrive late in the horizon and the search is cheaper: Improve and Crossover account for 85.0% of the total validation gain on leaf-classification and 91.9% on the audio task (held-out Human Rank 0.9455 Bronze and 0.8889 Silver, vs best comparisons 0.732 / 0.2963 with no medal); versus original AIRA-Evo at the same checkpoint, seed and 12 h, total model tokens fall 129.3M -> 75.3M (-41.7%) and Improve prompt mean 102.8K -> 35.7K characters (-65.3%) while evaluated nodes drop only 3430 -> 3004 (-12.4%), so new-best validation updates per million tokens rise 1.77 -> 3.27 (+84.3%) and Improve calls setting a new best go 4.73% -> 9.36%.

Held-out transfer on the 10-task NatureBench Lite subset (4 h per task): with the adapter fixed, swapping in the trained model raises Match-SOTA 50% -> 70% (5/10 -> 7/10) and Surpass-SOTA 20% -> 30% (2/10 -> 3/10); with the base model fixed, swapping in the OpenMLE-Evo adapter raises Match-SOTA 20% -> 50% (2/10 -> 5/10) and Surpass-SOTA 10% -> 20%.
advantages: The two gains are measured independently and compose, which is what makes the meta-evolution claim testable: at fixed harness, post-training buys +21.22 pp (39.39% -> 60.61%); at fixed model, Evo-Max buys +10.60 pp (60.61% -> 71.21%). Both are controlled replications (35B and 30B backbones), and the modality stratification attributes the 14 extra medals across every group (+2/+4/+1/+4/+3 image/text/tabular/audio/multimodal) with no group-level Medal Rate lowered.

Open-weight post-training, not scaffolding: under one common harness the post-trained 35B-A3B model (60.61%) beats MiniMax M3 (59.09%), Doubao Seed 2.1 Pro (56.06%) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (54.55%), and with Evo-Max (71.21%) exceeds GLM-5.2 and MiniMax M3 under the same enhanced harness.

The harness itself is the contribution and is domain-specialised rather than model-specific: at fixed model, OpenMLE-Evo beats original AIRA-Evo (53.03% -> 60.61%) and beats Claude Code / Codex scaffolds on four frontier models, so the gain is not a single favourable model-harness pairing.

Cheap in both senses: 12 hours per task on a single RTX 4090 capped at 12 GB VRAM, a smaller sandbox budget than most reported MLE-Bench runs; and the bounded, operator-conditioned context cuts total model tokens 41.7% and prompt tokens 50.3% while raising discoveries per token 84.3%, so the mechanism improves search productivity rather than merely truncating it.
limitations: Not RSI yet, per the paper's own section 8 list of five boundaries: training learns only from executed outcome, not whether a direction is promising, generalisable or robust; the trained operators are composed by an external harness rather than a general coding agent; the agent improves external ML artifacts but not language models themselves; evolution operates over candidate solutions while the evolutionary system stays fixed; and parent selection uses only three of the recorded experience signals.

Breadth is thin where it matters: the headline is one 22-task MLE-Bench Lite split and the transfer study is a fixed 10-task NatureBench Lite subset, where the reported gains are one or two tasks (7/10 vs 5/10; 2/10 vs 5/10). The authors state that small modality groups and the ten-task transfer set limit both conclusions.

The compute comparison is deliberately unnormalised: footnote 3 of section 6.1 says it uses per-run accelerator allocation and wall-clock budget from the official MLE-Bench runs registry and explicitly does not compare model-inference cost or normalise different accelerators to FLOPs.

Reproducibility is partial and the release is described inconsistently: licensing limits full task-package data to 1,415 of 5,758 tasks (the rest ship only prepare.py and metric.py), the SFT corpus is distilled from proprietary teachers with DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the trajectory annotator, Evo-Max's gain partly rests on priors distilled from public competition artifacts, and section 1 promises the release in the future tense while the abstract states it as done.
2607.28568.fits: Stage 8 (Automated AI R&D), at the meta-evolution rung: it turns test-time MLE search into weights and back, one level above AIRA-Evo-style fixed-model harnesses and one below agents that improve the model itself. Pairs with MLE-Bench, MLE-Dojo, MLEvolve and FT-Dojo (2606.06473, 2603.01712), OpenEvolve/DGM, and stage 5's harness-evolution cards.
2607.28568.reading: Section 2 for the formal SFT/RL objective, sections 4.2-4.3 for budget-adaptive SFT and the adaptive-bounds + entropic-advantage RL (Eq. 2-3), sections 5.1-5.4 for experience cards and three-factor selection, section 6.2 Table 1, section 6.5 Figure 16, section 8.

2603.01712.tldr: FT-Dojo is the first interactive benchmark for end-to-end LLM fine-tuning agents — 13 tasks across 5 domains with a shared raw-data pool, Docker sandbox and held-out evaluator; FT-Agent, a planning/fail-fast/feedback framework, wins 10 of 13 tasks.
2603.01712.method: FT-Dojo formalizes fine-tuning as argmax over data strategy θd and training hyperparameters θt, given structured feedback f(t). Each task supplies a natural-language objective plus an evaluation script; agents work inside a GPU-limited Docker sandbox against three interfaces — a Meta API (task spec, data descriptions, API docs), a shared raw-Data Repository (not per-task splits, so source selection is itself an optimization target), and an Evaluator built on OpenCompass returning aggregate metrics, per-instance predictions with correctness labels, and training loss curves. Validation and test splits are non-overlapping, each min(100, ⌊n/2⌋); training is capped at 2,000 self-constructed samples via SFT or LoRA on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct within a 12-hour single-B200 budget. FT-Agent adds structured iteration planning (compact data-strategy + training-config + rationale plans instead of verbose logs), three-stage fail-fast validation (schema/syntax, mini-run format check, runtime sanity), and multi-level feedback diagnosis that promotes a new best configuration when Fτ improves.
results: Best on 10 of 13 tasks (mean±std over 3 runs). AIME 2025: 0.00 → 11.11±3.82 accuracy, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, constrained Manual SFT and tool-augmented OpenHands all stay at 0.00 — the agent diagnosed missing reasoning supervision and synthesized CoT from a pool where 82% of samples lack solutions

Strongest where code or structural constraints are strict: Table QA Visualization Pass@1 29.33±6.11 vs OpenHands 24.00; Chemistry Molecule Editing 54.44±2.94 vs OpenHands 40.00. The losses are reported honestly — OpenHands wins both Reaction metrics (FTS 35.59 vs 30.92, Acc 60.00 vs 35.33) and Manual SFT wins Financial QA (71.68 vs 67.20)

Fail-fast validation converts budget into iterations: 6.0 vs 2.75 effective iterations inside the same 12h (2.2×; Table QA FC 7 vs 2), avg loops 8.77 vs 3.69, improvement rate 24.37% vs 17.31%, for $5.73 vs $3.92 of iterative spend

Five-task controlled comparison (same data repo, Docker env, LlamaFactory/OpenCompass wrappers, 12h): FT-Agent+GPT-5.2 averages 42.83, above Claude Code Sonnet-4.6-thinking (39.86), LLM-assisted Manual SFT (37.11), Codex GPT-5.2 (36.06) and OpenHands GPT-5.2 (34.55); swapping the planner to DeepSeek-V3.2 (35.83), GPT-4o (36.65) or Qwen3.5-397B (31.97) keeps it in range

Case-study duality: on Mol Edit the agent recovers from a 2% vocabulary-corruption collapse to 56% accuracy via format fixes and RDKit SMILES validation, but on PI4PC it shotguns generic fixes (NEFTune −11pp, collapse to 8%) and returns to the 34% baseline after 8 loops; on Visualization a locally-sane filter chain cut ~1,800 samples to 27 (98.5%) and dropped Pass@1 20% → 4%
advantages: First interactive, protocol-standardized environment for end-to-end fine-tuning: rather than per-task static datasets, it makes data curation and training configuration joint optimization targets under one fixed 2,000-sample budget, with a two-phase validation/test protocol that keeps the test set inaccessible during optimization

Unusually clean factorization — base model, raw data repository, Docker sandbox, training/eval wrappers, GPU, splits and wall clock are held fixed so only the agent framework varies — plus honest negative controls: doubling OpenHands to 24h on AIME changes nothing (best checkpoint lands in the first 6 hours), and scaling data 2k → 5k can hurt under a fixed budget because processing squeezes iteration time

Documents emergent autonomous cross-domain data transfer: for Numerical Reasoning the agent mixed in 10% out-of-domain DeepScaleR (AIME/AMC math) for 32.00 → 46.00 accuracy; for Mol Opt it built a 70/25/5 composite of mol_opt/mol_edit/mol_und for SR 23.33 → 36.67 with valid-SMILES 68.67 → 91.67 — and it stays selective, using only in-domain data on Reaction, Mol Edit and Mol Und

No black box: the paper's conflict-of-interest disclosure names the Microsoft authors behind FT-Agent, and the harness is released at github.com/microsoft/rd-agent with pluggable task-objective and evaluation-script modules, so new fine-tuning tasks need no core infrastructure changes
limitations: A benchmark, not a method, and the authors say so: the constituent datasets are pre-existing held-out evaluators (PANORAMA, ChemCoTBench, FinanceIQ, TableBench, AIME 2025), only the protocol is new; 13 tasks in 5 domains with pools from 4,497 to 136,211 raw samples is still narrow coverage

Causal diagnosis is the headline deficit: on PI4PC the agent describes symptoms with hedging language ('likely', 'appears') and applies generic ML techniques without asking why the task overfits, never operationalizing the train–eval mismatch it correctly named in Loop 2; net gain was zero

Planning myopia: the agent optimizes each pipeline step locally without modeling cumulative state changes, which is exactly how the Visualization dataset collapsed 98.5%; a 3-stage validation gate cannot catch joint effects that only appear after composition

Statistics are uneven by necessity: 3 seeds for FT-Agent only (full coverage would cost 1,500+ GPU-hours, so baselines are single controlled runs) and chemistry reaction similarity is volatile (30.92±11.22), which the paper flags as large variance; one author group also built both the benchmark and the winning agent
2603.01712.fits: Stage 8 (Automated AI R&D) — the 'fine-tuning as an agent task' environment, one level above MLE-Bench/DSBench and below MLEvolve. Pairs with MLE-Dojo and MLE-Bench as the fixed-data vs open-data contrast, and with the autoresearch/rd-agent harnesses: FT-Agent is the feedback-and-reward-signal half, hyperagents the self-modification half.
2603.01712.reading: Read §2.1–2.4 for the task formulation, two-phase validation/test protocol and 2k budget; §3 for the three FT-Agent mechanisms; §4.2–4.5 with Tables 2–4; and Appendix D for the Mol Edit recovery vs PI4PC shotgun-debugging traces.

2606.06473.tldr: An LLM multi-agent framework that evolves end-to-end ML algorithms, reaching 65.3% average medal rate on MLE-Bench in a 12-hour budget — best among compared agents at half the standard 24h runtime — and the best result on 11 of 15 AlphaEvolve math-optimization tasks.
2606.06473.method: Three coupled mechanisms per task (500 steps, 12h). A branch is a root-to-leaf trajectory of candidate solutions (3 initial drafts, max 5 branches plus 2 fusion). (1) Progressive MCGS: primary edges carry UCT selection and backpropagation; reference edges — never backpropagated — point from other branches' top nodes, so cross-branch transfer conditions generation on retrieved solutions, not scalar rewards. A soft switch w(t) decays 1.0→0.2, blending UCT exploration into Elite-Guided picks from the global top-3 by inverse rank; two-level stagnation detection (τ_branch=3, τ_global=6) triggers intra-branch evolution, cross-branch fusion, or multi-branch aggregation at the root. (2) Retrospective Memory: curated cold-start knowledge base plus a dynamic global store of per-node records (plan, outcome, metric, analysis), retrieved by BM25+FAISS fused via RRF at planning/debugging stages — records persist across the run, replacing memoryless scalar-only search. (3) Planner-coder decoupling: planner decides what/why at module level; coder implements via Base/Stepwise/Diff modes chosen by search state.
results: MLE-Bench (75 tasks, 12h budget, 3 seeds): 65.3% average medal rate, 34.7% gold, 100% valid submissions, 76.0% above-median — vs. best 24h baselines MARS+ 62.7% medal / 33.8% gold and AIBuildAI 63.1% / 25.8%; by complexity 80.3% low, 64.0% medium, 46.7% high.

AlphaEvolve's 15 math-optimization tasks: best result on 11 of 15 vs. AlphaEvolve, AlphaEvolve-v2, SimpleTES, TTT-Discover, and OpenEvolve (e.g., sums-differences problem 1: 1.1901774219 vs. AlphaEvolve's 1.1479889651; circle packing in a rectangle: 2.3658323759 vs. 2.3658321334).

Component ablation on MLE-Bench Lite (22 tasks): medal 81.82% full → 68.18% w/o Progressive MCGS, 68.18% w/o Retrospective Memory (the paper's cited 13.64% drop), 72.73% w/o adaptive code generation; beat ratio 88.39% vs. 79.91/81.90/84.14.

Search dynamics: effective active branches exp(H(π)) falls 4.8 → 2.8 over the run (vanilla MCTS flat at ~4.3); on representative tasks beat ratio reaches 98.2% vs. ~70% for vanilla MCTS, which plateaus early.

Mechanism-level ablation (9-task subset): removing intra-branch evolution drops medal 66.67% → 33.33% (largest single factor); removing the knowledge base or the global memory each drops it to 44.44%.
advantages: State-of-the-art MLE-Bench result at half the standard 24-hour budget (65.3% vs. MARS+ 62.7% and AIBuildAI 63.1%, both at 24h) with 100% valid submissions — an efficiency claim, not just a score claim.

Cross-domain check most MLE agents skip: unchanged, it beats specialized algorithm-discovery systems (AlphaEvolve, AlphaEvolve-v2, OpenEvolve) on 11/15 math tasks, evidence the search machinery generalizes past Kaggle.

Reference edges are a clean way to get cross-branch information flow without corrupting credit assignment — backpropagation stays strictly on primary edges — and every mechanism ablates positively, with intra-branch evolution isolated as the critical one.

Memory accumulates without extra reflection LLM calls: records are logged by a Result Parse Agent and retrieved by BM25+FAISS/RRF, unlike MARS/ROME-style reflection memory, and the two memory halves (static KB vs. dynamic store) are separately ablatable.
limitations: Expensive per task: up to 500 expansion steps over 12h on 21 vCPUs / 234GB RAM, an H200 GPU, and a frontier backbone (Gemini-3.1-Pro-preview); baseline numbers are taken from leaderboards or papers, so comparisons confound framework with different backbone LLMs and budgets.

The edge shrinks with difficulty: 46.7% medal on high-complexity tasks only ties AIBuildAI's 46.7% (at 24h), vs. 80.3% on low-complexity — most of the gain over MARS+ comes from medium tasks (64.0% vs. 60.5%).

The cold-start knowledge base is manually curated per task type from repositories and competition platforms, so part of performance is static human prior rather than self-evolved; the dynamic memory is task-scoped, not accumulated across tasks (ML-Master 2.0's cross-task caching is the contrast).
Ablation statistics are thin: 22 tasks (Lite) for component removal, 9 tasks for mechanism analysis, and some headline cells carry ±0.0 SEM over 3 seeds (gold rate, valid rate, high-complexity).
2606.06473.fits: Stage-8 descendant of AutoML-Zero/AlphaEvolve for whole-ML-algorithm discovery (the repo positions it as AutoMLGen's successor): it keeps the propose-execute-evaluate loop but adds machinery that makes long-horizon search persistent — graph reference edges for cross-branch reuse, an entropy schedule shifting exploration toward exploitation, run-length experience memory, and planner/coder decoupling.
2606.06473.reading: §3.2 (Progressive MCGS, Eqs. 3–7, four expansion types), §3.3 (memory + RRF retrieval), §4.2 Tables 1–2, §4.3 Table 3 plus Appendix E Table 5, §4.4 Fig 3 (entropy dynamics).

2601.10657.tldr: PACEvolve diagnoses three failure modes of LLM-driven evolutionary search — context pollution, mode collapse, weak collaboration — and fixes them with hierarchical idea memory, momentum-triggered backtracking, and self-adaptive cross-island crossover, reaching state-of-the-art on symbolic regression, KernelBench, and Modded NanoGPT.
2601.10657.method: From 200+ 1000-step evolution runs the authors find append-only history contexts saturate with failed trials (context pollution), agents anchor to locally similar hypotheses (mode collapse), and static periodic crossover wastes parallel compute (weak collaboration). PACEvolve evolves candidate solutions (equations, GPU kernels, training code) via three mechanisms. HCM decouples idea generation from selection over a persistent idea pool (caps: 5 ideas, 20 hypotheses each): an LLM classifier merges conceptually duplicate ideas, caps trigger summarization and LLM pruning, and a permanent failure log preserves consistency by blocking rediscovery of dead ends. MBB computes scale-invariant Relative Progress R_t (fraction of remaining gap G_t = s_t − r closed), smoothed into momentum m_t by EWMA (β=0.85); when m_t < 0.001 the trajectory reverts to an ancestor state drawn from a power-law (α=1.5), resetting context. CE then samples backtrack vs. crossover from other islands with probability proportional to absolute-progress-based weights.
results: LLM-SR nonlinear-oscillator symbolic regression (Log10 NMSE, 10 runs × 1000 iterations, Gemini 2.5 Pro): PACEvolve-Multi best −8.24 / P75 −7.64 / mean −6.11 vs ShinkaEvolve −6.35 / −5.92 / −5.35, OpenEvolve −7.11 / −5.79 / −5.40, and non-LLM uDSR best −4.06; Multi finds 3 solutions below log10 NMSE −8.

KernelBench (16 kernels, 1000 iterations each, A100 40GB): beats the best KernelBench-leaderboard kernel on all 16, beats ShinkaEvolve on all 16 (PACE-Multi ≥ Single on 13/16, i.e. 81.25%), matches-or-beats OpenEvolve on 15/16 and CodeEvolve/ShinkaEvolve on 14/16; up to 17.38× over PyTorch (LayerNorm, 10.1ms → 0.581ms), though it loses to PyTorch on MLP/MatMul.

Modded NanoGPT (8×H100, Gemini 3 Pro): cuts time to val loss 3.28 on FineWeb from the heavily optimized v40 baseline 142.8s → 140.2s via data sharding/preloading, U-shaped skip-connection init (0.8→0.4→0.8), hyperparameter tuning, and dynamic context scheduling — on a benchmark already optimized from ~2700s (v1) to 142s.

Ablation (10 runs each): HCM lifts mean/best but worst runs still stall (a locally-optimal idea is never erased); adding MBB eliminates stalled trajectories yet slightly hurts best runs (exploration tax); adding CE recovers top-run performance while keeping the floor — full stack needed.
advantages: Real diagnosis, not anecdote: 200+ 1000-step runs show trajectories that fail to find low-NMSE solutions in the first few iterations rarely recover, with large variance across independent runs (Fig. 2) — grounding context pollution and mode collapse in measured search dynamics.
Each failure mode gets a matched, ablation-isolated fix: HCM's bi-level pruning cleans context, and MBB's progress-aware trigger removes the worst-run tail that context erasure alone cannot (§4.3).

The scale-invariant Relative Progress metric lets one stagnation trigger work across tasks without task-specific thresholds, unlike fixed-schedule resets in ShinkaEvolve/FunSearch-style loops that ignore search state.
Same scaffold achieves SOTA across three distinct domains — scientific equation discovery, GPU kernel optimization, and full-stack distributed training engineering — suggesting the recipe transfers.
limitations: By the paper's own ablation, backtracking 'slightly affected the best-performing processes' (exploration taxes exploitation), and CE only helps 'provided that at least one island discovers a promising direction' — joint all-island stagnation remains a risk.

No explicit limitations section; the authors flag KernelBench/Modded-NanoGPT world knowledge as 'questionable' (Table 5) since optimization strategies likely sit in LLM pretraining corpora, so gains may partly reflect retrieval rather than search.

Tasks need smooth rewards and cheap evaluation per the paper's own criteria; Modded NanoGPT needs 8 H100s and its gain is incremental (142.8s → 140.2s, conceded as 'this improvement looks incremental').

Mechanism assumes a known metric lower bound r and tuned constants (β=0.85, ε_rel=0.001, caps 5/20, power-law exponent 1.5); a sweep (Fig. 5) reports robustness but values are still benchmark-derived.
2601.10657.fits: Stage-9 prerequisite: open-ended evolution stalls without memory governance — long-horizon search needs structured, pruned idea memory plus a progress signal that decides when to abandon a line of work. Its diagnosis-first methodology (measure failure modes across 200+ runs, then derive the scaffold) pairs naturally with PACE-style diagnosis in this catalog.
2601.10657.reading: Read §2 (failure-mode study), §3.1–3.3 (HCM, MBB, CE with the Relative Progress equations), §4.3 (ablation), and Appendix A (case-study insights); Appendix B has pseudocode and hyperparameters (β=0.85, ε=0.001, caps 5/20).

openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.tldr: Higher-order evolution: evolve the mutation rate, recursively the meta-mutation rate, up to a self-referential top-level parameter that modifies itself.
openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.method: Evolves higher-order parameters (mutation rate → meta-mutation rate → … up to a self-referential top-level parameter that modifies itself), showing this improves robustness in Population-Based Training and Unsupervised Environment Design.
results: Self-referential mutation improves robustness to initial hyperparameters and enables complex adaptation in competitive multi-agent settings.
limitations: Small-scale domains (PBT/UED); self-referential levels are still bounded in practice.
openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.fits: The evolutionary-computation counterpart to the Gödel Agent — the meta-parameters of evolution are themselves evolved, one step toward self-referential search.
openreview-higher-order-evolution-2024.reading: Read the higher-order/self-referential mutation definitions (§2–3) and the PBT/UED results.

1901.01753.tldr: POET co-evolves a population of obstacle-course environments and their neural walker controllers in one run, transferring solutions between environments; it invents and solves challenges that neither from-scratch ES nor a direct-path curriculum can reach.
1901.01753.method: POET keeps a list of active environment-agent pairs, starting from one flat course and a random weight vector. Each iteration does three things. (1) Every paired agent takes one ES step (512-sample population, Adam, lr 0.01->0.001, sigma 0.1->0.01) maximizing forward reward in its own environment. (2) Every N_mutate iterations, environments whose agent scores >=200 become parents; their encodings are mutated (stump height, gap width, step height, step number, roughness genes), 512 children are generated, then filtered by a minimal criterion 50 <= E_child(theta) <= 300, ranked by novelty, and admitted until the active population cap (20) is reached; oldest environments are evicted as a queue. (3) Every N_transfer iterations, all agents are tried in all other environments: the best of the M agents plus M one-ES-step proposals replaces the target's champion if better (direct or proposal transfer).
results: Direct ES cannot solve the environments POET produces: for the five POET-created courses in Figures 2-3, the best of five ES runs of up to 16,000 steps each (twice the budget Ha [64] gives in the same domain) scores 17.9, 39.6, 13.6, 24.0 and 19.2, versus POET exceeding the 230 success threshold on each; ES agents converge on freezing before obstacles to avoid the -100 fall penalty. Single-sample t-tests give p < 0.01 on all five.

A direct-path curriculum control (flat ground, then one mutation-step increment at a time toward the target, advancing at the same score-200 threshold POET uses for reproduction, and given POET's full ES-step budget along the ancestral line) solves only the lowest difficulty tier; at very and extremely challenging tiers it falls short, and Mann-Whitney U tests show the distance-to-target grows significantly with difficulty level (p < 0.01).

Challenges are calibrated far above the OpenAI Gym Bipedal Walker Hardcore reference: difficulty gates are 1.2x, 2.0x and 4.5x the reference top-of-range values (stump height >= 2.4 vs 2.0, gap width >= 6.0 vs 3.0, roughness >= 4.5 vs 1.0). Three runs of 25,200 iterations with 20 active environments took about 10 days each on 256 CPU cores; mean iterations from creation to solve were 638 +/- 133 (challenging), 1,180 +/- 343 (very challenging) and 2,178 +/- 368 (extremely challenging).

Transfer is load-bearing, not cosmetic: in three runs there were 18,894 / 19,014 / 18,798 replacement attempts, of which 53.62% / 49.26% / 48.89% succeeded, and a no-transfer control solved zero extremely challenging environments while covering the environment space significantly worse (Mann-Whitney U, p < 2.2e-16).

Two-way transfer creates non-obvious stepping stones: a flat-ground parent whose agent walked in a crouch (a local optimum) mutated at iteration 400 into a child with small stumps; the child learned to stand and jump, and transferring that gait back at iteration 1,175 let the parent reach a score of 349 over 3,000 iterations versus 309 for the original gait, while the kneeling agent run for 3,000 iterations with transfer off never improved.
advantages: Demonstrates in a single run that an algorithm can invent, diversify and solve an increasingly hard set of problems that neither from-scratch optimization nor a directed curriculum reaches, with each claim backed by an explicit control (ES-alone, direct-path curriculum, no-transfer).

The acceptance gates are the mechanism, not the population alone: requiring the parent agent to have scored >=200 before reproducing, filtering children into the 50-300 minimal-criterion band, ranking by novelty and evicting oldest-first at capacity 20 lets POET keep children that are unsolved but improvable, which MCC would have deleted, so difficulty can rise faster than drift.

Backward (child-to-parent) transfer plus periodic all-pairs transfer attempts turns the population into an archive of reusable stepping stones; the paper shows a transfer can rescue an agent stuck at a local optimum that direct optimization provably never leaves.

The skeleton is domain- and optimizer-agnostic: ES is the inner loop here, but the paper argues any RL or search algorithm (PPO, TRPO, genetic algorithms) can be substituted, which is why the environment/solution co-evolution pattern recurs in unsupervised environment design.
limitations: The problem space is bounded by the environment genome's maximum values (gap width, stump height), so difficulty can eventually 'max out'; the authors propose CPPN-style indirect or unbounded encodings as the fix, left to future work.
The agent's body is fixed, which caps the obstacles it can ever surmount (e.g. how wide a gap can be jumped); co-evolving morphology with the controller is future work.

The reward function is not evolved: one shared reward (forward progress minus hull angle and torque) applies to every environment, so POET generates new challenges but not new objectives, unlike the reward-generating work it cites.

Evaluation is a single 2-D bipedal-walker domain with only three runs, and the comparison is post-hoc: each POET environment is unique, so results rest on single-sample t-tests anchored to a single POET score rather than a fixed benchmark.
1901.01753.fits: Stage 9 (Evolutionary & Open-Ended RSI): the transfer-enabled evolutionary descendant of POWERPLAY (1112.5309), which the catalog already names as POET's ancestor. Pairs with MCC (its minimal-criterion parent), MAP-Elites and the Innovation Engine (goal-switching and archive ideas it borrows), and the stage-10 POET/Enhanced POET repo card.
1901.01753.reading: Read Section 3 (Algorithm 2 main loop) and 4.1-4.2 for the domain, reward and Table 1 gene encoding; then 4.3 for the ES-alone, curriculum-control and no-transfer ablations. Supplemental Algorithms 3-4 give MUTATE_ENVS and EVALUATE_CANDIDATES.

agent-zero.what: MIT-licensed Python framework that runs the agent inside its own Dockerized Linux computer — XFCE desktop over Xpra, a Patchright/Chromium browser exposing numbered element references, LibreOffice/Markdown cowork, SKILL.md skills, 40 built-in plugins plus a 100+ Plugin Hub, and an A0 CLI bridge onto your host.
architecture: The harness *is* the machine: the image (docker/run, agent0ai/agent-zero, config repo at /a0, user data at /a0/usr) runs a persistent XFCE desktop on an Xpra display (session agent-zero-desktop, DISPLAY :120) that the agent drives through plugins/_desktop/skills/linux-desktop/scripts/desktopctl.sh — launch writer|calc|impress|terminal, wait-window, focus, key, paste-text, `sequence` batches, plus an app-native calc-set-cell UNO helper — reading state back with check / state --json / windows / geometry. The skill imposes a structured-first ladder: office_artifact and plain file edits before GUI, screenshots only for pixel evidence, coordinate clicks as last resort after a fresh observation, and explicit verification (saved file, window title, screenshot) after every GUI action.

Browser is Patchright/Chromium (patchright==1.61.2) whose injected page-content script inventories interactive elements and tags each with a numeric reference id — `[link 1]`, `[button 2]` — so the ~20 browser actions (click, type, hover, drag, scroll, evaluate, key_chord, clipboard, multi, select_option, set_checked, upload_file, mouse, wheel) address refs rather than coordinates; each step keeps a history screenshot so an older chat still shows the page as the agent saw it. Annotate mode reverses the channel: the human clicks an element and files the instruction as inspect, change, lift, or comment. The same surface can drive the user's own Chrome/Edge/Brave/Opera/Vivaldi over CDP (Bring Your Own Browser), with a page-content policy (local-models-only / warn / allow) governing host page text and screenshots.

Skills are SKILL.md folders (YAML frontmatter + markdown body) discovered across ten roots — skills/, usr/skills/, usr/projects/*/.a0proj/skills, usr/agents/*/skills, agents/*/skills, plugins/*/skills and their usr/ and nested-agent variants — ranked by a weighted lexical scorer in helpers/skills.py (exact name 10, exact trigger 9, trigger overlap 8, name substring 6, description 4, tag 3; query terms must be ≥4 chars), then either loaded on demand by the agent through skills_tool (list/search/load/read_file) or pinned into the prompt Protocol; max_active_skills defaults to 20. The repo ships 25 SKILL.md files, including a0-development, build-skill, a0-create-plugin and a0-manage-plugin — the agent's own instructions for extending the framework — alongside 40 _-prefixed built-in plugin trees (each with tools/, prompts/, skills/, extensions/ hooks) and an install-by-click Plugin Hub over 100+ community plugins.

The A0 CLI Connector is a scoped bridge, not a second agent: a host-installed `a0` joins one running instance over WebSocket/HTTP and exposes host file read, file write and code execution as separate scopes (write requires read, execution requires write), with a CLI session toggling host file access (F3) and remote code execution (F4) live. Transfers declare size and SHA-256, and are bounded by per-SID ceilings, four concurrent transfers per SID, a 30 s idle timeout, disk spooling above 1 MiB, a 256 KiB write / 2,000-line read text-editor ceiling and a 10 MiB File Browser text limit. Self-extension is gated the same way: _tool_access enforces per-project/per-profile tool and MCP allow/block policy, _infection_check checks streamed reasoning for prompt injection before tool execution, _plugin_validator plus the LLM-guided _plugin_scan vet community plugins without executing them, and Time Travel snapshots /a0/usr (6-hour retention sweeps; history kept forever by default) with diff, preview and revert.
advantages: A whole-computer substrate with the discipline written down. desktopctl's structured-first ladder and the browser's ref-id inventory are concrete, inspectable answers to 'how should an agent act on a machine' — the harness behavior RSI papers assume but rarely specify. Pair it with the papers that evolve harnesses: this is the environment those loops would have to operate on, complete with state read-back and post-action verification.

The strongest in-tree example of an agent that can rewrite its own scaffolding: prompts/, tools/, plugins/, skills/ and agents/ are plain files inside the same container the agent has shell access to, and the shipped a0-development / build-skill / a0-create-plugin / a0-manage-plugin skills teach it how to author skills and plugins while Plugin Hub installs more at runtime. Time Travel (snapshot, diff, revert of /a0/usr) plus the plugin scanners and tool policy are what keep those self-edits diffable, revertible and reviewed rather than silent.

Model-agnostic where research scaffolds are wired to one lab's API: conf/model_providers.yaml registers 29 chat and 16 embedding providers through LiteLLM (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure, Bedrock, OpenRouter, xAI, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai plus local ollama, lm_studio, llama_cpp, vllm, omlx) with projects isolating workspaces, memory, secrets, knowledge and model presets, and an OpenAI Codex OAuth plan path. Distinct from the same-named paper Agent0 (arXiv 2511.16043), whose co-evolution method is data-free but not model-free — it needs a GPT-4o judge; this repo has no training loop and no judge.
agent-zero.run:
# recommended: download the A0 Launcher desktop app (v1.7; macOS/Linux/Windows, x64 + ARM64)
# terminal install — macOS / Linux:
curl -fsSL https://bash.agent-zero.ai | bash
# headless / scripted:
curl -fsSL https://bash.agent-zero.ai | bash -s -- --quick-start --name agent-zero --port 5080
# Windows PowerShell: irm https://ps.agent-zero.ai | iex   (headless: -QuickStart -Name agent-zero -Port 5080)
# Docker already installed, run directly:
docker run -p 80:80 -v a0_usr:/a0/usr agent0ai/agent-zero
# host bridge (install on YOUR machine, not in the container), then connect:
curl -LsSf https://cli.agent-zero.ai/install.sh | sh && a0
agent-zero.note: Study the container/host boundary: desktopctl.sh's structured-first GUI ladder, the browser ref-id inventory, the A0 CLI scope chain (read → write → execute, F3/F4), and _plugin_scan / _infection_check as gates on self-extension. Contrast with the same-named paper Agent0 (2511.16043): no training loop here, only editable scaffolding.

deepseek-harness.what: DeepSeek's open-source agent harness (`dsh`): a TypeScript monorepo where every component — model adapters, tool registry, session log, the agent loop itself — is a Cordis plugin, composed at boot into replaceable profiles (web, headless, sdk, sdk-minimal, acp). MIT, developer preview.
architecture: Everything-is-a-plugin via Cordis (its design is formalized in arXiv 2608.25512, 'A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability'): plugins contribute services, typed events, and reversible effects to one shared context; there is no privileged core — the model adapter, tool registry, session log, and agent loop (`ctx.agentLoop`) are all rows replaceable from config, and registrations unwind when their plugin unloads.

Boot composition is ordered layers: each profile stacks bundles, then the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, then the home-level one, then `--patch` overlays; a patch targets a config row by id and replaces its whole config, and `dsh --profile web --dump-config` prints the exact tree your machine boots.

The session log is the source of truth: an append-only `SessionEvent` log under a runtime invariant that anything reaching a model request must be reconstructable from it ('model-visible means logged'); `deriveMessages()` projects model history, and storage is versioned `session.vN.jsonl[.zstd]` generations with one-step migration chains — fork, resume, transcripts, and telemetry all derive from it.

Tools register with `defineTool` (typed params, validated calls, allow/deny/ask policy) and their schemas join prompt assembly automatically; native function-calling or PTC mode, where a `run_code` program calls registry tools through nested sub-dispatches — each logged for reconstruction, only the outer curated result entering model history; `maxParallelToolCalls` defaults to 10. Capability seams (Service Definition + Provider + Consumer) swap fs and subprocess together, so one provider change moves Bash, PTY, and LSP to a remote sandbox with no forks.
advantages: The interception surface a self-modification experiment needs is first-class, not monkey-patched: `agent/pre-step` rewrites or rejects claimed input, `agent/request` reroutes model calls, `tools/pre-execute|execute|post-execute` guard tool runs, and `agent/turn-stopping` stops a turn — every extension point is a typed event with a documented producer/consumer map.

Harness-as-data: because the running agent is a patchable config tree with YAML-driven HMR, you can inspect, re-compose, or shrink the harness itself (`sdk-minimal` is a complete explicit SDK tree that omits `dsh-base`) through the same mechanism plugins use to extend it.

A coordination substrate for multi-agent RSI: experimental Agent Teams on `ctx.agentTeams` (durable roster, task board, mailbox over continuable subagents), forkable sessions at turn boundaries, and swappable subagent providers — including a one-shot provider that delegates a task to a fresh, unattended Claude Code session in the parent workspace.
deepseek-harness.run: `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` — Web UI at http://127.0.0.1:3080 (needs Node.js; `--no-open` skips the browser). From source: `git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness && cd deepseek-harness && pnpm install && pnpm run build && pnpm dsh web`. Other profiles: `dsh --profile headless|sdk|sdk-minimal|acp`.
deepseek-harness.note: Read docs/architecture.md first — its turn-flow event map and 'where new behavior goes' table are the real spec. Then trace one turn's events end-to-end and study the patch mechanism as the harness self-modification seam. Mind SAFETY.md: unaudited preview that executes model-generated code and third-party plugins.

openclaw.what: Open-source, self-hosted personal AI assistant (TypeScript on Node, MIT, stewarded by the OpenClaw Foundation 501(c)(3)): an always-on local Gateway drives agent sessions from your existing chats — WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, iMessage, 20+ more — with state, memory, and credentials on your own hardware.
architecture: The Gateway is the whole architecture: one local, always-on control plane for sessions, tools, events, and channel connections; CLI, TUI, and Control UI attach to it, and the identical Gateway runs a laptop assistant or a shared team deployment — configuration is the only difference. Channels bring it to 20+ chat networks; companion apps and nodes add voice, Canvas, camera, screen, and device-local actions.

Trusted gateway / untrusted execution with policy as code: denial is structural, not a request the model is asked to honor — src/gateway/agent-turn/agent-admission-controller.ts admits runs through session-work admission leases and dedupe reservations that fail closed (aborted/timeout/superseded outcomes, fail on deleted or archived sessions). Sandboxing (docker or OpenShell kernel-level backends, agents.defaults.sandbox.mode: "all"), exec approvals, DM sender pairing, and `openclaw security audit --deep` are explicit configuration, off by default.

Vendor harnesses are first-class swappable plugins, not API endpoints: the Codex plugin drives Codex's own app-server loop, the Anthropic plugin drives the installed Claude Code executable over its structured stdio protocol, while OpenClaw keeps ownership of channels, sessions, policy, and state. The core stays deliberately small — channels, memory, and harnesses are all plugins behind capability-registration points enforced by CI import guards, with a public plugin SDK of about 150 entrypoints under shrink-only surface budgets.

Extensibility and state have their own mechanisms: skills follow the AgentSkills spec and ship through the ClawHub registry (moderation, VirusTotal/ClawScan/static-analysis scan status, `openclaw skills verify`); memory carries provenance with explicit deletion (`openclaw memory forget`); state is schema-versioned with guarded migrations owned by `openclaw doctor`; interoperates over MCP (client and server), A2A 1.0, and ACP. Default telemetry is a single daily version check; `update.checkOnStart: false` disables it.
advantages: The clearest production answer to what an always-on, credential-holding personal agent must fix before self-improvement is safe: secrets via handles with egress substitution so the model never sees them, versioned state with guarded upgrades, purgeable memory with reingestion barriers, recorded provenance and audit — each a named, code-level mechanism, formalized as seven testable harness properties in Why OpenClaw.

Harness portability made concrete: one operator-owned loop that can drive Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, or local models as plugins keeps harness, policy, and state as inspectable, separately-replaceable layers — the exact factoring that harness-evolving RSI work tends to blur.

A field-tested threat model for long-lived autonomous agents: ~390k stars with chat-network ingress and real credentials, 647 published security advisories (as of 2026-08-27), public trust model, and an academic security case study of the architecture (arXiv 2603.12644); NVIDIA's NemoClaw distribution hardens it with OpenShell sandboxing.
openclaw.run:
curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash   # macOS / Linux / WSL2 (Windows PowerShell: iwr -useb https://openclaw.ai/install.ps1 | iex)
npm install -g openclaw@latest --allow-scripts=openclaw   # if you manage Node yourself (24.16+ or 26.1+; 26 recommended)
openclaw onboard --install-daemon   # after install; then: openclaw gateway status && openclaw dashboard
openclaw.note: Read the seven testable harness properties in Why OpenClaw, then check them against code: agent-admission-controller.ts (fail-closed admission), the plugin capability-registration points, ClawHub skill verification. Policy-in-code vs policy-in-prompt is where it becomes functions — what a self-modifying agent may touch, what persists, who approves.

pi.what: Minimal, extensible terminal coding agent and harness (pi.dev) whose centerpiece is a self-extensible agent: it writes its own TypeScript extensions, skills, and prompt templates, layered on a stateful agent runtime and a unified multi-provider LLM API.
architecture: Layered monorepo: `pi-coding-agent` (interactive CLI, bin `pi`) builds on `pi-agent-core` (stateful `Agent` with tool execution and event streaming), which builds on `pi-ai` (unified multi-provider LLM API: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, …); sibling packages add `pi-tui`, `pi-durable`, `pi-telemetry`, and `chord`.

Self-extension = in-process TypeScript extensions: a default factory receives `ExtensionAPI` and registers tools (`pi.registerTool()`), commands, providers, and event handlers; loaded via `jiti` (no compile step) from `~/.pi/agent/extensions/` or project dirs, or ad hoc with `pi --extension ./hello.ts`. The README's pitch: 'Ask Pi to create the prompt templates, skills, extensions, and themes you need.'

The agent mutates its own tool set at runtime: register every tool, keep optional ones inactive, and a loader tool calls `pi.setActiveTools()`; `examples/extensions/dynamic-tools.ts` registers brand-new tools mid-session. Pi logs the initial prompt/tool set in the transcript's first system message and appends each tool/prompt change before the next model request.

Sessions are JSONL trees — every entry has an ID and parent, branches fork from any entry, compaction inserts summary entries — and all five interfaces (interactive, print, JSON, RPC, TypeScript SDK) share the same agent/session mechanisms. Skills inject instructions on demand.
advantages: The extension API is ordinary in-process TypeScript the agent itself can author and reload (`ctx.reload()`), so self-extension is a first-class loop — a concrete substrate for studying agents that grow their own tool sets rather than a metaphor.
Each layer is independently reusable: build a custom agent on `pi-agent-core` + `pi-ai` (a dozen lines to stream a tool-calling agent) without adopting the coding agent.
Branch-tree sessions with compaction and forking yield durable, inspectable transcripts; the project actively curates real OSS agent sessions as datasets (badlogicgames/pi-mono on Hugging Face).
pi.run:
npm install -g --ignore-scripts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent  # Node >= 22.19; or: curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh
cd /path/to/project && pi   # then /login to attach a provider
pi.note: Read packages/coding-agent/docs/extensions.md and how-pi-works.md, then examples/extensions/dynamic-tools.ts: new tools registered mid-session, active set switched via pi.setActiveTools(). Deliberately ships no built-in permission system — docs/containerization.md covers micro-VM/Docker sandboxing.

hermes-agent.what: Nous Research's MIT-licensed general-purpose Python agent — AIAgent core behind a CLI, messaging gateway, and Electron desktop shell — whose headline is a closed self-improvement loop: the agent writes its own skills, curates its bounded memory, searches its past sessions, and prunes both in the background.
architecture: AIAgent core (run_agent.py facade; loop in agent/conversation_loop.py + turn_*.py): 3 API modes (chat completions, codex responses, anthropic), 70+ tools across 28 toolsets, `delegate_task` subagents, and 7 terminal backends (local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona, Vercel Sandbox), fronted by CLI/TUI, an Electron shell (apps/desktop), and one gateway process bridging Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp/Signal/email; session storage is SQLite + FTS5.

Procedural memory: agentskills.io-compatible SKILL.md files in ~/.hermes/skills loaded by progressive disclosure (a ≤60-char description indexed every session — past char 60 it is silently cut and never routes; `skill_view` loads bodies on demand). The agent authors its own via `skill_manage` (create/patch/delete/write_file) under HARDLINE authoring standards, with an advisory linter (incident-log-shape, references-sprawl >60 files, oversized-body ~24k chars); `/learn` distills any source into a skill or a lean-index knowledge base (SKILL.md + per-chapter references/).

Episodic memory: MEMORY.md (2,200 chars ≈800 tokens) and USER.md (1,375 chars ≈500 tokens) injected as a frozen session-start snapshot (preserves prefix cache); the `memory` tool does add/replace/remove only — no read — and returns an error when full, forcing the agent to consolidate in-turn before retrying. `session_search` (FTS5, custom fts5_cjk extension) with LLM summarization recalls past sessions; Honcho supplies dialectic user modeling.

The learning loop is background machinery, not a training loop: after each turn a forked AIAgent (agent/background_review.py, auxiliary.background_review.enabled default true) replays the conversation snapshot asking 'should any skill/memory be saved or updated?' and writes straight to the stores — inheriting the parent's runtime and prompt-cache prefix, whitelist-gated tools, isolated session id — gated by nudge counters (memory.nudge_interval default 10; skills.creation_nudge_interval); plus the inactivity-triggered Curator (agent/curator.py): 7-day interval, 2h min idle, stale after 14 unused days, archived (never deleted) after 30, opt-in aux-model consolidation fork, before/after-hash ledger with rollback.
